docs.title: What you’ll build
docs.text:
You’ll work through the bundled Leavenworth, WA network in one notebook session and produce, in order:

  1. A folium / matplotlib map of the full network.
  2. A validation report rendered as an HTML card.
  3. A data-quality report grouped by severity.
  4. A simplify-geometry edit, rendered as a before/after diff (then rolled back).
  5. A scoped subgraph around a single node, rendered side-by-side with the original.

Total runtime: under two minutes on a laptop. The fixture ships inside the netstead wheel (the CSV flavour is about 140 KB).

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
The [clean] extra brings in shapely + geopandas + pyproj for the geometry edit; [graph] brings in scipy for the scope step and the data-quality rule pack; [notebook] is reserved for future widgets — the _repr_html_ cards used below render without it.

netstead 1.0.0b2 is not on PyPI yet, so the beta installs from GitHub (both packages in one command; see Install and troubleshoot):

pip install \
  "dbcorral @ git+https://github.com/e-lo/netstead.git@main#subdirectory=packages/corral" \
  "netstead[clean,graph,notebook] @ git+https://github.com/e-lo/netstead.git@main#subdirectory=packages/netstead"

For the map steps, either folium (interactive Leaflet) or matplotlib (static fallback) works — pick one:

pip install folium       # interactive Leaflet map
pip install matplotlib   # static fallback

The steps below show both paths.

docs.title: 1. Load the fixture
docs.text:
Start by loading the bundled Leavenworth network. Network.from_source returns a lazy Network — no rows have been read from disk yet; net.links is a lazy Table (the underlying ibis expression is at net.links.expr).

from netstead import Network
from netstead.fixtures import leavenworth

net = Network.from_source(leavenworth.csv_dir())
print(f"{net.spec_version}: {net.links.count()} links, {net.nodes.count()} nodes")

You should see:

0.97: 339 links, 121 nodes

In a notebook, evaluating net on its own renders an HTML summary card with the spec version, the 9 tables with their row counts, and a preview of the first rows.

Network summary card (net.repr_html()) — spec 0.97, 9 tables, 339 links / 121 nodes, first-rows preview

docs.title: 2. Render the network as a map
docs.text:
The link table is keyed to geometry by geometry_id; the geometry.geometry column carries each link’s LineString as WKB bytes in memory (the CSV on disk stores WKT; netstead decodes it on load). Materialize both with .to_pandas(), join them, and decode the WKB with shapely before plotting.

import pandas as pd
from shapely import wkb

links = net.links.to_pandas()
geoms = net.tables["geometry"].to_pandas().set_index("geometry_id")
links = links.join(geoms[["geometry"]], on="geometry_id")
links["shape"] = links["geometry"].map(wkb.loads)

For an interactive Leaflet map, use folium. Compute the centroid from the node table, then add one PolyLine per link.

import folium

# Centroid of the network — average node y/x
nodes = net.nodes.to_pandas()
center = [nodes["y_coord"].mean(), nodes["x_coord"].mean()]

m = folium.Map(location=center, zoom_start=15, tiles="OpenStreetMap")
for shape in links["shape"]:
    coords = [(y, x) for x, y in shape.coords]  # folium wants (lat, lon)
    folium.PolyLine(coords, color="#1f77b4", weight=2, opacity=0.8).add_to(m)
m  # in a notebook, this renders the map inline

You should see the downtown Leavenworth grid — a compact, walkable core wrapped around Highway 2 / Front Street, surrounded by a few residential tertiary streets.

Folium map of the full Leavenworth fixture — downtown grid around Highway 2 with residential streets fanning out

If folium isn’t available, the static matplotlib fallback gives an equivalent view (without basemap tiles):

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 8))
for shape in links["shape"]:
    xs, ys = shape.xy
    ax.plot(xs, ys, color="#1f77b4", linewidth=1.0, alpha=0.8)
ax.set_aspect("equal")
ax.set_title(f"Leavenworth GMNS fixture — {len(links)} links")
plt.show()

Either way: a recognizable Bavarian-themed downtown core in an OSM-derived street network roughly 2 km across.

docs.title: 3. Validate and display the report
docs.text:
net.validate() runs the four-pass validator (structural / schema / FK / sync-state) and returns a ValidationReport. In a notebook, evaluating the report on its own renders a styled HTML card.

report = net.validate()
report  # in a notebook, the _repr_html_ renders a styled card

You should see a card with no ERRORs, no WARNINGs and 16 INFO findings. The INFOs are structural.missing_optional_resource, one per optional GMNS table the fixture doesn’t include. INFO findings don’t count against cleanliness, so report.is_clean is True.

Validation report card — 0 ERRORs, 0 WARNINGs, 16 INFO structural.missing_optional_resource across 9 tables

In a non-notebook context, drop down to the text representation:

print(f"{report.spec_version}: {len(report.issues)} issues")
for issue in report.issues[:5]:
    print(f"  {issue.severity.value:9} {issue.code:30} {issue.message[:60]}")

docs.title: 4. Run quality and display
docs.text:
The data-quality pack flags things the spec is silent on but every real network has — disconnected components, lane-count mismatches, high speeds on residential facilities, near-duplicate nodes. Run it the same way as validation; the result has its own _repr_html_.

from corral.quality import run_quality

qreport = run_quality(net)
qreport  # _repr_html_ renders severity-grouped findings

You should see a card of WARNING findings (no ERRORs): 271 links with facility_type=residential carry free_speed=40, above the default 35 mph threshold of quality.high_speed_residential — useful for seeing what a real finding looks like, with its fix_hint.

Quality report card — 271 WARNING quality.high_speed_residential findings (residential links with free_speed=40, default 35 mph threshold)

To see the top findings in detail, iterate over qreport.issues:

for issue in qreport.issues[:3]:
    print(f"  {issue.severity.value:9} {issue.code:35} {issue.message}")

docs.title: 5. Simplify geometry and render before/after
docs.text:
The simplify_geometry op in netstead.clean removes redundant vertices from link geometries. Leavenworth keeps its shapes in the geometry table (keyed by link.geometry_id), so the op edits that table directly; no inline link.geometry column is needed. Wrap it in a Session so the edit can be rolled back atomically.

from corral.editing import Session
from netstead.clean import simplify_geometry

with Session(net) as s:
    edit = simplify_geometry(net, s, mode="redundant_only", tolerance=0.000001)
    edit  # in a notebook, _repr_html_ shows the diff card (the edit targets the geometry table)

You should see an EditResult card for the geometry table: the op and table, the +added / -removed / ~changed row counts, the session id and the timestamp. mode="redundant_only" drops vertices that sit on the chord through their neighbours; with tolerance=0.0 it is loss-free, and the 0.000001-degree (about 10 cm) tolerance here also catches the near-collinear vertices OSM traces leave behind, removing about a third of Leavenworth’s 2,132 vertices. mode="douglas_peucker" is the lossy alternative with an explicit tolerance.

EditResult card for the simplify-geometry edit: the op and the geometry table, the changed-row count, session id and timestamp.

To visualize before-and-after on one map, keep the decoded shapes from step 2 as the “before” set, then read the edited geometry table as the “after” set:

links_before = links[["link_id", "shape"]].copy()
# (run the simplify edit above inside the Session)
geoms_after = net.tables["geometry"].to_pandas().set_index("geometry_id")
links_after = links.copy()
links_after["shape"] = links_after["geometry_id"].map(lambda gid: wkb.loads(geoms_after.loc[gid, "geometry"]))

m = folium.Map(location=center, zoom_start=15, tiles="OpenStreetMap")
for shape in links_before["shape"]:
    folium.PolyLine([(y, x) for x, y in shape.coords],
                    color="#888", weight=4, opacity=0.4).add_to(m)
for shape in links_after["shape"]:
    folium.PolyLine([(y, x) for x, y in shape.coords],
                    color="#d62728", weight=1.5, opacity=0.9).add_to(m)
m

Grey underneath = before; red on top = after. The two overlays sit almost exactly on top of each other, because the dropped vertices were within 10 cm of a straight line, so look for the red line cutting the tiny kinks on the curved tertiary links.

To restore the original state, roll the session back:

s.rollback()

The session’s chronological log reverses the edit, so the network returns to step 1: 339 links, with every vertex back in the geometry table.

docs.title: 6. Build a scope from a single node and render
docs.text:
from_node builds a network-distance-bounded subgraph around a seed node. The 200 m buffer below is Dijkstra-bounded along the routable graph — links that are spatially close but only reachable via long detours fall outside.

from netstead.scope import from_node

scoped = from_node(net, node_id=1, network_buffer="200m").apply()
print(f"scoped: {scoped.links.count()} links, {scoped.nodes.count()} nodes")

You should see scoped: 8 links, 5 nodes. Every related table (lane, link_tod, movement, signal tables) is pre-filtered by FK chain, so the result is a self-consistent GMNS network you can write back out.

Render the scope side-by-side with the original to see the contrast — full network as grey context, scoped subgraph highlighted.

scoped_links = scoped.links.to_pandas().join(geoms[["geometry"]], on="geometry_id")
scoped_links["shape"] = scoped_links["geometry"].map(wkb.loads)

m = folium.Map(location=center, zoom_start=15, tiles="OpenStreetMap")
# Full network, faint
for shape in links["shape"]:
    folium.PolyLine([(y, x) for x, y in shape.coords],
                    color="#bbb", weight=1, opacity=0.5).add_to(m)
# Scope, highlighted
for shape in scoped_links["shape"]:
    folium.PolyLine([(y, x) for x, y in shape.coords],
                    color="#2ca02c", weight=3, opacity=0.95).add_to(m)
m

You should see a small green subgraph centered on one intersection, with the rest of the network greyed out as context.

Scoped subgraph (200 m network buffer around node 1, green) over the full Leavenworth network (grey)

docs.title: Variations you might try
docs.text:
Each accordion below is a one-line tweak that shows off a different facet of the toolkit. Pick whichever matches what you want to learn next.

Try a different fixture or your own network

The bundled fixture is Leavenworth. Point Network.from_source at any GMNS package on disk or in cloud storage to repeat the tour with your own data — every step above is fixture-agnostic.

```python
net = Network.from_source("./my-network/")
net = Network.from_source("s3://my-bucket/network.parquet/")
```
Configure a custom quality threshold

Override the quality.high_speed_residential threshold (default is conservative). Tightening it surfaces more findings on a network with mixed posted speeds.

```python
from corral.quality import RuleConfig, run_quality

qreport = run_quality(
    net,
    config={
        "quality.high_speed_residential": RuleConfig(
            thresholds={"speed_limit_mph": 30.0}
        )
    },
)
```

docs.title: Quickstart: the Workbench
docs.text: Prefer code? → Quickstart: Python does the same work from a Python session.

docs.title: What you’ll build
docs.text:
The whole tutorial in a minute: open, select, validate, fix, replay. (screenshot predates the panel restructure)

In ten minutes, with nothing but a browser, you will:

  1. Open the bundled Leavenworth, WA network (339 links, 121 nodes) in the Workbench.
  2. Pick a link on the map and see its row in the table, and the other way round.
  3. Select a street by name, then resolve a selection the resolver found ambiguous.
  4. Validate the network against the GMNS spec and the quality rules.
  5. Fix a finding, see the edit tracked, and undo it.
  6. See every step as a Python script you can run again.
  7. Save the edited network as a copy, with the original untouched.

Everything runs on your machine. With --provider stub the selection box uses an offline pattern parser, so nothing leaves your computer and you need no API key.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Python 3.11 or newer, and netstead with four extras: [server] is the Workbench itself, [graph] runs the quality rules inside validation and the path search behind “between”, [nl] adds the language-model providers you can switch to later (the offline parser needs none of them), and [osm] powers Open → Place search and building a network from OpenStreetMap. If anything below fails to install or start, see Install and troubleshoot.

docs.title: 1. Install and open the network
docs.text:
Install with the tool you already use. netstead 1.0.0b2 is not on PyPI yet, so the beta installs from GitHub, both packages in one command (pip install takes the same two arguments). The quotes matter on macOS (zsh): see Install and troubleshoot.

uv init --bare
uv add \
  "dbcorral @ git+https://github.com/e-lo/netstead.git@main#subdirectory=packages/corral" \
  "netstead[server,graph,nl,osm] @ git+https://github.com/e-lo/netstead.git@main#subdirectory=packages/netstead"

uv init --bare makes a new folder a uv project, which uv add needs; skip it when you add netstead to a project you already have.

(Once the PyPI release is out: uv add 'netstead[server,graph,nl,osm]'.)

The Leavenworth fixture ships inside the netstead wheel, so there is nothing to download. Ask Python where it landed and keep the path in a shell variable:

LV=$(uv run python -c "from netstead.fixtures import leavenworth; print(leavenworth.csv_dir())")
echo "$LV"

Start the Workbench on that folder. --provider stub picks the offline parser so the tutorial works without a network connection or a key.

uv run netstead app "$LV" --provider stub

Open http://127.0.0.1:8850 in your browser.

(You can also start uv run netstead app with nothing open and pick Leavenworth, WA from Included examples in the Open / Import wizard (Open → Browse / import…); the path above is only needed to pass the fixture on the command line. Included examples also lists RDU I-40, NC and Market Street, San Francisco, a small Overture-derived network with GERS ids (overture_segment_id, overture_connector_id) for trying the Find tab’s Overture GERS id system.)

You should see the Netstead Workbench header with the network picker showing leavenworth, the count 339 links · 121 nodes, the Map / Split / Table view buttons, and the map below. If the map opens zoomed out, press the map’s Zoom to full network button (the second of the small buttons on the map) and the downtown Leavenworth grid fills the view. The side panel on the right has five tabs — Find, Inspect, Edit, Cards, Validate — plus Assistant; the selection box with Select and Ask lives in the Find tab, not the header.

The Workbench with the Leavenworth network open: header, network picker, counts, and the map. (screenshot predates the panel restructure)

docs.title: 2. Link the map and the table
docs.text:
Press Split in the header. The map stays on the left and the link table opens on the right, with a rail listing every table in the network and its row count.

Click a link on the map. The Inspect tab comes forward in the dock and shows that link’s record (its facility_type, free_speed, lanes, and so on), and the table outlines its row and scrolls to it, on whichever page it sits. Now click a different row in the table: it becomes the focused record and the map flies to it.

Clicking never changes the selection; focus is just a view. That matters in step 3, where the selection is the thing the Workbench records.

Split view: a link picked on the map, its row focused in the table, its record in Inspect. (screenshot predates the panel restructure)

docs.title: 3. Select a street by name
docs.text:
Open the Find tab in the side panel. With the offline pattern parser it shows a small form: leave Find on Street, start typing Ski Hill Drive in Street (the open network’s street names are suggested), and press Select (or Enter). The sentence it sends, Ski Hill Drive, shows under the form. (With a language model chosen in the header, the Find tab has a free-text box instead.)

Twenty links light up in the selection color, and the Find tab shows the status resolved, the phrase you typed, a diagnostic line facility ['Ski Hill Drive']: 20 link(s), and the Fragment: the GMNS selection fragment as JSON (as a Segment, the street name plus its from and to nodes; switch to Link list for the twenty link_ids, and use the copy button to take it elsewhere). In the table bar, Show → Selection lists just those rows. The strip at the bottom of the window now reads app.do(Select(utterance='Ski Hill Drive')): the same selection as Python, which step 7 comes back to.

Ski Hill Drive selected: 20 links on the map, the status and fragment in the Find tab. (screenshot predates the panel restructure)

docs.title: 4. Resolve an ambiguous selection
docs.text:
Set Find to Street between two cross streets, then choose Street Cherry Street, From cross street Prospect Street and To cross street West Center Street (once the street is chosen, the cross streets offered are the ones that meet it), and press Select. The sentence under the form reads Cherry Street between Prospect Street and West Center Street.

This time the status is ambiguous and the Find tab’s badge shows ?. Under Anchors, the from anchor resolved cleanly (Prospect Street → node 53 · intersection), but the to anchor has more than one intersection that could be “West Center Street”: the resolver picked the nearest, node 60, and lists the other candidate, node 61, after Or:. The candidates are drawn as rings on the map (the Anchor candidates overlay), and the diagnostics say why: multiple intersection candidates; picked nearest (see candidates).

Pin the anchor to settle it. Click node 61 to choose the other intersection, or press Pin node 60 to keep the resolver’s choice. The selection is resolved again: the status becomes resolved, the rings disappear, and three links of Cherry Street are selected between the two pinned intersections. Unpin returns to the resolver’s choice. The strip shows app.do(PinAnchor(role='to', node_id=60)), so the pin is part of the recorded selection, not a one-off click.

An ambiguous selection: the to anchor’s candidate nodes drawn as rings, with Pin buttons in the Find tab. (screenshot predates the panel restructure)

docs.title: 5. Validate the network
docs.text:
Open the Validate tab in the dock and press the run icon (Run validation). It runs as a background job (the Jobs count in the header ticks while it works) and takes a few seconds on Leavenworth.

When it finishes the status line reads Validated v0: 271 warnings, 16 info. That is two reports in one list. The spec checks find 0 errors, 0 warnings and 16 info: the 16 info findings are structural.missing_optional_resource, one per optional GMNS table that is absent. The quality rules add 271 warnings of quality.high_speed_residential: residential links whose free_speed of 40 is above the default 35 mph threshold. The Severity, Table and Code filters show the same counts, for example quality.high_speed_residential (271).

Every located issue is a dot on the map. Click an issue in the list: the map flies to its link (or use the crosshair “zoom to” icon on a located finding), Inspect shows the record, and the table scrolls to its row and marks it. The 16 table-level findings have no place on the map, so they sit grouped under a collapsed Unlocated findings group at the bottom of the panel (expand with --all-style grouping, or the group’s disclosure triangle).

The Validate panel after Run validation: 271 warnings and 16 info, each located issue a dot on the map. (screenshot predates the panel restructure)

docs.title: 6. Fix a finding
docs.text:
Pick any quality.high_speed_residential issue and press its Fix button. The fix editor opens at the top of the Validate panel on that link and that column (link 1 · free_speed, for the first one), with the current value 40 filled in and the issue text as the edit’s note. Replace the note with your own reason if you like (Residential street: posted 35 mph); it is kept with the edit.

Change free_speed to 35 and press Apply. One edit is sent with only the value you changed. Three things update at once:

  • The Edit tab lists the edit (#1 link 1: free_speed = 35.0 (Residential street: posted 35 mph), 1 link · v1), the status reads 1 unsaved, the network picker reads leavenworth • 1 unsaved, and the undo icon is enabled. The network’s version moved from v0 to v1; nothing on disk changed. The header’s validity light turns amber-outlined (Validated vN, the network changed since: re-run).
  • The Validate panel re-checks the rows you touched straight away: a value the spec disagrees with would appear under Edit warnings with its own Fix button. This one is fine, so the count stays at 0. The stored validation is now stale, and the run icon’s tooltip becomes Re-run validation; the list stays so you can work down it.
  • The strip shows the edit as Python: app.do(EditCells(ids=[1], values={'free_speed': 35}, note='Residential street: posted 35 mph')).

Press the undo icon and the value goes back to 40, recorded as app.do(UndoEdit()). A redo icon beside it becomes active and would reapply the edit (app.do(RedoEdit())); instead, press Fix and apply the change once more, so there is an edit to save in step 8.

Fixing a free_speed value from an issue; the Edit tab shows the pending edit and the undo/redo icons. (screenshot predates the panel restructure)

docs.title: 7. Replay the session as Python
docs.text:
The strip at the bottom always shows the last action as Python, with its sequence number (#8); Copy copies that one line. Press the code icon in the footer (tooltip “Copy session as Python”) to see the whole session as a script: the imports, then app = Session(), then one app.do(...) line per action you took, from OpenNetwork(source=…) through the selects, the pin, the validation, the edit, the undo and the edit again. Copy all puts it on the clipboard.

Run that script with uv run python and it repeats your session without the browser. Everything in the Workbench is a typed action, so there is no “export” step to remember.

Session as Python: the whole session as a replayable script. (screenshot predates the panel restructure)

docs.title: 8. Save a copy
docs.text:
Press the Save icon in the header (tooltip “Save a copy…”) to open the save dialog. Name it (leavenworth-fixed), leave the format on Parquet folder, and press Choose folder…. A file browser opens; move to a folder inside your home directory and press Use this folder, then Save.

The save runs as a job. When it finishes, a toast reads Saved a copy to <folder>/leavenworth-fixed (1 edit). and names the tables that differ from the source (link). In the Edit tab the edit is now marked saved and the unsaved badge clears. The folder you opened in step 1 is untouched: the Workbench never writes to the network it opened, and never overwrites an existing copy. A folder outside your home directory is refused (… is outside the allowed folders), which io.allowed_roots can widen: see Which folders the app can read and write.

Save a copy: the edited network written to a new folder; the original stays as it was. (screenshot predates the panel restructure)

Stop the server with Ctrl+C in the terminal when you are done.

docs.title: Quickstart: Python
docs.text: Prefer a browser? → Quickstart: the Workbench does the same work with no code.

docs.title: When to use this
docs.text: You’re new to netstead and want to see what it does on a real GMNS network before reading anything else. Time budget: five minutes.

docs.title: Quick example
docs.text:
The fastest way to confirm netstead is wired up correctly is to install it, load the bundled Leavenworth, WA fixture, and print a one-line summary. netstead 1.0.0b2 is not on PyPI yet, so the beta installs from GitHub (both packages in one command; see Install and troubleshoot):

pip install \
  "dbcorral @ git+https://github.com/e-lo/netstead.git@main#subdirectory=packages/corral" \
  "netstead[clean,graph] @ git+https://github.com/e-lo/netstead.git@main#subdirectory=packages/netstead"

Then in Python:

from netstead import Network
from netstead.fixtures import leavenworth

net = Network.from_source(leavenworth.csv_dir())
print(f"{net.spec_version}: {net.links.count()} links, {net.nodes.count()} nodes")

Expected:

0.97: 339 links, 121 nodes

You just loaded the bundled Leavenworth network through the default ibis + DuckDB engine. Nothing was materialized — net.links is a lazy expression; only the integer count came back from DuckDB to Python.

docs.title: 1. Install
docs.text:
The bare netstead install is enough for read-only validation. Add [clean,graph] to unlock the ops the rest of this guide uses: [clean] brings in shapely + geopandas + pyproj for the geometry edits; [graph] brings in scipy (+ numpy + pandas) for the scope graph, connected components, and the data-quality rule pack.

uv init --bare
uv add \
  "dbcorral @ git+https://github.com/e-lo/netstead.git@main#subdirectory=packages/corral" \
  "netstead[clean,graph] @ git+https://github.com/e-lo/netstead.git@main#subdirectory=packages/netstead"

uv init --bare makes a new folder a uv project, which uv add needs; skip it when you add netstead to a project you already have.

This is the GitHub form the beta uses until the PyPI release is out; it then becomes uv add 'netstead[clean,graph]', with corral coming along as a transitive dependency. For the other install tools (uv pip, pip, pipx), the full list of extras and what each pulls in, netstead doctor, and the zsh bracket-quoting rule, see Install and troubleshoot.

docs.title: 2. Load the bundled fixture
docs.text:
The fixture is a small real network (Leavenworth, WA — an OSM-derived street grid roughly 2 km across) bundled inside the netstead wheel, so the example below runs without any download. Network.from_source accepts the same surface as corral.Package.from_source: local paths, URLs (s3://, https://, duckdb://), or directories of CSV / Parquet / DuckDB / zip-CSV.

from netstead import Network
from netstead.fixtures import leavenworth

net = Network.from_source(leavenworth.csv_dir())

The result is a lazy Network object — its tables haven’t been read yet. Print a quick summary to confirm it loaded:

print(f"{net.spec_version}: {net.links.count()} links, {net.nodes.count()} nodes")

Expected:

0.97: 339 links, 121 nodes

In a Jupyter notebook, evaluating net on its own renders an HTML summary card with the spec version, per-table row counts, and a preview of the first rows.

Network summary card (net.repr_html() in a notebook) — spec version, table inventory with row counts, first-rows preview

docs.title: 3. Validate against the spec
docs.text:
Validation runs four passes in a single call: structural (required tables and files), schema (per-field types and constraints), foreign-key (cross-table integrity), and sync-state (have any FKs gone stale since a previous edit?). The Leavenworth fixture has no ERRORs, but it is not spotless: expect 16 INFO findings (structural.missing_optional_resource, one per optional GMNS table the fixture doesn’t ship) and 1 WARNING (fk.unverifiable: node.zone_id can’t be checked because there is no zone table). That WARNING is why report.is_clean is False — is_clean means no ERRORs and no WARNINGs.

report = net.validate()
print(f"issues: {len(report.issues)} ({report.spec_version})")

In a notebook, report on its own renders an HTML card grouped by severity.

Validation report card (report.repr_html() in a notebook) — 0 ERRORs, 0 WARNINGs, 16 INFO structural.missing_optional_resource

docs.title: 4. Run data-quality checks
docs.text:
The data-quality rule pack covers things the spec is silent on but every real network gets wrong sooner or later. Its nine rules cover high-speed-residential, lane-count mismatch, sharp-angle bends, near-duplicate nodes, disconnected components, implausible v/c ratios, missing critical fields, overlapping links and non-unique combinations (see Customize the quality pack). Findings come back as WARNING or INFO by default and carry category=DATA_QUALITY. The rule pack needs the [graph] extra. On Leavenworth, quality.high_speed_residential fires on 271 residential links whose free_speed is 40 — above the default 35 mph threshold.

from corral.quality import run_quality

qreport = run_quality(net)
for issue in qreport.issues[:5]:
    print(f"  {issue.severity.value:9} {issue.code:35} {issue.message[:60]}")

Quality report card (qreport.repr_html() in a notebook) — 271 WARNING quality.high_speed_residential findings on residential links with free_speed=40 at the default 35 mph threshold

docs.title: 5. Scope to a subgraph
docs.text:
The scope module lets you carve a smaller network out of a larger one without writing FK-pushdown SQL by hand. from_node builds a network-distance-bounded subgraph around a seed node; every related table (lane, link_tod, movement, signal control) is pre-filtered so the result is still a self-consistent GMNS network.

from netstead.scope import from_node

scoped = from_node(net, 1, network_buffer="200m").apply()
print(f"scoped: {scoped.links.count()} links, {scoped.nodes.count()} nodes")

That’s a 200-metre Dijkstra-bounded buffer around node 1. Expected:

scoped: 8 links, 5 nodes

Scoped subgraph (200 m network buffer around node 1, green) over the full Leavenworth network (grey context)

docs.title: 6. Or run the same thing from the CLI
docs.text:
The CLI mirrors the Python API one-for-one. The same fixture lives at packages/netstead/netstead/fixtures/leavenworth/csv in the repo, so you can point the CLI at it directly.

netstead info packages/netstead/netstead/fixtures/leavenworth/csv
netstead validate packages/netstead/netstead/fixtures/leavenworth/csv
netstead quality packages/netstead/netstead/fixtures/leavenworth/csv
netstead scope from-node packages/netstead/netstead/fixtures/leavenworth/csv 1 --network-buffer 200m

quality and scope need the [graph] extra; info and validate run on the bare install.

By default netstead prints colorized tables and panels for humans. Add --json and you get a single machine-readable JSON document on stdout instead — useful for scripting, CI checks, or feeding the output to an AI agent.

netstead validate --json packages/netstead/netstead/fixtures/leavenworth/csv | jq '.issues | length'

docs.title: Common variations
docs.text:
Each accordion below is one alternative to the defaults used above. The first (most common) is expanded; the rest are collapsed — open the one that matches your situation.

Pick a different GMNS spec version

The vendored versions are 0.95, 0.96, and 0.97; default is 0.97. Networks load against the version they were written against — no silent upgrades.

net = Network.from_source(leavenworth.csv_dir(), spec_version="0.96")
Get a pandas (or polars) frame

DuckDB (via ibis) is the only compute engine, and every table stays lazy until you ask. When downstream code wants a DataFrame, materialize just that table with .to_pandas() or .to_polars().

links_df = net.links.to_pandas()
Read from S3 with credentials

Credentials resolve via a cascade: keyword arg → CORRAL_CRED_<host>_TOKEN env var → OS keyring → .netrc. No code changes if your environment is already set up.

```python
net = Network.from_source("s3://bucket/network/")
```
Write the scoped network out

The output format follows the destination: an extension-less path or .parquet writes a directory of GeoParquet files (one per table); .csv writes a CSV directory; .duckdb writes a single DuckDB file; .zip writes zipped CSV.

```python
scoped.write("./scoped.parquet")
```
Run the data-quality pack with custom thresholds

Per-rule config keys override defaults. The example below tightens the residential-speed threshold to 30 mph.

from corral.quality import RuleConfig, run_quality

qreport = run_quality(
    net,
    config={
        "quality.high_speed_residential": RuleConfig(
            thresholds={"speed_limit_mph": 30.0}
        )
    },
)

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• Auto-build of the graph index on large networks. The first from_node or connected_component call on a network larger than 50k nodes builds the scipy GMNSGraph adjacency on the spot and logs an INFO notice. Pre-build with net.build_indexes(graph=True) if you want to control the timing, or set NETSTEAD_AUTO_INDEX_THRESHOLD to raise the auto-build bar.
  • Duplicate-near-nodes default threshold is tight (epsilon_units=1e-5). Networks in WGS84 degrees barely trigger it; networks in projected meters need an explicit threshold via RuleConfig.
  • Editing requires a Session. Don’t mutate tables directly — open with corral.editing.Session(net) as s: and pass s into the netstead.clean.* ops. See Edit a network with atomic rollback.

docs.title: Why we have it
docs.text: netstead is in public beta (1.0.0b2). The library surface (read, validate, scope, edit) is stable enough to build on; the Workbench grows by phases, and each phase lands as one pull request. Knowing which phase is on main tells you which cookbook pages apply to the version you installed.

docs.title: Mental model
docs.text:
Three layers, maturing at different speeds:

Layer Status Where documented Library (netstead.Network, validation, quality rules, scope, edit with rollback, GeoParquet I/O) beta, API frozen for v1.0 Quickstart, Cookbook, API Builders and surfaces (OSM and Overture builds, natural-language selection, CLI --json, HTTP server, MCP server) beta Build a network, Self-host, MCP Workbench (netstead app) and its plugin API beta; phased; the plugin API is provisional until v1.0 Explore in the Workbench, Write a plugin

docs.title: Shipped
docs.text:
Everything below is on main and in the current beta.

  • Library. DuckDB is the single compute engine (via ibis); pandas, polars and Arrow are in/out formats. Geometry is WKB in memory, WKT in CSV and GeoParquet on disk.
  • Builders. netstead build from OpenStreetMap (place, bbox, point and buffer, or a local .osm file) and from Overture Maps.
  • Natural-language selection. netstead select and the Workbench resolve a phrase such as “I-90 EB between Exit 85 and Exit 87” to links, with Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini or a local Ollama model; keys are write-only and nothing leaves the machine unless you opt in.
  • Workbench phases P0 to P3. Open or import a network (local, URL, OSM, Overture) with estimate and approval; linked map and tables with foreign-key navigation; layered settings; validation with an issues panel; table edits with live warnings, undo and “save a copy”; selection verification with pinned anchors, saved selections and export; style, filter and navigate actions; the natural-language assistant with approved drafts. Every action is recorded and replayable as Python.
  • Plugins. Python entry-point plugins with a versioned Host API (currently 1.7) and browser slots for workspaces, panels, commands and map layers.
  • Project cards plugin. Lives in the repository at plugins/project-cards and authors ProjectCards from Workbench edits: the change model, draft cards written as YAML or JSON in Wrangler names, import of card files and of the offline edit log, the project_cards.* Actions (add a change, undo, commit, import, preview), a catalog of cards checked against the open network and applied with a session summary, and the Cards panel in the Workbench. See Author ProjectCards in the Workbench.
  • AI surface. --json on every data command, llms.txt, an MCP server with seven tools, and Claude Code skills in the repository.

docs.text:
In the order the design records schedule them. None of these are on main yet, so no cookbook page describes them.

  1. Workbench P4: live Python session. An app(net) helper in the top-level package starts the Workbench from a notebook on the same Network objects, with a handle offering the live selection, show(...) for temporary layers, do(action) and an optional Python console.

  3. Workbench P6: Transit. A GTFS component beside the roadway network: routes and stops layers, transit selections, roadway-to-transit consistency checks.

docs.title: What you’ll build
docs.text:
Open, select, validate, fix, replay: the tour in a minute. (screenshot predates the panel restructure)

By the end you will be able to read the Workbench the way a modeler reads it: a GMNS network on a map, its tables beside it, a selection with a status you can trust, a validation report whose severities mean something, an edit log with versions, and a script that reproduces all of it.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Follow step 1 of the Workbench quickstart to install netstead with the [server,graph,nl] extras and open the Leavenworth fixture with --provider stub. This page doesn’t repeat the commands; if the install or the first run fails, see Install and troubleshoot.

docs.title: 1. A GMNS network on a map
docs.text:
Leavenworth, WA: 339 links and 121 nodes, drawn from the link, node and geometry tables. (screenshot predates the panel restructure)

What you see is a small, real street network: downtown Leavenworth, an OSM-derived grid about 2 km across, with Highway 2 along the south and residential streets fanning north. The header says what it is made of: 339 links · 121 nodes. In GMNS a node is a point (an intersection, a dead end, a change of attributes) and a link is a directed edge between two nodes with the attributes a model needs: facility_type, lanes, free_speed, capacity, directed. Each link’s shape comes from the geometry table, keyed by geometry_id, which is why a link can bend without extra nodes.

Why it matters: everything else in the Workbench is a view of those tables. The map is not a separate GIS layer that can drift from the data; it is drawn from the link rows you are about to edit, and it redraws when they change. If the map opened zoomed out, Zoom to full network fits the view to the network’s bounding box: the first thing to try whenever the map looks empty.

docs.title: 2. The linked table
docs.text:
Split view. One record, three views: the link on the map, its row in the table, its attributes in Inspect. (screenshot predates the panel restructure)

Split puts the link table next to the map. The rail on the left of the table lists every table in the network with its row count: link, node, geometry, lane, link_tod and the rest. Click a link on the map and three things agree on which record you mean: the map outlines it, the table scrolls to and outlines its row, and the Inspect tab comes forward and lists its attributes. Click a row and the map flies to it.

What the linked table gives you is the half of a network that a map can’t show. A speed, a lane count, a time-of-day override or a foreign key are table facts; the map can color by one of them at a time (Find → View → Color links by), but the table shows them all, sortable and pageable, with the key columns (from_node_id, geometry_id) as links you can follow into the other tables. Rows a foreign key away from the focused record, such as the link’s two end nodes or its lanes, are tinted in every table and on the map. GMNS is a relational spec, and the Workbench treats it as one.

One rule keeps this simple: clicking never changes the selection. The focused record is a view. The selection, next, is the thing the Workbench records and can replay.

docs.title: 3. A selection you can read back
docs.text:
Ski Hill Drive: 20 links, status resolved, and the GMNS selection fragment that names them. (screenshot predates the panel restructure)

Type Ski Hill Drive into the Find tab’s box and press Select. The resolver matches the phrase against the network’s own street names, finds the facility, and marks its 20 links. The Find tab shows three things worth reading:

  • The status, resolved: the phrase mapped to one unambiguous set of links. Other statuses are ambiguous (next step) and the empty result when nothing matched.
  • The diagnostics: how it got there (facility ['Ski Hill Drive']: 20 link(s)).
  • The fragment: a JSON document in the GMNS selection schema, the portable form of the selection. As a Link list it holds only the link_ids; as a Segment it keeps the street name and the from/to nodes instead, so another tool, or a later version of this network, can resolve it again. Pick the form and the ID system (GMNS, OpenStreetMap or Overture GERS) under Export, or a ProjectCard facility instead, and use the copy button on the box.

Why it matters: a selection made by name is reproducible in a way a hand-drawn box is not. The strip at the bottom already shows it as app.do(Select(utterance='Ski Hill Drive')); after an edit, a query selection is resolved again against the edited network. With --provider stub the phrase is parsed by an offline pattern matcher; the same box can use a local model through Ollama or a hosted one, and the selection object looks the same either way.

docs.title: 4. What an ambiguous anchor means
docs.text:
“Cherry Street between Prospect Street and West Center Street”: the to anchor could be node 60 or node 61. (screenshot predates the panel restructure)

Now select Cherry Street between Prospect Street and West Center Street. A “between” phrase has a facility (Cherry Street) and two anchors, the cross streets that bound the stretch; each anchor must resolve to one node on the facility. The from anchor does (Prospect Street → node 53). The to anchor doesn’t: West Center Street meets Cherry Street at more than one node, so the resolver picks the nearest (node 60) and reports the status ambiguous, with node 61 listed as the other candidate and both drawn as rings on the map.

That status is the point. The resolver could have quietly taken its best guess, and three links would have lit up looking exactly like a confident answer. Instead the selection says it is a guess, the tab badge shows ?, and export is refused until you settle it. Settling it is a pin: click node 61 to choose it, or Pin node 60 to keep the resolver’s choice. The selection is resolved again, the status becomes resolved, and the pin becomes part of the selection’s query (app.do(PinAnchor(role='to', node_id=60))), so it survives an edit and comes back when you reuse a saved selection. Unpin returns to the resolver’s choice.

Real networks are full of this: a cross street that crosses twice, a divided road with two carriageways, a name shared by a street and a ramp. A selection status you can read is what lets you trust the selections you didn’t check by hand.

docs.title: 5. What validation severities mean
docs.text:
After Run validation: 271 warnings and 16 info, and a dot on the map for every issue with a place. (screenshot predates the panel restructure)

Run validation (the play icon in the Validate tab) runs two kinds of check and lists them together, each with a severity:

  • error — the network breaks the spec in a way a consumer can’t work around: a required table or field is missing, a value has the wrong type, a foreign key points at a row that doesn’t exist. Leavenworth has none.
  • warning — something is wrong or can’t be shown to be right. The spec check finds none on Leavenworth. The quality rules add 271: quality.high_speed_residential, a residential link whose free_speed (40) is above the 35 mph threshold. The spec allows it; the rule says it is probably a coding mistake, and its fix_hint says what to do if the speed is right (raise the facility class instead).
  • info — worth knowing, not wrong: 16 structural.missing_optional_resource findings, one per optional GMNS table (movement, segment, signal_*, zone, …) that this network doesn’t include.

The status line sums them: Validated v0: 271 warnings, 16 info, the v0 being the version of the network that was checked. Spec checks are about whether the file is valid GMNS; quality rules are about whether the network is plausible, and they are configurable (Settings → Validation, keyed by rule code), so a region with 40 mph residential streets can raise the threshold instead of silencing the rule.

Each located issue is a dot on the map, colored by severity; click one in the list (or its crosshair “zoom to” icon) and the map flies to its link, Inspect shows the record, and the table scrolls to the row. Findings about a whole table, like the missing-resource notes, have no place on the map; findings that share a code and differ only by resource are grouped into one row under a collapsed Unlocated findings block. The filters (severity, table, code) carry counts, so quality.high_speed_residential (271) is one click away from being the only thing in the list.

docs.title: 6. What an edit does to the network
docs.text:
Fix on an issue: the editor opens on the issue’s column; Apply sends one edit; the Edit tab records it at v1. (screenshot predates the panel restructure)

Press Fix on a quality.high_speed_residential issue. The editor opens on that record and that column (link 1 · free_speed), prefilled with 40, and with the issue as the edit’s note, which you can replace with your own reason (Residential street: posted 35 mph). Change the value to 35 and press Apply.

Three things happen, and each is visible:

  • The network version moves. The network you opened was v0; it is now v1. Edits change the network in memory only; nothing on disk is touched until you save a copy, and the source is never overwritten. The version is what the rest of the Workbench keys on: the map and table redraw for v1, the stored validation is marked stale (the network changed since: re-run), and a delete planned on v0 would be refused.
  • The edit log grows. The Edit tab lists #1 link 1: free_speed = 35.0 (Residential street: posted 35 mph), with the rows it touched (1 link) and the version it produced (v1), and says 1 unsaved; the network picker says the same, and the header’s validity light turns amber-outlined. The undo icon reverses the newest edit; undo is last-in, first-out and is itself recorded (app.do(UndoEdit())). A redo icon beside it would reapply that edit (app.do(RedoEdit())) until any other change clears it.
  • The edited rows are re-checked at once. A value the spec disagrees with, such as a foreign key to a row that doesn’t exist or a required field left empty, is applied anyway and listed under Edit warnings in the Edit tab with its own Fix, so you can put it right where you found it. A speed of 35 raises no warning, so the count stays at 0.

Why it matters: an edit in the Workbench is a typed action with a note, a version and an undo, not a cell changed in a spreadsheet. That is what makes the next two steps possible.

docs.title: 7. What “Session as Python” is for
docs.text:
Every action you took, as the script that repeats it. (screenshot predates the panel restructure)

The strip at the bottom of the window shows the last action as Python; the code icon in the footer (tooltip “Copy session as Python”) shows the whole session as one script: the imports, app = Session(), and one app.do(...) line per action, from OpenNetwork(source=...) through Select, PinAnchor, RunValidation, EditCells and UndoEdit.

It exists because clicking is a bad way to document work. The script is the record of what you did to the network, in the form a reviewer can read, a colleague can run on the next quarter’s network, and a CI job can run on every one. A build you approved replays with approved=True; a save replays as a new copy. The one thing to know before replaying: a folder you trusted on the netstead app command line is not in the script, so a fresh Session() needs it in io.allowed_roots (see Every action is replayable).

docs.title: 8. Saving a copy, and what stays the same
docs.text:
Save a copy as a Parquet folder. The source folder is never written to. (screenshot predates the panel restructure)

The Save icon in the header opens a dialog that writes the network as it is now (v1, with your fix) to a new folder or file: name it, choose Parquet, CSV, DuckDB or Zip, and pick a folder inside your home directory with Choose folder… and Use this folder, then Save. The save is a job; when it finishes a toast says where the copy went and which tables differ from the source, the edit is marked saved in the Edit tab, and the unsaved badge clears.

What stays the same is the network you opened. The Workbench never writes to its source, local or remote, and never overwrites an existing copy, so an afternoon of edits can’t damage the file you started from. Open warnings are listed and confirmed before a save goes ahead. A Parquet copy opens directly in GeoLibre, QGIS or ArcGIS Pro, and feeds AequilibraE, DTALite and Path4GMNS; see The Workbench and other tools for how to move between them.

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
The General Modeling Network Specification (GMNS) is an open standard, maintained by the Zephyr Foundation, for representing routable transportation networks as a small set of related tables. The spec lives at github.com/zephyr-data-specs/GMNS and is versioned (current vendored versions: 0.95, 0.96, 0.97).

A GMNS network is a directory of CSVs (or Parquet, or any tabular store) plus a datapackage.json manifest that describes the schema. The required core is just two tables:

  • link — directed edges of the routable graph (one row per road segment between two intersections).
  • node — vertices of the graph (intersections, dead-ends, zone centroids).

Layered on top of that core, the spec defines optional tables for the things real transportation models need:

  • Geometry detail — geometry (WKT shapes per link), segment and segment_lane (sub-link partitioning for places where lane geometry changes).
  • Lane detail — lane (one row per travel lane), movement (turning movements at a node).
  • Time-of-day overrides — link_tod, lane_tod, segment_tod, segment_lane_tod, movement_tod — per-period overrides on capacity, allowed uses, lane assignments.
  • Signal control — signal_controller, signal_coordination, signal_detector, signal_phase_mvmt, signal_timing_phase, signal_timing_plan.
  • Demand context — zone (traffic analysis zones), location (curb-side points), curb_seg (curb space management).
  • Dimension tables — time_set_definitions (period definitions), use_definition and use_group (vehicle / mode classes), config (network-wide configuration).

The full set across the 0.97 spec is 25 resource files. See Table of tables for the catalog and Schema reference for field-level detail.

The spec ships as a Frictionless Data Package — datapackage.json declares each resource, its CSV schema, primary keys, and foreign-key relationships in a machine-readable form.

docs.title: Why we have it
docs.text:
Before GMNS, every traffic simulator, travel-demand model, and routing engine carried its own network format. A network exported from Cube didn’t load in TransCAD; a Visum file didn’t open in SUMO; a TomTom routing graph wasn’t a TransModeler input. Modelers spent more time writing conversion scripts than running models, and every conversion silently dropped information.

GMNS exists so a network produced for one tool travels to another with zero conversion code. The interop story is the whole story:

  1. Producers (state DOTs, MPOs, OSM derivative pipelines) publish in GMNS.
  2. Consumers (modelers, routing services, analysis tools) read GMNS directly.
  3. The spec is small enough that bespoke conversions are practical when a tool doesn’t speak GMNS natively — but the goal is that they don’t have to be written twice.

GMNS is not a modeling format with semantics baked in (capacity calculations, BPR functions, signal optimisation). It is the substrate on which those tools operate. The same GMNS network feeds a microsimulation, a static-equilibrium assignment, and an active-transportation accessibility analysis.

docs.title: Mental model
docs.text:
• Tables, not files — a GMNS network is a set of relations, not a binary blob. Any tabular store works (CSV, Parquet, DuckDB, zipped CSV).
  • Two required tables, the rest optional — the minimum viable GMNS network is link + node. Every other table layers detail onto that spine.
  • Foreign keys are the API — relationships between tables (lane.link_id → link.link_id, link.from_node_id → node.node_id) are declared in datapackage.json and machine-checkable.

The core relationships:

erDiagram node ||--o{ link : "from_node_id / to_node_id" link ||--o{ lane : "link_id" link ||--o{ link_tod : "link_id" link }o--|| geometry : "geometry_id (optional)" node ||--o{ movement : "node_id" link ||--o{ movement : "ib_link_id / ob_link_id"

A real network has more edges in this diagram (signal tables hang off node, segment tables sub-divide link, zone tables hang off node) but the four cardinal relations above carry most of the routing semantics.

docs.title: The Frictionless Data Package format
docs.text:
GMNS is a Frictionless Data Package. The spec is not a custom serialization — it’s a datapackage.json that declares 25 resources, each with a Table Schema (field types, constraints, primary key, foreign keys). Any Frictionless-compatible reader can parse a GMNS package’s structure without knowing what GMNS is.

This is why the Netstead validator’s structural and schema passes are inherited verbatim from corral (the generic toolkit underneath); only the foreign-key chains and the data-quality rules are GMNS-specific.

docs.title: GTFS
docs.text:
GTFS (General Transit Feed Specification) is a separate spec, scoped to scheduled public transit — routes, stops, trips, stop-times. GMNS is scoped to the routable roadway / street network — links, nodes, lanes, signals.

The two are complementary and frequently combined: GMNS for the street network the bus drives on, GTFS for the bus schedule. Bridging tools like openmobilitydata.org and the in-development GTFS-GMNS reconciliation patterns let a transit assignment use both.

GMNS deliberately does not duplicate GTFS. A transit_route table is not in GMNS — that’s GTFS’s job.

docs.title: OpenStreetMap
docs.text:
OpenStreetMap (OSM) is a global, crowdsourced geographic database. It is not a network spec — OSM tags are loose, regionally inconsistent, and not designed for routing-grade modeling out of the box.

GMNS is the standardized target for the conversion. Tools like osm2gmns and osmnx (used to build the bundled Leavenworth fixture — see its README) consume OSM, infer link attributes (lanes, free-flow speed, facility type) from OSM tags, and emit GMNS. netstead’s own Overture builder produced the bundled Market Street, San Francisco fixture (Overture Maps, an ODbL-licensed OpenStreetMap derivative; see its README).

OSM → GMNS is lossy and opinionated (tag inference is heuristic; OSM doesn’t carry signal timing or TOD restrictions). The point is that the output is a single standardized format that every downstream consumer understands, regardless of where the source data came from.

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
The Netstead Workbench is a network session, not a GIS. It holds one or more GMNS networks in a live DuckDB session and gives them a map and linked tables. What it adds that a GIS does not:

  • Spec-aware tables. Foreign keys from the GMNS spec drive navigation, related-row tints, validation and cascading deletes across link, node, lane, segment and the rest.
  • Selections that resolve. A phrase such as “I-90 EB between Exit 85 and Exit 87” becomes a path with anchors, candidates, confidence and diagnostics, and can be pinned, saved and exported.
  • Edits with an audit trail. Every change is a typed action with undo, lineage, “copy as Python” and, through plugins, ProjectCard output.
  • Validation on the map. Issues link to rows and markers; a fix is an edit, not a redraw.

What it deliberately leaves to other tools: cartography beyond color-by, width-by and filter; context layers such as aerials, land use or census data; printing; 3D; and running a model.

docs.title: Why we have it
docs.text: Transportation networks are relational, and GIS tools see one layer at a time. The Workbench exists so that the relational work (does this lane belong to that link, does this edit break a movement, which links does this phrase mean) happens in one place with a map attached, and so that the result can be handed to a GIS or a model in a format it already reads.

docs.title: Mental model
docs.text:
Three roles, one network:

Role Tool Owns Network session Netstead Workbench tables, selection, validation, edits, history GIS canvas GeoLibre, QGIS, ArcGIS Pro symbology, legends, context layers, print, 3D Model engine AequilibraE, DTALite, Path4GMNS, commercial packages assignment, simulation, skims

The hand-off between roles is a file. A network saved from the Workbench as Parquet is a directory of one GeoParquet file per table, which every GIS canvas and most model engines open directly. Save it from Edits → Save a copy with the Parquet format, or from Python:

from netstead import Network
from netstead.fixtures import leavenworth

net = Network.from_source(leavenworth.csv_dir())
net.write("./leavenworth.parquet")

Expected: a leavenworth.parquet/ directory holding link.parquet, node.parquet, geometry.parquet and the other tables the network carries. Shapes live wherever the network keeps them: on link when it has its own geometry column, otherwise in geometry keyed by geometry_id, with nodes as x_coord / y_coord points.

docs.title: GeoLibre
docs.text:
GeoLibre is a client-side GIS from the opengeos group: MapLibre and deck.gl rendering, DuckDB-WASM for import and SQL, a large toolbox compiled to WebAssembly, and the same React app shipped as a desktop program, a web app and a Jupyter widget. Its plugins are JavaScript bundles that add panels, controls and layers; Python drives it as a widget but cannot extend its UI.

The two are complementary rather than competing. GeoLibre is the better canvas: categorised and graduated symbology, legends, print layouts, basemaps, time slider, 3D, and any GeoParquet, COG, PMTiles or service layer dropped beside the network. The Workbench is the better session: it keeps the network’s tables, selection and edit history, which GeoLibre’s per-layer feature model has no place for.

Use them together by saving from the Workbench and opening in GeoLibre, on the desktop or from a notebook with its add_geoparquet. A thin GeoLibre plugin that connects to a running netstead app and mirrors the selection both ways is a natural later step; the Workbench’s action API is designed to be driven that way.

docs.title: QGIS
docs.text:
QGIS reads GeoParquet natively in recent releases (3.36 and later, where its GDAL build includes the Arrow driver) and CSV with WKT through its delimited-text layer. It is the usual desktop home for cartography and for joining a network to parcels, zones or counts. The GMNS community’s NeXTA4GMNS notes describe viewing and editing GMNS in QGIS.

Edits made in QGIS do not come back with lineage. Make attribute edits in the Workbench and use QGIS for geometry work and maps.

docs.title: ArcGIS Pro
docs.text: ArcGIS Pro reads GeoParquet from 3.3 on, and its Network Analyst extension builds routable network datasets from feature classes. The Workbench is the place to validate and fix a GMNS network before it becomes such a dataset; ArcGIS is the place to publish it as a feature service or run Network Analyst solvers on it.

docs.title: Network Wrangler and ProjectCard
docs.text: Network Wrangler manages scenarios as a base network plus an ordered set of ProjectCards. Netstead reads and writes the card format rather than depending on Wrangler’s pandas stack: Workbench selections export as card facility objects, the fix workflow downloads a card, and the project-cards plugin (plugins/project-cards in the repository) authors cards from Workbench edits. See Triage and fix findings for the field mapping.

docs.title: Model engines
docs.text:
• AequilibraE imports a network with create_from_gmns (link, node, use_group and geometry tables) and exports with export_to_gmns. Validate in the Workbench, then build the AequilibraE project from the saved CSV folder.
  • DTALite and Path4GMNS read node.csv and link.csv directly; save as CSV and point them at the folder.
  • Commercial packages (Cube, Visum, TransCAD, Emme) generally import GMNS link and node tables through their own scripting interfaces rather than a native reader. What is GMNS? explains why the spec exists as the common target.

docs.title: Builders and notebook maps
docs.text: osm2gmns and osmnx build GMNS from OpenStreetMap, as does netstead build. For a quick map inside a notebook without the Workbench, View a network on a map covers the built-in viewer, and a GeoDataFrame from netstead[clean] drops into lonboard, pydeck or kepler.gl.

docs.text:

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
netstead mcp serve runs a stdio MCP server that exposes seven tools: three generic Frictionless-package tools inherited from corral.mcp (describe_package, validate_package, list_tables), plus four GMNS-aware tools (describe_network, quality_check, connected_components, scope_from_nodes). Every tool is stateless — each call takes a source (path or URL) and loads the package fresh. No session, no cache, no cross-call mutation. A stateful surface (editing sessions, indexed scope ops) is deferred.

All tools return JSON-shaped dicts (or, for list_tables, a list of strings); shapes are stable inside a major version. The example outputs below are what the tools return for the bundled Leavenworth fixture (packages/netstead/netstead/fixtures/leavenworth/csv: 339 links, 121 nodes, nine CSV tables, no datapackage.json). For wiring the server into Claude Desktop or Claude Code, see Wire the MCP server.

docs.title: describe_package(source)
docs.text:
Generic package overview. Available on any Frictionless package, not just GMNS. It loads the source as a bare corral.dataset.Package, so on a CSV directory without a datapackage.json the inferred package name is "auto"; describe_network is the GMNS-aware variant.

Parameters

Name Type Description source string Filesystem path or URL to a package directory / datapackage.json

Returns — dict:

{
  "source": "<echoed input>",
  "name": "auto",
  "engine": "IbisEngine",
  "table_count": 9,
  "tables": [
    {"name": "geometry", "rows": 339, "columns": ["geometry_id", "geometry"]},
    {"name": "lane", "rows": 429, "columns": ["lane_id", "link_id", "lane_num", "allowed_uses", "width"]},
    {"name": "link", "rows": 339, "columns": ["link_id", "name", "from_node_id", "to_node_id", "..."]},
    {"name": "node", "rows": 121, "columns": ["node_id", "name", "x_coord", "y_coord", "node_type", "ctrl_type", "osm_node_id"]}
  ]
}

rows / columns may be null for an individual table if its count fails (e.g. unreadable file).

Example

{"name": "describe_package", "arguments": {"source": "packages/netstead/netstead/fixtures/leavenworth/csv"}}

docs.title: validate_package(source)
docs.text:
Run corral’s generic validation pipeline (structural + schema + foreign-key + sync-state) against whatever spec the source carries, and return the report. It does not apply the GMNS spec: on a bare CSV directory such as the Leavenworth fixture there is no spec to check against, so spec_version is null and the findings are one structural.spec_missing info (no datapackage.json, no spec given) and nine structural.unexpected_resource warnings (one per CSV the empty spec does not declare). For GMNS validation use netstead validate <source> --json, which emits the same report shape with the vendored spec applied.

Parameters

Name Type Description source string Path or URL to the package

Returns — dict, the canonical ValidationReport.to_dict() shape:

{
  "report_version": 1,
  "spec_version": null,
  "source": "<echoed input>",
  "created_at": "2026-10-19T13:12:08.078865",
  "metadata": {},
  "summary": {"error": 0, "warning": 9, "info": 1, "data_quality": 0, "is_clean": false},
  "issues": [
    {
      "severity": "info",
      "category": "structural",
      "code": "structural.spec_missing",
      "message": "package source '...': no spec was given and none was found beside the source, so no table was checked against a schema",
      "table": null,
      "column": null,
      "row": null,
      "fix_hint": "Pass spec= to Package.from_source. Only a datapackage.json inside a source directory is discovered automatically; one inside a zip, next to a single file, or at a remote prefix is not.",
      "extra": {}
    },
    {
      "severity": "warning",
      "category": "structural",
      "code": "structural.unexpected_resource",
      "message": "package source '...': resource 'geometry' was found but is not declared in the spec",
      "table": "geometry",
      "column": null,
      "row": null,
      "fix_hint": "Add geometry to the spec, rename it to match an existing declared resource, or remove it from the source.",
      "extra": {"path": ".../geometry.csv", "format": "csv"}
    }
  ]
}

severity is one of error, warning, info; category is one of schema, structural, foreign_key, sync_state, data_quality. summary.is_clean is true when there are no error or warning issues; info issues do not affect it. The example above shows the spec_missing info and the first of the nine warnings.

Example

{"name": "validate_package", "arguments": {"source": "s3://my-bucket/regional/datapackage.json"}}

docs.title: list_tables(source)
docs.text:
Cheap variant of describe_package — returns just the sorted list of table names with no row counts. Useful as a first call when the agent doesn’t know what’s in a package.

Parameters

Name Type Description source string Path or URL

Returns — list[str]:

["geometry", "lane", "link", "link_tod", "node", "signal_controller", "time_set_definitions", "use_definition", "use_group"]

Example

{"name": "list_tables", "arguments": {"source": "packages/netstead/netstead/fixtures/leavenworth/csv"}}

docs.title: describe_network(source)
docs.text:
GMNS-aware version of describe_package. Loads the source as a netstead.Network (so the GMNS spec is applied and name is "gmns") and surfaces the fields an agent typically wants up front — spec version, link/node counts — without iterating tables.

Parameters

Name Type Description source string Path or URL to a GMNS network

Returns — dict:

{
  "source": "<echoed input>",
  "name": "gmns",
  "spec_version": "0.97",
  "engine": "IbisEngine",
  "links": 339,
  "nodes": 121,
  "table_count": 9,
  "tables": ["geometry", "lane", "link", "link_tod", "node", "signal_controller", "time_set_definitions", "use_definition", "use_group"]
}

links / nodes may be null if the network doesn’t have those tables or the count fails.

Example

{"name": "describe_network", "arguments": {"source": "packages/netstead/netstead/fixtures/leavenworth/csv"}}

docs.title: quality_check(source)
docs.text:
Run the GMNS data-quality rule pack (high-speed-residential, disconnected components, lane-count mismatch, duplicate-near-nodes, sharp-angle bends, implausible v/c, missing critical fields). Requires the [graph] extra (scipy) on the server side for the connectivity rule.

Parameters

Name Type Description source string Path or URL to a GMNS network

Returns — same ValidationReport.to_dict() shape as validate_package. The report’s own spec_version and source are null (the rule runner does not fill them in); every issue has category: "data_quality":

{
  "report_version": 1,
  "spec_version": null,
  "source": null,
  "created_at": "2026-10-19T13:12:08.141843",

docs.title: connected_components(source)
docs.text:
Count weakly-connected components in the network graph. Requires the [graph] extra (scipy) on the server side.

Parameters

Name Type Description source string Path or URL to a GMNS network

Returns — dict:

{
  "source": "<echoed input>",
  "component_count": 1,
  "sizes": [121]
}

component_count == 1 means the network is fully connected. sizes is the descending list of node counts per component — [121] for the fully-connected 121-node Leavenworth fixture; [60, 12, 3] for a three-component network whose largest piece has 60 nodes.

Example

{"name": "connected_components", "arguments": {"source": "packages/netstead/netstead/fixtures/leavenworth/csv"}}

docs.title: scope_from_nodes(source, node_ids, path_between)
docs.text:
Build a network-aware scope from a list of seed node ids and return the resulting node + link sets.

Parameters

Name Type Default Description source string — Path or URL to a GMNS network node_ids list[int] — Seed node ids path_between bool true If true, includes all nodes/links on shortest paths between every pair of seeds. If false, the docstring promises the seeds plus their incident links, but today the scope holds only the seed nodes and no links (seeds [1, 25, 50] on Leavenworth give 3 nodes, 0 links, although 20 links touch them).

Returns — dict (intended; see the known issue). For seeds [1, 25, 50] on Leavenworth the scope has 14 nodes and 28 links:

{
  "source": "<echoed input>",
  "seed_node_ids": [1, 25, 50],
  "path_between": true,
  "result_node_count": 14,
  "result_link_count": 28,
  "node_ids": [1, 2, 3, 10, 11, 15, 25, 50, 63, 74, 78, 96, 99, 100],
  "link_ids": [1, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 27, 29, "..."]
}

The returned ids are sorted. For chaining (union / intersect / buffer), drop into the Python API — the MCP surface only exposes the leaf operation.

Example

{"name": "scope_from_nodes", "arguments": {"source": "packages/netstead/netstead/fixtures/leavenworth/csv", "node_ids": [1, 25, 50], "path_between": true}}
