docs.title: Build a GMNS network from OpenStreetMap or Overture
Build a GMNS network from OpenStreetMap or Overture
When to use this
docs.text:
You need a GMNS network for a study area and don’t have one yet. Point netstead at a place name, a bounding box, or a lat/lon + buffer and it fetches the road network — from OpenStreetMap via Overpass (--source osm, the default) or from Overture Maps’ transportation theme (--source overture) — and writes a validated GMNS node + link package. No osmnx or osm2gmns required.

Requires the matching optional extra: pip install 'netstead[osm]' or pip install 'netstead[overture]'.

docs.title: Quick example
docs.text:
Build the drivable network for a place and write it as CSV. The area is geocoded via Nominatim, the road network is fetched from Overpass, and the result is a GMNS package on disk:

netstead build --place "Leavenworth, WA" --network-type roads --source osm --format csv ./leavenworth-osm

The command prints a summary (nodes, links, spec_version); add --json for a machine-readable document.

docs.title: 1. Install the extra
docs.text:
pip install 'netstead[osm]'        # --source osm (default)
pip install 'netstead[overture]'   # --source overture

Overture is read as GeoParquet straight through corral’s bundled DuckDB, so [overture] adds only the mapping-data loader. Geocoding a --place string uses Nominatim from the [osm] extra, so an Overture build by place name needs both.

docs.title: 2. Pick how you specify the area
docs.text:
One of three, mutually exclusive:

# A place name (city / county / neighborhood) — geocoded to a boundary polygon.
netstead build --place "Leavenworth, WA" ./net

# A bounding box: west,south,east,north (EPSG:4326).
netstead build --bbox -120.67,47.58,-120.64,47.61 ./net

# A point (lat,lon) plus a buffer in metres.
netstead build --point 47.596,-120.66 --buffer 800 ./net

docs.title: 3. Choose the source
docs.text:
--source osm (the default) fetches from Overpass. --source overture reads the pinned Overture release from cloud GeoParquet; --overture-release moves the pin and --data-root points at an alternative base URI or a local snapshot directory holding segment.parquet / connector.parquet. Both flags are rejected with --source osm:

netstead build --source overture --bbox -120.67,47.58,-120.64,47.61 ./leavenworth-overture
netstead build --source overture --overture-release 2026-09-23.1 --data-root /data/overture-snapshot --bbox -120.67,47.58,-120.64,47.61 ./net

docs.title: 4. Choose modes and output format
docs.text:
--network-type is roads (motorway through residential, service and other roads, links and busways), paths (footways, paths, pedestrian ways, steps, tracks, cycleways and bridleways), or both: repeat the option or comma-separate (--network-type roads,paths). Proposed, construction and corridor ways are never built. The old names still work but are deprecated: drive means roads; walk, bike and all mean roads,paths. Overture builds use the same two types, mapped onto Overture road classes (no busway class exists there). The output format is inferred from the destination extension, or set it explicitly with --format (csv / parquet / duckdb / zip). A destination with no extension — ./net in the examples above — is written as a Parquet directory; pass --format csv for CSV:

netstead build --place "Leavenworth, WA" --network-type roads,paths --format parquet ./full-net

docs.title: 5. Validate what you built
docs.text:
The build already produces a schema-valid package; run netstead validate any time to confirm and to see the report:

netstead validate ./leavenworth-osm

docs.title: Python API
docs.text:
Programmatic equivalent — netstead.osm.build_network_from_osm returns a Network (a corral package) you can validate, scope, or write. The area is a place string, a (lat, lon) point with buffer_m, or a (west, south, east, north) bbox:

from netstead.osm import build_network_from_osm

net = build_network_from_osm("Leavenworth, WA", network_type="roads")
print(net.links.count(), net.nodes.count())
net.write("leavenworth-osm", format="csv", overwrite=True)

netstead.overture.build_network_from_overture has the same shape, plus overture_release (the pinned release string) and data_root (alternative base URI or local snapshot directory). Its extra_tags are Overture segment property paths (e.g. "subclass", "road_surface") rather than OSM tag keys:

from netstead.overture import build_network_from_overture

net = build_network_from_overture((-120.67, 47.58, -120.64, 47.61), network_type="roads")
net.write("leavenworth-overture")   # no extension → Parquet directory

If you already have node/link records (e.g. from your own fetch, or to benchmark the build path without the network), assemble a Network directly with netstead.osm.network_from_records:

from netstead.osm import network_from_records

nodes = [
    {"node_id": 1, "x_coord": -120.66, "y_coord": 47.60},
    {"node_id": 2, "x_coord": -120.65, "y_coord": 47.60},
]
links = [
    {"link_id": 1, "from_node_id": 1, "to_node_id": 2, "directed": True,
     "facility_type": "residential", "geometry": "LINESTRING (-120.66 47.6, -120.65 47.6)"},
    {"link_id": 2, "from_node_id": 2, "to_node_id": 1, "directed": True,
     "facility_type": "residential", "geometry": "LINESTRING (-120.65 47.6, -120.66 47.6)"},
]
net = network_from_records(nodes, links)
print(net.links.count())

docs.title: How the conversion works
docs.text:
• Topology. A GMNS node is created at every OSM intersection (a node shared by two or more ways) and at each way’s endpoints. Intermediate shape points are dropped as nodes and kept as the link’s WKT geometry; their OSM ids are retained on the link’s osm_node_ids column for provenance, alongside osm_way_id.
  • Direction. Every link is directed=True. A two-way street becomes two directed links (one per direction); a oneway street becomes one, honoring oneway=-1 and implied-oneway (motorways, roundabouts).
  • Attributes. name, lanes, free_speed, and facility_type are mapped from OSM tags via the maintained data file netstead/osm/mappings/osm_to_gmns.yaml. Pass --extra-tags surface,bridge (or extra_tags=[...]) to carry additional OSM tags through as extra columns. Edit the YAML to change or extend the mapping — no code change needed.

docs.title: Common variations
docs.text:
Point + buffer

A circle of road around a coordinate (metres).

netstead build --point 47.596,-120.66 --buffer 800 ./net
Carry extra OSM tags

Add columns to the link table verbatim.

netstead build --bbox -120.67,47.58,-120.64,47.61 --extra-tags surface,bridge ./net
Build from a local .osm XML or Overpass JSON file

No network access: build_network_from_osm_file reads an .osm XML file or an Overpass [out:json] export (.json) and applies the same network_type filter and tag mapping. It is Python-only (no netstead build flag) and still needs the [osm] extra for the mapping loader.

from netstead.osm import build_network_from_osm_file

net = build_network_from_osm_file("leavenworth.osm", network_type="roads", extra_tags=["surface"])
net.write("leavenworth-osm", format="csv")

Build from Overture Maps

Same area options; swap the source. Overture link geometry comes from segment shapes and nodes from Overture connectors.

netstead build --source overture --bbox -120.67,47.58,-120.64,47.61 --format csv ./leavenworth-overture
Benchmark the build

The scripts/bench_osm_build.py harness times the convert + build path (DuckDB is the single compute engine); add --baselines for directional osmnx / osm2gmns comparisons.

uv run python scripts/bench_osm_build.py --grids 10,40,120 --json

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• Units. GMNS is unit-agnostic — units are declared per-dataset, so the build writes a config table stating them: free_speed is mph (faithful to US OSM maxspeed tags; unit-less values are treated as km/h and converted), length is geodesic metres, crs is EPSG:4326. Re-unit downstream if your convention differs.
  • Overpass limits. The public Overpass endpoint rate-limits and times out on large areas. For regional extracts (e.g. a metro), point at a self-hosted endpoint (endpoint= in the Python API) rather than hammering the public server.
  • Nominatim policy. Place-name geocoding uses the public Nominatim, which is not for bulk/automated use. Prefer --bbox for scripted/repeated runs.
  • Attribution. OSM data is ODbL-licensed — attribute OpenStreetMap in anything you publish from these networks. Overture data is ODbL too: derived products must credit “© OpenStreetMap contributors, © Overture Maps Foundation” (see Overture’s attribution page); netstead reads Overture data and does not redistribute it.
  • netstead[osm] / netstead[overture] required. Without the matching extra the command exits with an install hint.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Run validation and read the report — interpret the report from netstead validate.
  • Run the bundled benchmarks — netstead bench for load/validate timings on an existing network.

docs.title: When to use this
docs.text:
GMNS defaults are designed for typical mid-sized urban networks. Override them when:

  • Your network’s speed limits, lane counts, or geometry tolerances differ from the defaults (a 30 mph residential cap, or a CRS in degrees instead of meters).
  • You want to silence a rule that’s noise on your data.
  • You want to plug in a project-specific quality rule.

docs.title: Quick example
docs.text:
Raise the residential-speed threshold from the default 35 mph to 45 mph. RuleConfig.thresholds merges into the rule’s defaults — you only specify the keys you want to change. Every residential link in Leavenworth is posted at 40 mph, so the default fires 271 warnings and 45 mph silences all of them:

from netstead import Network
from netstead.fixtures import leavenworth
from corral.quality import run_quality, RuleConfig

net = Network.from_source(leavenworth.csv_dir())
default = run_quality(net)
relaxed = run_quality(
    net,
    config={"quality.high_speed_residential": RuleConfig(thresholds={"speed_limit_mph": 45.0})},
)
print(f"{len(default.issues)} issues at 35 mph, {len(relaxed.issues)} at 45 mph")

Expected:

271 issues at 35 mph, 0 at 45 mph

Quality report card at the default thresholds: 271 quality.high_speed_residential WARNINGs, one per residential link posted at 40 mph. Raising speed_limit_mph to 45 silences them all; lowering it to 30 changes nothing, because no residential link sits between 30 and 35 mph.

docs.title: 1. List the rules currently registered
docs.text:
Inspect the registered rule pack to see codes, defaults, and severities. The GMNS pack ships nine rules out of the box:

from corral.quality import list_rules, get_rule
from netstead.quality import register_all

register_all()                                   # populate the registry
for code in list_rules():
    rule = get_rule(code)
    print(f"{rule.code:42} {rule.severity.value:8} {rule.description[:50]}")
Code Threshold key Default Severity quality.high_speed_residential speed_limit_mph 35 WARNING quality.disconnected_components (no threshold) — INFO quality.lane_count_mismatch (no threshold) — WARNING quality.duplicate_near_nodes epsilon_units 1e-5 WARNING quality.sharp_angle_bends min_angle_degrees 30 WARNING quality.implausible_vc vc_max 1.5 WARNING quality.missing_critical_fields coverage_min 0.90 INFO quality.non_unique_combination combinations see below WARNING quality.overlapping_links min_overlap_units 0 WARNING

Three of these are conditional: quality.disconnected_components builds the scipy graph index, so run_quality needs the [graph] extra; quality.overlapping_links needs shapely (the [clean] extra) and link shapes, inline or in the geometry table; quality.sharp_angle_bends only applies when the link table carries an inline geometry column (Leavenworth keeps geometry in a separate table, so the rule is skipped there).

quality.non_unique_combination catches rows that repeat a column combination GMNS expects to be unique even though the table’s primary key is a surrogate id: two link_tod rows for the same link_id and time_day pass spec validation but contradict each other. It emits one issue per repeated combination, with the row positions in extra["rows"]. By default it checks (<parent id>, time_day) and (<parent id>, timeday_id) on every time-of-day table (link_tod, lane_tod, segment_tod, segment_lane_tod, movement_tod, signal_timing_plan), plus (link_id, lane_num) on lane, (segment_id, lane_num) on segment_lane and (timing_plan_id, signal_phase_num) on signal_timing_phase (read-only, as netstead.quality.DEFAULT_UNIQUE_COMBINATIONS). Setting combinations replaces that list, so name every combination you still want. A configured combination whose table or columns the network lacks is logged as a warning on the netstead.quality.rules logger (probably a typo). It is deliberately not an issue: severity_override applies to every issue a rule emits, so promoting this rule to ERROR in CI fails only on real duplicates, never on a network that lacks an optional table. A value that is not a mapping of table name to lists of column names raises ValueError, and the Workbench rejects it (and a negative epsilon_units) when the setting is saved:

report = run_quality(
    net,
    config={
        "quality.non_unique_combination": RuleConfig(
            thresholds={"combinations": {"link_tod": [["link_id", "time_day"]], "link": [["osm_way_id", "from_node_id"]]}}
        )
    },
)

docs.title: 2. Override a threshold
docs.text:
RuleConfig.thresholds is merged into the rule’s defaults — you only specify the keys you want to change. Override multiple rules in one call:

report = run_quality(
    net,
    config={
        "quality.high_speed_residential": RuleConfig(thresholds={"speed_limit_mph": 25.0}),
        "quality.sharp_angle_bends": RuleConfig(thresholds={"min_angle_degrees": 45.0}),
    },
)

The Workbench applies the same per-rule configuration from its validation.rules setting (Settings → Validation, keyed by rule code) — see Validate and fix in the Workbench.

docs.title: 3. Disable a rule entirely
docs.text:
A disabled rule produces no issues and isn’t listed in the report:

report = run_quality(
    net,
    config={"quality.missing_critical_fields": RuleConfig(enabled=False)},
)

docs.title: 4. Promote (or demote) severity
docs.text:
A common case: your CI pipeline should fail on lane-count mismatches even though the rule ships as WARNING. Use severity_override to promote, then check report.issues and exit non-zero accordingly:

import netstead
from netstead.fixtures import leavenworth
from corral.quality import RuleConfig, run_quality
from corral.reports import Severity

net = netstead.read(leavenworth.csv_dir())
report = run_quality(
    net,
    config={"quality.lane_count_mismatch": RuleConfig(severity_override=Severity.ERROR)},
)
has_errors = any(i.severity is Severity.ERROR for i in report.issues)
# In a CI script: sys.exit(1 if has_errors else 0)

docs.title: 5. Write your own rule and register it
docs.text:
A rule is a plain class (no base class needed — corral.quality.Rule is a Protocol) with three attributes, code, description and severity, and two methods: applies_to(package) -> bool, a cheap predicate the runner calls first, and run(package, report, config), which appends findings to report with report.add_issue(...). Accept the third config argument to read RuleConfig.thresholds; a rule with no thresholds may define run(self, package, report) and the runner passes two arguments. Don’t apply severity_override yourself — run_quality rewrites the severity of every issue your rule emitted after it returns.

Write the predicate against the table’s ibis expression (package.tables["link"].expr) so DuckDB filters the rows and only the offending ones reach Python; on a 200k-link network that is the difference between materializing every row and fetching a handful. Number the rows with ibis.row_number() before filtering so Issue.row is the row’s position in the whole table. This rule flags links longer than a configurable maximum (Leavenworth’s length column is in metres):

import ibis
from corral.quality import RuleConfig, register_rule, run_quality
from corral.reports import Category, Issue, Severity


class LongLinkRule:
    code = "quality.long_link"
    description = "Link longer than the configured maximum length."
    severity = Severity.WARNING

    def applies_to(self, package) -> bool:
        link = package.tables.get("link")
        return link is not None and {"link_id", "length"} <= set(link.columns())

    def run(self, package, report, config: RuleConfig | None = None) -> None:
        thresholds = config.thresholds if config else {}
        max_length = float(thresholds.get("max_length", 1000.0))
        link = package.tables["link"].expr
        link = link.mutate(row=ibis.row_number())
        offending = (
            link.filter(link.length.notnull(), link.length > max_length)
            .select("row", "link_id", "length")
            .order_by("row")
        )
        for row in offending.to_pyarrow().to_pylist():
            report.add_issue(
                Issue(
                    severity=self.severity,
                    category=Category.DATA_QUALITY,
                    code=self.code,
                    message=f"link {row['link_id']} is {row['length']:.0f} long (> {max_length:.0f})",
                    table="link",
                    column="length",
                    row=row["row"],
                    fix_hint="Split the link, or check its length.",
                )
            )


register_rule(LongLinkRule())
report = run_quality(net, config={"quality.long_link": RuleConfig(thresholds={"max_length": 500.0})})
print(sum(1 for i in report.issues if i.code == "quality.long_link"), "links over 500 m")

Expected:

4 links over 500 m

To ship the rule with a package, expose a zero-argument factory that returns list[Rule] and declare it under the corral.quality.rules entry point in your pyproject.toml. run_quality loads every entry point on its first call and registers each returned rule — this is exactly how netstead registers its own pack (netstead.quality:register_all):

# myproject/rules.py
def register_rules() -> list:
    return [LongLinkRule()]

[project.entry-points."corral.quality.rules"]
myproject = "myproject.rules:register_rules"

docs.title: Common variations
docs.text:
Default — override one threshold for one run

Most common pattern: tighten or loosen a single threshold without touching anything else.

report = run_quality(
    net,
    config={"quality.high_speed_residential": RuleConfig(thresholds={"speed_limit_mph": 30.0})},
)
Silence a noisy rule entirely

Disable it via RuleConfig(enabled=False); the rule contributes no issues and doesn’t appear in the report.

report = run_quality(net, config={"quality.missing_critical_fields": RuleConfig(enabled=False)})
Promote a WARNING to ERROR for CI

Use severity_override; then exit non-zero if any ERROR issue appears.

report = run_quality(
    net,
    config={"quality.lane_count_mismatch": RuleConfig(severity_override=Severity.ERROR)},
)
Ship a custom rule with your package

Point the corral.quality.rules entry point at a zero-argument callable that returns your rule instances; run_quality discovers and registers them on first call.

[project.entry-points."corral.quality.rules"]
myproject = "myproject.rules:register_rules"

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• epsilon_units is CRS-sensitive. The default 1e-5 is tight for WGS84 degrees (~1 metre near the equator). A network in projected meters needs something like epsilon_units=0.5 for the same intent. Always set this explicitly for non-WGS84 networks.
  • quality.overlapping_links measures overlap in CRS units too. It flags two links whose shapes share a stretch longer than min_overlap_units (default 0, so any shared stretch). Links that only meet at a node, cross, or carry the identical shape (the usual way two directions of a two-way street are drawn) are not flagged; a short link running along part of a longer one is. Raise min_overlap_units to ignore short shared stretches, e.g. 0.00002 (about 2 m) in WGS84 degrees or 2.0 in projected metres.
  • quality.overlapping_links matches exactly, with no tolerance. Only segments the two shapes share exactly are caught; two digitisations of the same road a hair apart, or whose vertices never line up on a common segment, are not flagged, and min_overlap_units does not widen the match. It can also get slow when many link bounding boxes overlap with real area, as long or diagonal links in WGS84 do; disable it with RuleConfig(enabled=False) if it dominates a run.
  • epsilon_units must not be negative. quality.duplicate_near_nodes raises ValueError for a negative value; 0 flags only exact duplicates.
  • severity_override doesn’t mute — it replaces. Setting severity_override=Severity.INFO on a WARNING rule still produces issues; if you want to drop them, use enabled=False.
  • applies_to is a method, not a tuple. The runner calls rule.applies_to(package) before run and skips the rule silently when it returns False. Check for the tables and columns you need there (a rule reading signal should return False when the table is absent) rather than raising inside run.

docs.title: Edit a network with atomic rollback
Edit a network with atomic rollback
When to use this
docs.text:
You’re applying a destructive, geometry-aware cleanup to a network — merge near-coincident nodes, drop orphan nodes, simplify link geometry, recompute lengths — and you want a safety net. The netstead.clean ops run inside a Session that records every change, so you can undo all of them in LIFO order: by raising inside the with block, by calling session.rollback(), or by replaying a persisted log later.

These ops are the geometry-aware layer on top of the raw edit primitives. For low-level row edits (update_rows, delete_rows, add_rows) and querying across foreign keys, see Query and update linked tables.

docs.title: Quick example
docs.text:
Open a session, merge nodes that sit almost on top of each other, and exit cleanly so the edit commits. merge_close_nodes rewrites the from_node_id / to_node_id foreign key on every incident link to point at the surviving node — the whole point of doing it inside a session:

import netstead
from netstead.fixtures import leavenworth
from netstead.clean import merge_close_nodes
from corral.editing import Session

net = netstead.read(leavenworth.csv_dir())
print(f"before: {net.nodes.count()} nodes, {net.links.count()} links")

# Leavenworth's coords are WGS84 degrees, so threshold_m is in degrees:
# 0.0005 deg ≈ 56 m at this latitude. Closest nodes are ~27 m apart, so
# this deliberately-large threshold collapses 22 of them (121 → 99 nodes).
with Session(net) as s:
    node_edit, link_edit = merge_close_nodes(net, s, threshold_m=0.0005)
    print(f"merged away {node_edit.diff.rows_removed} nodes; "
          f"link table replaced ({link_edit.diff.rows_changed} rows)")

print(f"after:  {net.nodes.count()} nodes")

Expected:

before: 121 nodes, 339 links
merged away 22 nodes; link table replaced (339 rows)
after:  99 nodes

Both ops are bulk replace_table edits, so rows_changed counts every row of the replaced table (339 links, 99 surviving nodes) — not just the 84 links whose end nodes were actually rewired. rows_removed on the node result is the number to read.

If the with block raises instead, the session reverses every op and net is back to its pre-edit state.

EditResult diff card: per-table row counts (added / removed / changed) and capped before/after row samples.

docs.title: 1. Install
docs.text:
The [clean] extra brings in the geometry stack the ops depend on — shapely, geopandas, pyproj:

pip install 'netstead[clean]'

docs.title: 2. Open a Session
docs.text:
A Session wraps the network in an editable, transactional view. Inside the with block you pass both net and s into each op — the op reads state from net and records its change on s so the session can undo it later:

import netstead
from netstead.fixtures import leavenworth
from corral.editing import Session

net = netstead.read(leavenworth.csv_dir())
with Session(net) as s:
    ...  # editing ops go here — see the next step

docs.title: 3. Apply one or more ops
docs.text:
Multiple ops in the same with block share one transactional boundary — rollback undoes all of them. A realistic cleanup pass merges coincident nodes, then sweeps up any node the merge left with no incident links:

import netstead
from netstead.fixtures import leavenworth
from netstead.clean import merge_close_nodes, remove_orphans
from corral.editing import Session

net = netstead.read(leavenworth.csv_dir())
with Session(net) as s:
    node_edit, link_edit = merge_close_nodes(net, s, threshold_m=0.0005)
    orphan_edit = remove_orphans(net, s)
    print(f"merge removed {node_edit.diff.rows_removed} nodes; "
          f"orphan sweep removed {orphan_edit.diff.rows_removed} more")

Each op returns an EditResult (note: merge_close_nodes touches two tables, so it returns a list of two — one for node, one for link). An EditResult carries three fields:

Field Type Description .diff Diff Per-table counts: rows_added, rows_removed, rows_changed, plus capped before/after samples. Cheap to print / log. .edit Edit The underlying op (op name, target table, payload). .rollback_data Any The state captured before the op ran — opaque, consumed by Session.rollback() / corral.editing.rollback.

EditResult also carries .applied_at (timestamp) and .session_id.

docs.title: 4. Commit or rollback
docs.text:
Clean exit from the with block commits all ops. An exception or an explicit s.rollback() reverses them in LIFO order:

import netstead
from netstead.fixtures import leavenworth
from netstead.clean import merge_close_nodes, remove_orphans
from corral.editing import Session

net = netstead.read(leavenworth.csv_dir())

# Commit:
with Session(net) as s:
    remove_orphans(net, s)
# committed at __exit__

# Rollback by raising — net is restored to the pre-edit state:
before = net.nodes.count()
try:
    with Session(net) as s:
        merge_close_nodes(net, s, threshold_m=0.0005)
        raise RuntimeError("changed my mind")
except RuntimeError:
    pass
assert net.nodes.count() == before

# Rollback explicitly while staying in the block:
with Session(net) as s:
    node_edit, _ = merge_close_nodes(net, s, threshold_m=0.0005)
    if node_edit.diff.rows_removed > 100:
        s.rollback()  # too aggressive — undo

docs.title: 5. Persist the edit log (optional)
docs.text:
Pass log_path= to write a chronological record of each op (name, params, diff, rollback blob) to a sidecar parquet. The log is the only way to undo edits across process boundaries:

with Session(net, log_path="history.parquet") as s:
    merge_close_nodes(net, s, threshold_m=0.0005)
    remove_orphans(net, s)

Later, in a fresh process, replay the log to undo every recorded op in LIFO order:

from netstead import Network
from corral.editing import rollback

net = Network.from_source("./edited.parquet")
rollback(net, log_path="history.parquet")  # replay in LIFO

docs.title: 6. Write the result
docs.text:
Persist the edited network with net.write(...). An edit marks the touched tables dirty, so writing emits a benign OutOfSyncWarning (the validator’s foreign-key index hasn’t been re-resolved against the edited rows — tracked in #164). Suppress it for the write, exactly as the CLI does:

import warnings
from corral.dataset.package import OutOfSyncWarning

with warnings.catch_warnings():
    warnings.simplefilter("ignore", OutOfSyncWarning)
    net.write("./leavenworth-edited.parquet", overwrite=False)

The warning is informational: it tells you the in-memory FK index reflects the pre-edit rows. A fresh netstead.read of the written network re-resolves the index from scratch, and netstead validate re-checks the foreign keys.

docs.title: Common variations
docs.text:
Default — transactional block with a single op

Most common pattern: open session, run one op, exit cleanly to commit.

import netstead
from netstead.fixtures import leavenworth
from netstead.clean import remove_orphans
from corral.editing import Session

net = netstead.read(leavenworth.csv_dir())
with Session(net) as s:
    remove_orphans(net, s)
Chain multiple ops in one atomic block

All-or-nothing: rollback undoes the whole batch.

import netstead
from netstead.fixtures import leavenworth
from netstead.clean import merge_close_nodes, remove_orphans
from corral.editing import Session

net = netstead.read(leavenworth.csv_dir())
with Session(net) as s:
    merge_close_nodes(net, s, threshold_m=0.0005)
    remove_orphans(net, s)
Preview without committing

--dry-run on the CLI runs the op, prints the diff, and reverts before exit.

netstead clean merge-close-nodes <src> --threshold-m 0.0005 --dry-run
Run one op from the shell

Useful in pipelines; the CLI opens the session, writes the result, and suppresses the dirty-write warning for you. Without --dest the edited network is written back over <src> in its own format.

netstead clean remove-orphans <src> --dest ./out.parquet
Capture the diff for a log line

EditResult renders as a card in notebooks (_repr_html_); in plain code, read the .diff counts directly.

import netstead
from netstead.fixtures import leavenworth
from netstead.clean import merge_close_nodes
from corral.editing import Session

net = netstead.read(leavenworth.csv_dir())
with Session(net) as s:
    node_edit, _ = merge_close_nodes(net, s, threshold_m=0.0005)
d = node_edit.diff
print(f"+{d.rows_added} / -{d.rows_removed} / ~{d.rows_changed}")
Geometry ops find the shapes wherever they live

GMNS lets a network keep link shapes inline (link.geometry) or in a separate geometry table keyed by link.geometry_id. Leavenworth uses the geometry table, and the geometry ops need no preparation for that: simplify_geometry edits the table that holds the shapes (so its EditResult targets geometry here, and rollback restores that table), while recompute_lengths resolves each link’s shape the way netstead.semantics.assemble_link_geometry does and writes link.length:

import netstead
from netstead.fixtures import leavenworth
from netstead.clean import recompute_lengths, simplify_geometry
from corral.editing import Session

net = netstead.read(leavenworth.csv_dir())
with Session(net) as s:
    shape_edit = simplify_geometry(net, s, mode="douglas_peucker", tolerance=0.00001)
    length_edit = recompute_lengths(net, s, geodesic=True)
print(f"simplified {shape_edit.edit.table}; recomputed length on {length_edit.edit.table}")

The CLI does the same; write to a new location so the source stays intact:

netstead clean simplify-geometry <src> --dest <out> --mode douglas_peucker --tolerance 0.00001

When the link table carries an inline geometry column, that column wins (the same priority as assemble_link_geometry). A network with shapes in neither place raises a CleanError that names both.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• threshold_m is in coordinate units, not always meters. The name reflects the common projected case. On a WGS84 (lat/lon) network like Leavenworth the units are degrees — 0.0005 ≈ 56 m. Pass a value in your network’s CRS units, not a string like "2m".
  • merge_close_nodes returns a list, not one EditResult. It touches two tables (node + link), so it returns [node_result, link_result]. The single-table ops (remove_orphans, simplify_geometry, recompute_lengths) return one EditResult.
  • simplify_geometry edits whichever table holds the shapes. Its EditResult targets link when geometry is inline and geometry when it is carried via geometry_id — read result.edit.table rather than assuming link. recompute_lengths always edits link, because that is where length lives (see the variation above).
  • Pass --dest to the CLI ops when the source is a CSV directory. Without it the op writes back over the source as parquet, and that in-place rewrite currently fails partway after the CSVs are gone (tracked as a follow-up). --dry-run is safe either way.
  • OutOfSyncWarning on write is expected after an edit (#164). It means the in-memory FK index still reflects the pre-edit rows; it is not an error. Suppress it for the write (step 6) — re-reading the written network rebuilds the index.
  • A 100%-null column can break the write (#163). Writing an edited table could fail when a column was entirely null. The issue’s original repro (netstead clean remove-orphans on the Leavenworth fixture) now succeeds. If you still hit it, cast the all-null column to a concrete type (or drop it) before the write, and add your case to the issue. The old --engine pandas workaround no longer exists: DuckDB is the only engine since #195.
  • The CLI ops overwrite <src> unless you pass --dest. The write is staged beside the source and swapped in once complete, so a failure leaves the original in place, and a directory source keeps its format (a CSV directory stays CSV). It is still an overwrite, though: there is no undo once the swap has happened. Pass --dest (or run with --dry-run first) to keep the original.
  • Don’t mutate tables outside the session. Direct net.links.expr.execute().assign(...) writes bypass the session entirely and aren’t rollback-able.
  • The session captures snapshots, not journals. Memory cost scales with the size of the tables an op touches; the bulk replace_table path snapshots the whole affected table. Long sessions over large networks should commit periodically.

docs.title: When to use this
docs.text: You want the links of a street, a stretch of a street between two cross streets, every link of a road type, or a handful of link ids, and would rather type it than click it. The same requests work in the Workbench’s Find tab, in netstead select from a terminal, and in Python.

docs.title: Quick example
docs.text:
With the bundled Leavenworth network open in the Workbench (uv run netstead app, then Included examples), type in Find:

Cedar Street between Central Avenue and Price Avenue

Two links (57 and 129) are selected, with no language model involved. From a terminal:

LEAVENWORTH=$(uv run python -c "from netstead.fixtures import leavenworth; print(leavenworth.csv_dir())")
uv run netstead select "Cedar Street between Central Avenue and Price Avenue" "$LEAVENWORTH"

Or in Python:

from netstead import Network
from netstead.fixtures import leavenworth
from netstead.select import StubParser, resolve

net = Network.from_source(leavenworth.csv_dir())
result = resolve(StubParser().parse("Cedar Street between Central Avenue and Price Avenue"), net)
print(result.status, result.link_ids)  # resolved [57, 129]

docs.title: What you can type
docs.text:
These forms are read by netstead’s built-in pattern parser. They work with no language model at all, and with one chosen, they are answered without calling it (see When the model is called).

Form Example (Leavenworth) Selects A street Cedar Street every link named Cedar Street A street and a direction Front Street eastbound (also EB, westbound, NB, SB, …) its links heading within 75° of east A stretch of a street Cedar Street between Central Avenue and Price Avenue, or … from Central Avenue to Price Avenue the shortest path along Cedar Street between the two intersections A route number I-40 EB between South Miami Boulevard and Airport Boulevard (route numbers starting I, US, SR, NC, CR, SH, CA or TX) the same, on a freeway, from the off-ramp to the on-ramp Every link all links the whole network Every link of a type all residential links links whose facility_type is residential Link ids links 57, 129 those links

The direction word goes after the street.

Anything else needs a language model. For example:

Request Why the pattern parser can’t read it bike lanes on Cedar Street a travel mode Cedar Street with 2 lanes an attribute filter northbound Cedar Street the direction comes first the stretch of Cedar near the school free phrasing

To choose a model, see Language models (cloud providers) or Run language models locally with Ollama.

docs.title: How names match
docs.text:
You don’t need to spell a street the way the network does. A name is looked up in this order, and the first rule that finds something wins:

Rule You type Network has Notes Exact cedar street Cedar Street case, spaces and punctuation ignored Abbreviation Cedar St, N Main St Cedar Street, North Main Street street types (St, Ave, Rd, Blvd, Dr, Ln, Ct, Pl, Pkwy, Hwy, …) and directions (N, S, E, W, NE, …) Direction left out Peace Street West Peace Street, East Peace Street selects every side; W Peace St selects only the West side Close spelling Ceder Street, Hilsborough St Cedar Street, Hillsborough Street the closest name at least 85% alike; never for names under 5 letters

Whenever a rule other than the exact one was used, the selection’s diagnostics say so, for example matched 'Ceder Street' to 'Cedar Street' (a close spelling). Cross-street names match the same way.

A route number matches the network’s ref column, so I-40 finds a link whose ref is I 40;US 64. Networks without a ref column (including those netstead build makes from OpenStreetMap today) can only be searched by street name.

docs.title: How a stretch between two cross streets is found
docs.text:
1. Each cross street is placed where it meets the street: an at-grade intersection, or for a freeway, the off-ramp where you leave (the first cross street) and the on-ramp where you join (the second).
  2. The selection is the shortest path along the street between those two nodes.
  3. A street that is partly a freeway (a trunk road with signals, like many US routes through town) tries its at-grade intersections when no ramp connects.
  4. When the street’s own links don’t join the two cross streets, the path may cross the short gaps where its name breaks off: unnamed links (a roundabout, a slip lane) or named links up to 20 m long (a cross street spanning a divided road’s median), within 3 links of the street. Service roads, paths and tracks never count. The diagnostics say how many links were used this way.
  5. If a cross street meets the street at more than one node, the selection is ambiguous: the nearest is used and the others are listed. See Verify a selection to pin one.

docs.title: When the model is called
docs.text:
With a language model chosen, every request is first read by the pattern parser. The model is called only when:

  • the pattern parser can’t read the request at all,
  • it reads it, but a street, cross street, route number or road type in it is not in the network (by the rules in How names match), or
  • its reading selects nothing.

A request answered this way records parsed_by: {"provider": "stub", "mode": "pattern", "grammar_first": true} in the history, so you can tell which requests went to the model.

Ask (the assistant) works the same way. A question the offline assistant reads in full (select Cedar St between Central Ave and Price Ave and color by lanes, filter lanes >= 2, zoom to the selection, save the selection as downtown), naming only streets and columns the network has, is planned without the model. Anything else (color by speed when the column is free_speed, which streets have the most lanes?) goes to the model.

Turn this off to send every request to the model:

# netstead.toml, or ~/.config/netstead/config.toml
[select]
grammar_first = false

docs.title: Performance
docs.text:
Measured on an Apple M3 laptop (16 GB) with an OpenStreetMap Raleigh–Durham roads network (303,000 links) and qwen2.5:7b in Ollama on the same machine, already loaded:

Request Pattern parser Local model (before this release, every request) Hillsborough Street 1 ms 6.7 s Capital Boulevard northbound 8 ms 2.8 s Western Boulevard between Gorman Street and Avent Ferry Road 4 ms 4.1 s all residential links (94,000 links) 32 ms 5.5 s Hillsborough St between Oberlin Rd and Gorman St 16 ms 4.7 s, not found Glenwood Avenue between Peace Street and Wade Avenue 31 ms 13.6 s, not found (two model calls) bike lanes on Hillsborough Street needs the model: 2.1 s 2.7 s
  • The model’s time is almost all generating its answer, about 2–5 s per call for a 7-billion-parameter model on a laptop. The first request after Ollama loads a model also waits for the load: 35–40 s here.
  • Looking up names is fast in both cases. The network’s street names are indexed once per network version (0.16 s for this network) and then each lookup takes well under a millisecond, where the previous release spent 0.2–0.8 s per request re-reading every link’s name.
  • A cloud model skips the load wait but adds a network round trip; we haven’t measured one here.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• An exact name always wins. Leavenworth has both Center Street and West Center Street; Center Street selects only Center Street. Likewise a misspelling that happens to be another street’s real name finds that street, not the one you meant.
  • A close spelling is a guess. When the diagnostics say (a close spelling), check the map.
  • Route numbers need a ref column. Without one, I-40 goes to the model, which can’t find it either.

docs.title: Triage findings, propose fixes, apply them
Triage findings, propose fixes, apply them
When to use this
docs.text:
You ran netstead validate and you have findings to address. You want to triage them visually, propose fixes one at a time without writing Python for each, then apply them deterministically and save. The flow splits cleanly into two halves:

  1. Browser — open the HTML report, click each finding’s “Propose fix” button, accumulate an edit log.
  2. Python — load the log, replay it against your network, save (overwrite or save-as).

The split lets you triage clickwise but always end up with a structured, replay-able record of what changed.

docs.title: Quick example
docs.text:
# 1. Generate the validation report
uv run netstead validate ./my-net --html /tmp/report.html
open /tmp/report.html

In the browser:

  • Each finding marker → click → popup with Propose fix button
  • Click Propose fix → inline editor with the column pre-filled and the current value loaded → enter new value + reason → Add to edit log
  • Bottom-right floating sidebar tracks your edits — Download YAML when done

Then back in Python:

from netstead import Network
from netstead.map.edits import apply_edits, load_edit_log

net = Network.from_source("./my-net")
log = load_edit_log("/path/to/edits-2026-06-30T19-00-00.yaml")
result = apply_edits(net, log)

print(result.summary())                # "12 applied, 2 skipped"
for s in result.skipped:               # inspect anything that didn't apply
    print(s.edit.id, "→", s.reason)

# Save either way — Network.write() takes a destination path. The format is
# inferred from the extension; a bare directory name writes Parquet, so pass
# format="csv" when you want to keep a CSV package.
result.net.write("./my-net", format="csv", overwrite=True)   # overwrite the CSV source
result.net.write("./my-net-v2")                              # new directory, Parquet

docs.title: The edit log shape
docs.text:
The download is a network-wrangler ProjectCard: one card per session, with a top-level changes: array of roadway_property_change entries. Each fix targets a single row via its primary key (not positional row index — PKs survive row reordering and partial reloads):

project: netstead edits 2026-06-30T19:00:00.000Z
tags: [netstead, edit-log]
notes: |
  created_at: 2026-06-30T19:00:00.000Z
  client: netstead.map (browser)
  netstead.note[0]: schema.required: free_speed missing · issue_id=i0 · edit_id=el7f9c3a
changes:
  - roadway_property_change:
      facility:
        links:
          model_link_id: [42]
          ignore_missing: false     # a clicked id (see below for what a missing link 42 does)
      property_changes:
        free_speed:
          existing: 40              # netstead "from" — drift check on apply
          set: 25                   # netstead "to"

Interop with network-wrangler. The file is a schema-valid ProjectCard; you can pipe it into network-wrangler’s own tooling or import it with the project cards plugin. GMNS link_id maps to model_link_id under the facility’s links (node_id to model_node_id under nodes), with ignore_missing: false because the ids were clicked. When a listed link is gone, network-wrangler and the project cards plugin refuse the change; netstead’s own apply_edits skips that edit and reports it in result.skipped (see Pitfalls). Per-cell values live under property_changes.<column>.set with an optional existing drift check. A change cannot carry its own notes, so each fix’s reason, issue id and edit id are one netstead.note[<i>]: line of the card’s notes, where <i> is the change’s position in changes. load_edit_log still reads logs written before this shape (ids at the top of the facility, a notes on each change).

existing: is the value the browser-side editor thought was there when you proposed the fix. apply_edits uses it for a drift check — if the table’s current value differs, the edit is skipped (with a reason) rather than silently clobbering a concurrent change. Omit existing: (or send null) to disable the check.

docs.title: Variations
docs.text:
Pass the log to a colleague (review workflow)

Don’t apply anything locally. Download the YAML, email it (or open a PR with it). They run apply_edits against their copy of the network when they’re ready.

Replay against a newer version of the same network

The vendor sent you v2 of the network. Run apply_edits(v2_net, log) — every edit whose PK still exists and whose existing: still matches applies cleanly. Anything that drifted shows up in result.skipped with a precise reason.

Bulk fixes from Python

Edit is a plain dataclass — build a list[Edit] programmatically (“every residential link with free_speed > 25 should be set to 25”), wrap it in an EditLog, and apply with the same apply_edits path. No browser needed. pk is a dict of primary-key columns, to_value the new cell value; from_value is optional and turns on the drift check.

import netstead
from netstead.fixtures import leavenworth
from netstead.map.edits import Edit, EditLog, apply_edits

net = netstead.read(leavenworth.csv_dir())
links = net.links.to_pandas()
too_fast = links[(links.facility_type == "residential") & (links.free_speed > 25)].link_id

edits = [
    Edit(id=f"cap-{lid}", kind="fix", table="link", pk={"link_id": int(lid)},
         column="free_speed", to_value=25.0, reason="residential cap")
    for lid in too_fast
]
result = apply_edits(net, EditLog(edits=edits))
print(result.summary())   # "271 applied, 0 skipped" on Leavenworth
Clear the log mid-session

The browser persists edits in sessionStorage. A page refresh keeps them. The sidebar’s Clear button drops them (with a confirm prompt).

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• The browser-side log is per-session. It lives in sessionStorage, so opening the report in a different tab gives you a fresh log. Always Download YAML before closing the tab if you want to keep the work.
  • Edits identify rows by PK, not row index. That’s deliberate — row index isn’t stable across reloads. If your edit log targets facility: {links: {model_link_id: [42], ignore_missing: false}} and link_id 42 no longer exists in the destination network, apply_edits skips that edit and reports it in result.skipped as pk {'link_id': 42} not found in 'link' (whatever ignore_missing says). network-wrangler and the project cards plugin follow ignore_missing: false and refuse the change instead.
  • Drift checks compare values pre-cast. When the source column is a number, the editor coerces the new value to a number too. When in doubt, look at the YAML — existing: 40 vs existing: '40' matter for the strict drift check (only null and NaN are treated as the same “missing” value).

docs.title: Run language models locally with Ollama
Run language models locally with Ollama
When to use this
docs.text: You want natural-language selection (“I-40 EB between South Miami Boulevard and Airport Boulevard”) without sending anything to a cloud provider and without an API key. Ollama runs open models such as Qwen on your own computer, and netstead talks to it over http://localhost:11434.

docs.title: Why local
docs.text:
• Nothing leaves your machine. Your utterances, street names and project notes go to a server on localhost, not to a vendor.
  • Better answers by default — in the Workbench. Because nothing leaves the machine, the "auto" quality settings turn on for a local endpoint there: grounding (the network’s street names and route numbers), project notes (NETSTEAD.md) and the close-match retry. See What is sent, and quality settings. The CLI’s netstead select sends only your utterance to the parser, with none of that extra context, whichever provider you choose.
  • No API key. There is nothing to store or rotate.

The trade-off is that a small local model is slower than a hosted one on most laptops, and makes more mistakes. See Troubleshooting.

docs.title: Install Ollama
docs.text:
Use the installer for your system from ollama.com/download. The commands below come from Ollama’s own download page and docs; if they have moved on, follow ollama.com instead.

macOSLinuxWindows

Download the app from ollama.com/download, open the .dmg and drag Ollama into Applications. Ollama’s docs list macOS 14 Sonoma or newer. When the app first starts, it offers to put the ollama command on your PATH.

Ollama’s download page also offers the same install script as Linux. A Homebrew formula exists too, but it is community-maintained and isn’t covered by Ollama’s docs; the app is the supported route.

Ollama’s install script:

curl -fsSL https://ollama.com/install.sh | sh

Piping a script into sh runs it with your permissions. Download it and read it first if you prefer:

curl -fsSL https://ollama.com/install.sh -o ollama-install.sh
less ollama-install.sh
sh ollama-install.sh

Ollama’s Linux docs also describe a manual install from a tarball.

Download and run OllamaSetup.exe from ollama.com/download. It installs for your account without administrator rights. Ollama’s docs list Windows 10 22H2 or newer. The download page also shows a PowerShell one-liner.

docs.title: Start it, then check it
docs.text:
• macOS and Windows: open the Ollama app. It runs the server in the background (on Windows, from the system tray).
  • Linux: the install script normally sets Ollama up as a service. If it isn’t running, start it with sudo systemctl start ollama, or run ollama serve in a terminal and leave it open.

By default the server listens on 127.0.0.1 port 11434, which is also netstead’s default llm.ollama.base_url. Then check each layer:

ollama list                    # Ollama answers, and shows the models you have (none yet is fine)
uv run netstead llm status       # netstead can reach it; prints the next step if it can't
uv run netstead llm test ollama  # a token-free connection test

If Ollama is reachable but has no models, netstead llm status says next step: run: netstead llm pull qwen3:4b. Once it has a model, the Ollama line names the model selections will use, e.g. running, 1 model(s); selections use qwen2.5:7b (qwen3:4b is not installed), and netstead llm test ollama says the same.

docs.title: Get a model
docs.text:
Already have a model? You may not need to download anything. When you haven’t chosen a model and the default (qwen3:4b) isn’t installed, netstead uses an installed one instead: the first model from the table below that you have (in table order), else the first installed model that Ollama reports as supporting tools. For example, if you only have qwen2.5:7b, the Workbench and netstead select --provider ollama use it as is. A model you chose yourself (--model, select.model, or the picker) is never replaced. If no installed model supports tools, netstead asks you to pull the default.

Otherwise, pull the default, Qwen 3 4B (qwen3:4b). Any one of these does the same thing:

  • In a terminal, with Ollama’s own command:

    ollama pull qwen3:4b

  • In a terminal, through netstead. It shows the size and asks before downloading (--yes skips the question), then shows a progress bar:

    uv run netstead llm pull qwen3:4b

  • In the Workbench: open Models…. On the Ollama row, choose a model and click Pull qwen3:4b. Progress shows in the Jobs panel, where you can cancel it. When the pull finishes, the model appears in the picker. With models already installed, use Pull another model.

Model Download When to choose it qwen3:4b (default) about 2.5 GB Most laptops. Enough for one selection at a time. qwen3:8b about 5.2 GB When qwen3:4b keeps misreading your phrases, and you have the memory to spare. Slower. qwen2.5:7b about 4.7 GB If you already have it installed, it works: no need to pull another model.

Sizes are the download sizes listed on ollama.com/library/qwen3 and ollama.com/library/qwen2.5 (checked 2026-10-05). Both library pages mark the models as supporting tools, which netstead uses. Ollama doesn’t publish memory requirements per model. As a rough guide, you need at least the download size free in memory, plus some overhead, to run a model comfortably. If your machine starts swapping, use the smaller model.

The Workbench only pulls into an Ollama on this machine, and only when the Workbench itself is bound to this machine (the default, 127.0.0.1). Otherwise, pull from a terminal.

docs.title: Use it in the Workbench
docs.text:
1. Start the Workbench: uv run netstead app ./my-network.
  2. Choose Ollama (local) in the provider picker next to the utterance box, then pick a model. The picker lists the models Ollama has installed, and starts on the model selections will use. If that isn’t the default because the default isn’t installed, hovering over the model says so.
  3. That choice applies to this session. Click Make default to save it to your user config.

Common requests (“Cedar St between Central Ave and Price Ave”, “all residential links”) are answered by the offline pattern parser without calling the model; the model is called for the rest. A local 7B model takes a few seconds per call on a laptop, plus the time to load it into memory on the first call (timings).

Or set it in a config file:

# ~/.config/netstead/config.toml (or ./netstead.toml for one project)
[select]
provider = "ollama"
model = "qwen3:4b"

From a terminal:

uv run netstead select "I-40 EB between South Miami Boulevard and Airport Boulevard" ./my-network --provider ollama --model qwen3:4b

Without --model (and with no select.model set), netstead select uses the model netstead llm status names.

docs.title: Ollama on another machine
docs.text:
A GPU workstation on your network can run the model for everyone. Point netstead at it, either in Models… → Ollama server or in the config file:

[llm.ollama]
base_url = "http://gpu-box.example:11434"

An address that isn’t this machine counts as remote: your utterances now leave your computer. So the "auto" quality settings turn off, the same as for a cloud provider, and the Workbench won’t pull models there (run ollama pull on that server). If you trust that server with your network’s street names and project notes, opt back in:

[llm.quality]
grounding = "on"        # send street names and route numbers
project_context = "on"  # send NETSTEAD.md / the ## netstead section
match_retry = "on"      # after a miss, retry with the closest real names

Ollama only listens on 127.0.0.1 unless it is told otherwise. Ollama’s FAQ explains how to expose it with OLLAMA_HOST.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
“could not reach Ollama at http://localhost:11434” / connection refused. Ollama isn’t running, or isn’t installed. Open the app (macOS/Windows), or run ollama serve (Linux), then uv run netstead llm test ollama. In the Workbench, click Check again. If you changed llm.ollama.base_url, check the address and port.

“model not found” / the model shows “(not installed)”. Pull it: ollama pull qwen3:4b, uv run netstead llm pull qwen3:4b, or Pull in the Workbench. Model names must match what ollama list prints, including the tag after the colon.

Slow answers. Without a supported GPU, Ollama runs on the CPU, and each selection can take many seconds. ollama ps shows whether a loaded model is on the GPU or CPU. Use qwen3:4b rather than a larger model. If requests time out, raise llm.ollama.timeout_s (default 120 seconds).

A model without tool support. netstead asks for a tool call first. If Ollama answers that the model “does not support tools”, netstead automatically retries the same model in JSON mode, constrained to the same schema. You don’t need to do anything.

More misreadings than a hosted model. Small models make more mistakes. Try, in order:

  1. Keep llm.quality.temperature at its default, 0. In our tests qwen2.5:7b read every one of a set of varied requests correctly at temperature 0, and misread a few street names as route numbers at Ollama’s own default temperature. When that happens and the “route number” matches no route in your network, netstead looks it up as a street name instead, and the selection’s diagnostics say so (treated ref 'Capital Blvd' as a street name). It does the same for a route number read as a street name. A value that does match its own column is used as is.

  2. Give the model another attempt after an invalid reply:

    [llm.quality]
max_repairs = 2

  3. Switch to qwen3:8b.

  4. Add a NETSTEAD.md with your local names (“the Beltline” is I 440). See Project notes.

docs.title: When to use this
docs.text: You want to ask questions that span tables (“which lanes sit on links faster than 45 mph?”) and make targeted edits (“set every residential link to 25 mph”) — the bread-and-butter of network analysis and the kind of thing Network Wrangler does. This page covers both: querying across foreign keys, looking at results without materializing a DataFrame you don’t need, and editing rows with an undo log.

docs.title: Quick example
docs.text:
Every table exposes a lazy ibis expression via .expr. Join two tables on their foreign key, filter, and look at the result — all lazy until the last line.

import netstead
from netstead.fixtures import leavenworth

net = netstead.read(leavenworth.csv_dir())
link = net.tables["link"].expr
lane = net.tables["lane"].expr

# "Which lanes sit on links faster than 45 mph?"  (lane.link_id → link.link_id)
fast_lanes = lane.join(
    link.filter(link.free_speed > 45),
    lane.link_id == link.link_id,
)
print(f"{fast_lanes.count().execute()} lanes on links over 45 mph")

docs.title: 1. The foreign-key map
docs.text:
The bundled Leavenworth fixture wires its tables together like this:

node ──< link >── node        link.from_node_id / to_node_id → node.node_id
         │
         ├──< lane             lane.link_id → link.link_id
         ├──< link_tod         link_tod.link_id → link.link_id
         └──< geometry         link.geometry_id → geometry.geometry_id

A join is just child.join(parent, child.fk == parent.pk). Reach the lazy expression with net.tables["link"].expr (or the named accessor’s .expr — net.links.expr).

docs.title: 2. Build the query — it stays lazy
docs.text:
.filter, .join, .select, .group_by, .order_by all add to a query plan. Nothing touches data until you call a terminal method. So you can compose as deep as you like for free — the whole chain compiles to a single DuckDB SQL statement:

import netstead
from netstead.fixtures import leavenworth

net = netstead.read(leavenworth.csv_dir())
link = net.tables["link"].expr
lane = net.tables["lane"].expr

q = (
    lane.join(link.filter(link.free_speed > 45), lane.link_id == link.link_id)
        .select("lane_id", "link_id", "lane_num", "width", "free_speed", "facility_type")
        .order_by("link_id", "lane_num")
)
# `q` is still just a plan — no data has been read yet.

docs.title: 3. Look at it interactively — no pandas needed
docs.text:
Turn on ibis interactive mode once per session and just evaluate the expression. It renders a rich table (via Arrow, not pandas); .head(n) pushes a LIMIT so DuckDB only returns those rows:

import ibis
import netstead
from netstead.fixtures import leavenworth

net = netstead.read(leavenworth.csv_dir())
link = net.tables["link"].expr
lane = net.tables["lane"].expr
q = lane.join(link.filter(link.free_speed > 45), lane.link_id == link.link_id)

ibis.options.interactive = True     # set once per session/notebook
print(q.head(5))                    # DuckDB runs LIMIT 5; renders a table

In a Jupyter notebook the same expression renders as an HTML table — no print, no .to_pandas(). Interactive mode is a global, session-wide switch; in a notebook you set it once at the top and leave it on.

docs.title: 4. Materialize only when you hand the result to other code
docs.text:
.execute() runs the query at any point. Pick the container that fits what comes next — you rarely need pandas:

n      = q.count().execute()       # Python int  — DuckDB COUNT(*), builds no table
arrow  = q.to_pyarrow()            # pa.Table     — zero-copy, no pandas dependency
# polars_df = q.to_polars()        # pl.DataFrame — if polars is your downstream
df     = q.to_pandas()             # pd.DataFrame — for plotting / sklearn / .describe()

.execute() is always available — call it the moment you want values, skip it while you’re still composing. Reach for .to_pandas() only when something downstream actually wants a pandas frame.

docs.title: 5. See the SQL (or drop to raw DuckDB)
docs.text:
To understand why a query is fast or slow, print the compiled SQL:

print(ibis.to_sql(q))   # the exact DuckDB SELECT ... JOIN ... WHERE ...

The predicate pushes down to DuckDB, so a bbox or facility-type filter on a partitioned-Parquet source prunes partitions before reading.

docs.title: 6. Update rows — Network-Wrangler style, with rollback
docs.text:
Edits go through a Session: every change is recorded with a before/after diff and an undo record, so a failed batch leaves the network untouched. The four ops are add_rows, update_rows, delete_rows, and replace_table.

The predicate for update_rows / delete_rows is a callable (table) -> boolean column — it’s re-applied against the table inside the edit, so write it as a lambda:

import netstead
from netstead.fixtures import leavenworth
from corral.editing import Session, Edit

net = netstead.read(leavenworth.csv_dir())

# "Set every residential link to 25 mph."
with Session(net) as s:
    result = s.add_edit(
        Edit(
            op="update_rows",
            table="link",
            payload={
                "predicate": lambda t: t.facility_type == "residential",
                "set": {"free_speed": 25.0},
            },
        )
    )

print(f"{result.diff.rows_changed} links updated")

# The network now reflects the change — re-query to confirm:
link = net.tables["link"].expr
still_40 = link.filter((link.facility_type == "residential") & (link.free_speed == 40.0))
print(f"residential links still at 40 mph: {still_40.count().execute()}")

result.diff carries rows_added / rows_removed / rows_changed plus capped before/after samples, and result.applied_at / result.session_id for the audit trail.

docs.title: 7. Undo a change
docs.text:
Call session.rollback() to reverse every edit applied in that session — useful when an edit didn’t do what you expected, or you’re exploring “what if”:

import netstead
from netstead.fixtures import leavenworth
from corral.editing import Session, Edit

net = netstead.read(leavenworth.csv_dir())
print(f"before: {net.tables['link'].count()} links")

with Session(net) as s:
    s.add_edit(Edit(op="delete_rows", table="link",
                    payload={"predicate": lambda t: t.facility_type == "primary"}))
    print(f"after delete: {net.tables['link'].count()} links")
    s.rollback()

print(f"after rollback: {net.tables['link'].count()} links")

A Session(net, log_path="edits.parquet") persists the audit log to disk alongside the network so the history survives the process.

docs.title: Common variations
docs.text:
Default — join, filter, count

The most common shape: join across the FK, filter the parent, count the survivors.

lane.join(link.filter(link.free_speed > 45), lane.link_id == link.link_id).count().execute()
Aggregate across a join

Group-by on a joined expression — e.g. average lane width per facility type.

joined = lane.join(link, lane.link_id == link.link_id)
joined.group_by(link.facility_type).aggregate(avg_width=lane.width.mean()).execute()
Two-hop traversal (lane → link → node)

Chain joins to reach a grandparent table — e.g. lanes on links that depart a 4-way stop.

node = net.tables["node"].expr
stop4 = node.filter(node.ctrl_type == "stop_4_way")
links_at_stop4 = link.join(stop4, link.from_node_id == stop4.node_id).select("link_id")
lane.join(links_at_stop4, lane.link_id == links_at_stop4.link_id).count().execute()
Add rows

add_rows appends; the payload is a list of dicts matching the table schema.

with Session(net) as s:
    s.add_edit(Edit(op="add_rows", table="node",
                    payload={"rows": [{"node_id": 9001, "x_coord": -120.66, "y_coord": 47.59}]}))
Higher-level cleanup ops

For geometry-aware edits (simplify, merge close nodes, drop orphans) use the netstead.clean helpers, which wrap these primitives with domain logic — see Edit with rollback.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• update_rows / delete_rows predicates are callables, not expressions. Write lambda t: t.col == x, not link.col == x. The edit re-applies the predicate against the table’s own expression.
  • Joins need the .expr, not the Table wrapper. net.links is the convenience wrapper (.count(), .columns(), .to_pandas()); net.links.expr (or net.tables["link"].expr) is the ibis expression you join + filter on.
  • A filter on a table with no geometry column silently returns everything for spatial predicates. For from_bbox-style spatial filters, run them on the table that actually carries the WKT (in Leavenworth that’s geometry, not link).
  • Materialize once, at the end. Calling .to_pandas() mid-chain forces a DuckDB→Arrow→pandas round-trip and then re-wraps for the next step. Compose lazily; execute last.

docs.text:

docs.title: When to use this
docs.text: You want a fast read on how netstead performs on your hardware against your network — sizing a server, comparing hardware or storage formats, or tracking CI regressions over time.

docs.title: Quick example
docs.text:
Run the bench against the bundled Leavenworth fixture. Add --json to any netstead (or corral) CLI command and the output becomes a single machine-readable JSON document on stdout — pipe into jq, save to a file, feed to a script or AI agent. Default output is human-readable rich panels:

netstead bench packages/netstead/netstead/fixtures/leavenworth/csv --json

Expected:

{
  "source": "packages/netstead/netstead/fixtures/leavenworth/csv",
  "engine": "IbisEngine",
  "total_seconds": "...",
  "phases": [
    {"phase": "load",         "seconds": "..."},
    {"phase": "validate",     "seconds": "..."},
    {"phase": "links_count",  "seconds": "..."},
    {"phase": "nodes_count",  "seconds": "..."},
    {"phase": "is_connected", "seconds": "..."}
  ]
}

The "..." values are timings in seconds (floats such as 0.112); they vary by machine and run, so they’re elided here.

docs.title: 1. Run against the bundled reference
docs.text:
The Leavenworth fixture is small (339 links / 121 nodes) — total runtime is under a second. It’s a baseline, not a benchmark; useful for confirming nothing’s wrong with the install:

netstead bench packages/netstead/netstead/fixtures/leavenworth/csv

docs.title: 2. Run against your own network
docs.text:
Same command, different path. The bench accepts the same source surface as Network.from_source — local dirs, s3://, duckdb://, etc.:

netstead bench /path/to/my/network --json > bench.json

docs.title: 3. Compare storage formats
docs.text:
DuckDB (via ibis) is the single compute engine, so there is no engine to sweep — --engine is accepted only for compatibility. What does move the numbers is the on-disk format you load from. Convert the same network to CSV and Parquet and bench each:

netstead bench /path/to/net-csv --json > csv.json
netstead bench /path/to/net-parquet --json > parquet.json

docs.title: 4. Capture a baseline for CI
docs.text:
For regression tracking, save a baseline JSON in-repo and compare on every PR. A 30% tolerance is reasonable for the Leavenworth fixture given timing noise; tighten on larger networks:

netstead bench packages/netstead/netstead/fixtures/leavenworth/csv --json > bench-baseline.json
# in CI:
netstead bench packages/netstead/netstead/fixtures/leavenworth/csv --json > bench-current.json
python -c "
import json
b = json.load(open('bench-baseline.json'))['total_seconds']
c = json.load(open('bench-current.json'))['total_seconds']
assert c < b * 1.3, f'regression: {c:.2f}s vs baseline {b:.2f}s (+{(c/b-1)*100:.0f}%)'
"

docs.title: 5. Read the JSON
docs.text:
The shape is stable inside a major version. Each phase is one logical operation: load opens the package; validate runs the structural + schema passes only (net.validate(foreign_keys=False, sync_state=False) — no FK or sync-state checks); links_count / nodes_count force a count on each table; is_connected builds the scipy GMNSGraph and checks that there is a single weakly-connected component:

{
  "source": "packages/netstead/netstead/fixtures/leavenworth/csv",
  "engine": "IbisEngine",
  "total_seconds": 0.555,
  "phases": [
    {"phase": "load",         "seconds": 0.112},
    {"phase": "validate",     "seconds": 0.130},
    {"phase": "links_count",  "seconds": 0.002},
    {"phase": "nodes_count",  "seconds": 0.001},
    {"phase": "is_connected", "seconds": 0.309}
  ]
}

docs.title: Common variations
docs.text:
Default — Leavenworth fixture, JSON out

Quickest smoke-test that the install works and the engine is wired up.

netstead bench packages/netstead/netstead/fixtures/leavenworth/csv --json
Just the total seconds (for shell pipelines)

Pipe through jq to extract a single number.

netstead bench ./my-net --json | jq -r .total_seconds
Phase breakdown as CSV

For charting or copying into a spreadsheet.

netstead bench ./my-net --json | jq -r '.phases[] | [.phase,.seconds] | @csv'
CI regression check (one-liner)

Fails the CI step if the total exceeds your budget.

netstead bench ./my-net --json | jq -e '.total_seconds < 5.0'
Format sweep

Loop over copies of the same network in different storage formats.

for d in ./my-net-csv ./my-net-parquet; do
  netstead bench "$d" --json > "bench-$(basename "$d").json"
done

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• Micro-network timing is noisy. On Leavenworth the absolute numbers fluctuate by ±30% between runs. Use it to confirm correctness, not for sizing decisions — switch to a regional-scale network before drawing conclusions.
  • Every CLI run is a cold start. Each netstead bench invocation is a fresh process, so the is_connected phase always includes building the scipy GMNSGraph — there is no cache to warm by running the command twice. The graph is cached on the Network object only within one Python process (a second is_connected(net) call on the same object is faster).
  • Connectivity requires [graph]. Without scipy the is_connected phase is skipped and reported as {"phase": "is_connected", "seconds": null, "skipped": "scipy not installed"}; total_seconds sums the phases that ran. Data-quality rules are not part of netstead bench.

docs.title: Run the benchmark suite (netstead bench-suite)
docs.text:
netstead bench times one network end to end. netstead bench-suite sweeps size tiers over three operation families — network_create (load the fixture from each committed storage format, with row counts asserted as a correctness check), selection (resolve the versioned natural-language selection cases through the stub parser, cold and warm) and viz_pack (pack the network into the browser payload, timing plus byte counts) — and emits one structured document with wall time and peak memory per case. It needs the [bench] extra (psutil, for process RSS); the selection family also wants [nl] and returns nothing without it, and live OSM builds want [osm]:

pip install 'netstead[bench]'
netstead bench-suite --sizes S,M --format md --output bench.md
Flag Default Meaning --sizes S,M Size tiers to sweep, comma-separated from S, M, L. --operations network_create,selection,viz_pack Operation families to run, comma-separated. --format json json (the canonical regression document), csv (flattened results) or md (a table with an environment stamp). --output / -o stdout Write the rendered document to this file. --repeats 3 Macro timing repeats (reported as median + min). --warm-repeats 20 Repeats for the warm selection number. --run-osm off Include live OSM builds (hits Overpass). --fixtures benchmarks/fixtures.toml Override the fixture registry file. --commit — Git SHA to stamp into the environment block.

Fixture definitions live in benchmarks/fixtures.toml at the repo root (a built-in default covering the bundled fixtures is used when the file isn’t found). The S tier (Leavenworth, 339 links) and M tier (rdu_i40) ship inside the wheel. The L tier is never committed: point NETSTEAD_BENCH_LARGE at a GMNS package directory or a .duckdb file, or set NETSTEAD_BENCH_LARGE_BBOX="west,south,east,north" and pass --run-osm to build it live from OpenStreetMap:

export NETSTEAD_BENCH_LARGE=/path/to/large-network
netstead bench-suite --sizes S,M,L --format json --output bench.json

docs.title: Bench the OSM build path (scripts/bench_osm_build.py)
docs.text:
A separate harness measures the construction of a network from OpenStreetMap (convert + Network assembly on the DuckDB engine) and, optionally, compares it against osmnx and osm2gmns as directional baselines. It lives at scripts/bench_osm_build.py. Examples:

# Synthetic grids (no network I/O — reproducible, fast).
uv run python scripts/bench_osm_build.py --grids 10,40,100

# Real bbox (one Overpass fetch, reused by the netstead build + the osmnx baseline).
uv run python scripts/bench_osm_build.py --bbox=-120.6794,47.5751,-120.6411,47.6082 --baselines

Representative numbers (M1 / macOS; absolute numbers are noisy ±30%). The first dataset in a run also pays one-time import / DuckDB warm-up, so treat it as a cold-start figure:

Dataset tool build peak mem result (nodes / links) grid 10×10 (100 nodes / 20 ways) netstead 0.17 s 2.6 MB 100 / 360 grid 40×40 (1.6k nodes / 80 ways) netstead 0.05 s 1.2 MB 1600 / 6240 grid 100×100 (10k nodes / 200 ways) netstead 0.08 s 5.3 MB 10000 / 39600 Leavenworth bbox (8.5k OSM nodes → 1.9k GMNS nodes / 4.3k directed links) netstead 0.13 s 2.6 MB 1871 / 4250 Leavenworth bbox (same area) osmnx 1.11 s 20.3 MB 1871 / ~4250 (directional)

Takeaways:

  • The osmnx baseline is intentionally directional, not apples-to-apples — osmnx performs its own simplification and uses a different directed-link convention. Use it as a sanity check that we’re in the same order of magnitude, not as a strict speed comparison.
  • The osm2gmns baseline needs a local --osm-file and a C/C++ toolchain to install; when it is missing, the harness prints the install command and skips that baseline cleanly.
  • There is no engine axis: DuckDB (via ibis) is the single compute engine. For the broader create / selection / viz-pack timing suite, use netstead bench-suite.
