docs.text:
• Convert CSV ↔ Parquet ↔ DuckDB — the format you load from dominates load time.
  • API reference — Network.from_source() + .validate() for programmatic equivalents. The timing harness is also importable: netstead.bench exports the capture primitives (time_call, memory_call, repeat_wall_seconds, …) and report renderers (build_document, render_json / render_csv / render_markdown), and netstead.bench.suite.run_suite(...) runs the same suite as netstead bench-suite.

docs.title: Build a scope from seed nodes
Build a scope from seed nodes
When to use this
docs.text: You have a list of node ids (e.g. study-area boundary nodes, signalised intersections, a corridor’s endpoints) and want the subgraph that connects them — every link on a shortest path, every dependent lane / link_tod / signal_* row, with foreign keys pre-filtered.

docs.title: Quick example
docs.text:
Build a scope from three seed nodes. With path_between=True (the default), BFS shortest paths between every pair of seeds determine what’s included; .apply() materializes the result as a normal Network:

from netstead import Network
from netstead.fixtures import leavenworth
from netstead.scope import from_nodes

net = Network.from_source(leavenworth.csv_dir())
sub = from_nodes(net, [1, 25, 50], path_between=True).apply()
print(f"scoped: {sub.links.count()} links, {sub.nodes.count()} nodes")

Expected:

scoped: 28 links, 14 nodes

The scope from seed nodes 1, 25, and 50. Shortest paths between the seeds determine which interior links are kept; every dependent lane, link_tod, and signal row is FK-filtered automatically.

docs.title: 1. Install the [graph] extra
docs.text:
from_nodes walks the network through a scipy sparse-graph index (netstead.graph.GMNSGraph); scipy ships in the [graph] extra. Without it the first scope call raises ImportError: netstead.graph requires the [graph] extra: pip install 'netstead[graph]':

pip install 'netstead[graph]'

docs.title: 2. Decide path_between=True vs False
docs.text:
• path_between=True (default) — runs BFS shortest paths between every pair of seed nodes and includes all nodes + links on those paths. Gives you the connected subgraph containing the seeds.
  • path_between=False — keeps just the seed nodes and their incident links. Useful when the seeds already describe a closed region and you don’t want extra interior links.

docs.title: 3. Build the scope (lazy)
docs.text:
A NetworkScope is a description of which rows belong to the subset, not the subset itself. scope.provenance records how it was built (operation, seeds, parameters) for audit / debugging:

import netstead
from netstead.fixtures import leavenworth
from netstead.scope import from_nodes

net = netstead.read(leavenworth.csv_dir())
scope = from_nodes(net, [1, 25, 50], path_between=True)

print(f"nodes in scope:    {len(scope.node_ids)}")
print(f"links in scope:    {len(scope.link_ids)}")
print(f"provenance:        {scope.provenance}")   # str describing the op

docs.title: 4. Apply to materialize a sub-network
docs.text:
.apply() returns a normal Network you can validate, run quality checks on, or write out. Every table is pre-filtered by FK chain — lane rows whose link_id isn’t in scope are dropped, signal rows for missing controllers are dropped, etc. A table the scope empties entirely (e.g. signal_controller when no signals fall in the subgraph) survives as a zero-row table with its schema intact:

import netstead
from netstead.fixtures import leavenworth
from netstead.scope import from_nodes

net = netstead.read(leavenworth.csv_dir())
scope = from_nodes(net, [1, 25, 50], path_between=True)

# Every table is FK-filtered to the scope:
#   link / node    — only ids in scope.link_ids / scope.node_ids
#   lane, link_tod — only rows whose link_id is in scope
#   geometry       — only ids referenced by surviving links
sub = scope.apply()
print(f"{sub.links.count()} links, {sub.nodes.count()} nodes")

docs.title: 5. Chain with set ops + buffers
docs.text:
Scopes compose with union / intersect / subtract and with network / spatial buffering. Build a corridor scope, union it with a second scope, then add a 100 m network buffer — all in one expression:

import netstead
from netstead.fixtures import leavenworth
from netstead.scope import from_nodes

net = netstead.read(leavenworth.csv_dir())
corridor = from_nodes(net, [1, 25, 50])
downtown = from_nodes(net, [10, 11, 12])

combined = corridor.union(downtown).buffer_network("100m")
# .intersect(other) and .subtract(other) compose the same way.
# .buffer_spatial(distance) buffers by straight-line distance in the geometry
# column's CRS units; it needs an inline link.geometry column and is a silent
# no-op on Leavenworth, which has none.
sub = combined.apply()
print(f"combined scope: {sub.links.count()} links, {sub.nodes.count()} nodes")

Expected:

combined scope: 58 links, 24 nodes

docs.title: 6. CLI equivalent
docs.text:
The same operation runs from the shell. Add --json to any netstead (or corral) CLI command and the output becomes a single machine-readable JSON document on stdout — pipe into jq, save to a file, feed to a script or AI agent. Default output is human-readable rich panels:

netstead scope from-nodes packages/netstead/netstead/fixtures/leavenworth/csv 1 25 50 --json

Expected:

{
  "node_count": 14,
  "link_count": 28,
  "node_ids": [1, 2, 3, 10, 11, 15, 25, 50, 63, 74, 78, 96, 99, 100],
  "link_ids": [1, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 27, 29, 30, 31, 34, 44, 46, 77, 79, 160, 196, 197, 225, 226, 238, 239, 283, 284, 290, 292, 293, 295],
  "provenance": "from_nodes([1, 25, 50], path_between=True)"
}

Every id in node_ids and link_ids is a plain integer.

docs.title: Common variations
docs.text:
Default — multi-node BFS with path_between

Most common pattern: a handful of seed ids, paths between them filled in automatically.

sub = from_nodes(net, [1, 25, 50], path_between=True).apply()
Single seed with a network-distance buffer

Expands outward from one node along network edges up to a budget.

from netstead.scope import from_node
sub = from_node(net, 1, network_buffer="200m").apply()
Single link with a network or spatial buffer

Useful for corridor studies. Pass exactly one of network_buffer (graph distance along link.length, metres or a string like "200m") or spatial_buffer_m (straight-line distance in the geometry column’s CRS units — degrees on an EPSG:4326 network, despite the name). The network form works on Leavenworth:

from netstead.scope import from_link
sub = from_link(net, 42, network_buffer="200m").apply()

The spatial form needs an inline link.geometry column. Leavenworth keeps its shapes in the geometry table, so this raises ScopeError: from_link(spatial_buffer_m=...) requires a geometry column on links.:

sub = from_link(net, 42, spatial_buffer_m=0.001).apply()   # ~100 m in degrees

Point with a spatial buffer

Scope = every link within spatial_buffer_m of an (x, y) point, in the geometry column’s CRS units. Like the spatial from_link, it needs an inline link.geometry column and raises ScopeError: from_point requires a geometry column on links. on Leavenworth:

from netstead.scope import from_point
sub = from_point(net, (-120.66, 47.59), spatial_buffer_m=0.005).apply()   # ~500 m in degrees

Whole connected component

Drops everything not reachable from the seed via the graph.

from netstead.scope import connected_component
sub = connected_component(net, seed_node_id=1).apply()
Nodes tagged with a zone id

from_zone keeps every node whose node.zone_id is in the list, plus the links between those nodes. It is an attribute filter, not a polygon scope, and it requires a zone_id column on the node table — Leavenworth has none, so this raises ScopeError: from_zone requires a 'zone_id' column on the node table.:

from netstead.scope import from_zone
sub = from_zone(net, [12]).apply()

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• Auto-build threshold. The scipy GMNSGraph is built on the first scope call and cached on the network. On networks above 50k nodes that first call logs an INFO notice (auto-building graph index over N nodes) because the build can take a few seconds. Pre-build with net.build_indexes(graph=True) to control timing, or raise the bar with NETSTEAD_AUTO_INDEX_THRESHOLD=200000.
  • scipy is in [graph]. On a pure pip install netstead the first scope call raises ImportError: netstead.graph requires the [graph] extra: pip install 'netstead[graph]'.
  • path_between=True is O(seeds²) in shortest-path calls. For 100s of seeds, prefer an attribute scope (from_zone) or the generic bounding-box scope, or build the graph index first.
  • Spatial scope (from_point, from_link(spatial_buffer_m=…), buffer_spatial) needs an inline geometry column on links, and the _m parameters are in the geometry column’s CRS units — degrees on an EPSG:4326 network, not metres. Leavenworth carries geometry in a separate geometry table via link.geometry_id, so from_point / from_link(spatial_buffer_m=…) raise ScopeError and buffer_spatial is a no-op. netstead.semantics.assemble_link_geometry(net) resolves each link’s shape into a (link_id, geometry, source) table, but nothing in netstead writes that back onto link.geometry for you. Network buffers (buffer_network, from_link(network_buffer=…)) work straight off the FK graph — no geometry needed.

docs.text:

  • API reference — netstead.scope.from_nodes, Scope.apply, Scope.union, …

docs.title: When to use this
docs.text: You want HTTP access to your GMNS networks — for dashboards, non-Python consumers, or a small team sharing a single curated set of packages. The server is read-only: it serves metadata, the resolved spec, validation reports and quality reports, never edits.

docs.title: Quick example
docs.text:
Write a minimal config that binds localhost on port 8000, requires a bearer token, and exposes one package. Start it with netstead server run:

# server.yaml
bind: 127.0.0.1
port: 8000
auth:
  kind: bearer
  token: "paste-the-output-of-generate_dev_token-here"
packages:
  - id: leavenworth
    source: packages/netstead/netstead/fixtures/leavenworth/csv

netstead server run --config server.yaml

Expected:

INFO:     Uvicorn running on http://127.0.0.1:8000

Interactive OpenAPI at /docs — every endpoint with try-it-out forms and the JSON response schema.

docs.title: 1. Install the [server] extra
docs.text:
[server] brings in FastAPI, uvicorn and pydantic-settings. Add [graph] as well if you want /networks/{id}/quality — the GMNS rule pack’s connectivity rule needs scipy:

pip install 'netstead[server,graph]'

docs.title: 2. Generate a dev token
docs.text:
generate_dev_token() returns one URL-safe random string (secrets.token_urlsafe(32)). The same string goes into the config and into every client’s Authorization header — the server stores it as given, it does not hash it:

python -c "from corral.api import generate_dev_token; print(generate_dev_token())"

Expected (yours will differ):

D--IvW8W34gDhwRQC2D9ro9mhSEfPXsPX8XnBV8UUaU

Paste it into auth.token in your config and keep it with the same care as any other shared secret.

docs.title: 3. Write a config YAML
docs.text:
A config is one ServerSettings document (corral.api.config): bind, port, an auth block and a packages list. Each package has a URL-safe id, a source that Network.from_source accepts, and an optional description echoed by /networks. There are no per-package engine or spec-version keys and no logging section — the spec version is detected from the data, and logging is uvicorn’s:

# server.yaml
bind: 127.0.0.1      # 0.0.0.0 to accept off-host requests (see pitfalls)
port: 8000

auth:
  kind: bearer       # or "none" — see pitfalls
  token: "paste-the-output-of-generate_dev_token-here"

packages:
  - id: leavenworth
    source: packages/netstead/netstead/fixtures/leavenworth/csv
    description: Bundled Leavenworth, WA fixture (GMNS 0.97)
  - id: regional
    source: s3://my-bucket/regional/datapackage.json

JSON works too (--config server.json). YAML parsing uses pyyaml, which uvicorn[standard] (part of the [server] extra) already installs.

docs.title: 4. Run it + verify
docs.text:
Start the server, then hit /health (the unauthenticated liveness probe) to confirm it’s up. --bind / --port override the config for a one-off run:

netstead server run --config server.yaml

curl http://127.0.0.1:8000/health

Expected:

{"status": "ok"}

docs.title: 5. Make authenticated requests
docs.text:
Pass the token from step 2 as a bearer header. Every response is JSON, whatever Accept header the client sends. /networks is the cheap listing — it echoes the config without loading anything:

TOKEN="paste-the-output-of-generate_dev_token-here"
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" http://127.0.0.1:8000/networks

Expected:

[{"id": "leavenworth", "source": "packages/netstead/netstead/fixtures/leavenworth/csv", "description": "Bundled Leavenworth, WA fixture (GMNS 0.97)"}]

Counts and the spec version are on the per-network endpoint, which loads the package on first access:

curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" http://127.0.0.1:8000/networks/leavenworth

Expected:

{"id": "leavenworth", "name": "gmns", "spec_version": "0.97", "engine": "IbisEngine", "links": 339, "nodes": 121, "table_count": 9, "tables": ["geometry", "lane", "link", "link_tod", "node", "signal_controller", "time_set_definitions", "use_definition", "use_group"]}

Quality checks are a POST (a GET returns 405 Method Not Allowed). The body is the same ValidationReport.to_dict() shape the CLI’s --json emits:

curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
     http://127.0.0.1:8000/networks/leavenworth/quality

docs.title: 6. Endpoint list
docs.text:
Endpoint Returns GET /health {"status": "ok"} (no auth) GET /packages [{id, source, description}] — configured packages, nothing loaded GET /packages/{id} {id, name, engine, table_count, tables: [{name, rows, columns}]} GET /packages/{id}/spec resolved Frictionless datapackage.json POST /packages/{id}/validate full validation report (ValidationReport.to_dict()); packages are loaded as Networks, so this is GMNS validation with spec_version set GET /networks same listing as /packages GET /networks/{id} {id, name, spec_version, engine, links, nodes, table_count, tables} POST /networks/{id}/quality the GMNS rule pack as a validation report (needs [graph])

Interactive OpenAPI at http://127.0.0.1:8000/docs.

docs.title: Common variations
docs.text:
Default — localhost bind with bearer auth

Safe default for dev and single-host production behind a reverse proxy.

bind: 127.0.0.1
auth: { kind: bearer, token: "..." }
Off-host access (LAN, etc.)

Bind 0.0.0.0 — but keep auth on.

bind: 0.0.0.0
auth: { kind: bearer, token: "..." }
Behind nginx / Caddy

Bind to 127.0.0.1; let the proxy terminate TLS and forward. No server-side TLS config needed.

bind: 127.0.0.1
port: 8000
One token per client

The config holds exactly one auth.token. To give each client its own credential, run one server process (and config) per client, or put an authenticating reverse proxy in front and let it hold the per-client secrets.

Disable auth (dev only)

The server still starts on a public bind with kind: none — it only logs a warning (see pitfalls) — so pair this with a localhost bind.

bind: 127.0.0.1
auth: { kind: none }
Docker

The repo ships a server image definition at packages/netstead/Dockerfile (plus docker-compose.example.yml beside it). Build it from the repo root — the build needs both workspace packages — and mount your config and data:

docker build -f packages/netstead/Dockerfile -t netstead-server .
docker run --rm -p 8000:8000 \
    -v $(pwd)/server.yaml:/etc/netstead/config.yml:ro \
    -v $(pwd)/data:/data:ro \
    netstead-server

A prebuilt ghcr.io image is not published yet (tracked in #104). Alternatively, pip install into your own image and copy the config alongside:

FROM python:3.12-slim
RUN pip install 'netstead[server,graph]'
COPY server.yaml /etc/netstead/server.yaml
CMD ["netstead", "server", "run", "--config", "/etc/netstead/server.yaml"]

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• auth.kind: none + non-localhost bind is a security footgun. The server logs a corral.api: auth.kind='none' with bind='0.0.0.0' exposes the server with NO authentication warning at startup and then runs anyway — there is no refuse-to-start guard and no override key. Treat the warning as a stop sign.
  • Bearer mode needs a token. kind: bearer without auth.token fails at app build time (AuthSettings(kind='bearer') requires token to be set), so a misconfigured server never silently lets requests through.
  • Tokens are compared in constant time, as plaintext. The server holds the token string from the config and checks the incoming Authorization: Bearer … header against it with hmac.compare_digest. There is no hashing — protect the config file as you would the token itself.
  • Packages are cached after first load. The PackageRegistry loads each package through Network.from_source the first time its id is requested and keeps it for the life of the process. Edit the files on disk, or the config, and you need to restart the server to see the change.
  • No write endpoints. The HTTP server is read-only by design. For editing, use the Python API + Session, or the Workbench.

docs.text:

docs.title: Wire the MCP server to Claude Code / Claude Desktop
Wire the MCP server to Claude Code / Claude Desktop
When to use this
docs.text: You want an AI agent (Claude Desktop, Claude Code, any MCP-aware host) to call netstead directly via tool calls — describe a package, run validation, scope a subgraph, run the quality pack — instead of you copying CLI output into the chat. The MCP server speaks the Model Context Protocol so the agent treats netstead as a first-class tool surface.

docs.title: Quick example
docs.text:
Add this entry to your MCP host config, restart the host, and ask the agent “describe the package at /tmp/leavenworth/csv”. The agent picks describe_package, calls it with {"source": "/tmp/leavenworth/csv"}, and surfaces the package name, engine, table count and each table’s row count and columns back in chat:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "netstead": {
      "command": "netstead",
      "args": ["mcp", "serve"]
    }
  }
}

Once connected, Claude lists the seven netstead tools and calls them with the source path you name; the tool name, its arguments and the JSON reply appear inline in the chat.

docs.title: 1. Install
docs.text:
The [mcp] extra brings in mcp (the official Python SDK, v1 API). Add [graph] too: connected_components and quality_check need scipy, and without it those two tools fail at call time:

pip install 'netstead[mcp,graph]'

docs.title: 2. Test the server runs
docs.text:
You don’t normally launch the server yourself — the MCP host does it. But --help confirms the entry point resolves and the SDK is importable:

netstead mcp serve --help

Expected:

Usage: netstead mcp serve [OPTIONS]

 Start the netstead MCP server on stdio (for Claude Desktop / Claude Code).
 ...
╭─ Options ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╮
│ --name          TEXT  MCP server display name. [default: netstead] │
│ --help  -h            Show this message and exit.                  │
╰───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯

docs.title: 3. Configure the MCP host
docs.text:
Claude Desktop (macOS): edit ~/Library/Application Support/Claude/claude_desktop_config.json. On Linux it’s ~/.config/Claude/claude_desktop_config.json; on Windows, %APPDATA%\Claude\claude_desktop_config.json. Restart Claude Desktop after editing; the tools show up under a hammer-icon in the chat input:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "netstead": {
      "command": "netstead",
      "args": ["mcp", "serve"]
    }
  }
}

Claude Code: register the server from the terminal — everything after -- is the command Claude Code launches:

claude mcp add netstead -- netstead mcp serve

--scope project writes it to a .mcp.json at the project root that teammates pick up on session start (the default scope is local to you); see claude mcp add --help. The equivalent hand-written .mcp.json is the same JSON as above. To use the version installed in a project venv, replace netstead with the absolute path to that venv’s netstead.

docs.title: 4. The tools shipped today
docs.text:
The server exposes seven stateless tools. Every tool takes a source — any path or URL that Network.from_source accepts — and returns JSON; only scope_from_nodes takes anything more. Full input and output shapes are in the MCP tools reference.

Name Summary Inputs Output describe_package Generic package overview: name, engine, table count, per-table rows + columns. source {source, name, engine, table_count, tables: [{name, rows, columns}]} validate_package Generic Frictionless validation (no GMNS spec). For GMNS use netstead validate --json. source ValidationReport.to_dict() list_tables Sorted table names, no row counts. source ["lane", "link", ...] describe_network GMNS-aware overview: spec version, link + node counts, table names. source {source, name, spec_version, engine, links, nodes, table_count, tables} quality_check The GMNS data-quality rule pack. Needs [graph]. source ValidationReport.to_dict() connected_components Count + sizes of weakly-connected components. Needs [graph]. source {source, component_count, sizes} scope_from_nodes Node-seeded scope; returns the resulting node + link id sets. source, node_ids: [int], path_between: bool = true {source, seed_node_ids, path_between, result_node_count, result_link_count, node_ids, link_ids}

docs.title: 5. Sample agent prompts
docs.text:
Each of these exercises a different tool — paste them into a chat with the server configured to see the agent pick the right call:

  • “What’s in the GMNS network at packages/netstead/netstead/fixtures/leavenworth/csv?” — agent calls describe_network, returns spec version 0.97, 339 links, 121 nodes and the nine table names.
  • “Run the quality rules on that network and summarize the warnings by code.” — agent calls quality_check, groups the issues list by code, and reports the counts.
  • “Scope the network to the shortest paths between nodes 1, 25 and 50 and tell me how many links that is.” — agent calls scope_from_nodes with node_ids=[1, 25, 50] and path_between=true (the default). See the known issue on this tool in the MCP tools reference.

docs.title: Common variations
Pitfalls
docs.text:
• Stdio transport only today. The HTTP MCP transport is a follow-up — track the open issues for progress. For now, every agent that wants to call netstead needs to launch its own subprocess.
  • Tools are stateless. There’s no persistent edit_session tool yet — every call is a one-shot load + read. The agent can’t mutate a network and inspect intermediate state across calls. See the issue tracker for the design discussion.
  • JSON-only return values. Tool outputs are summaries (counts, names, id lists, reports), never table rows. For the data itself, the agent should call the CLI or the Python API through a shell tool.
  • Config file path is case-sensitive on macOS. Claude vs claude matters. If the server doesn’t show up after a restart, check ~/Library/Logs/Claude/mcp*.log.

docs.text:

  • Drive the CLI from an AI agent loop — when you want an agent to drive netstead via shell instead of MCP.
  • API reference — the Python entry points the MCP tools wrap.

docs.title: Validate a network and read the report
Validate a network and read the report
When to use this
docs.text: You have a GMNS network — yours, a vendor’s, the output of an edit — and you need to know whether it conforms to the spec before downstream tools (assignment models, AI agents, regulators) touch it. Validation is fast (sub-second on Leavenworth, a few seconds on a regional network) and answers four questions at once: do all required tables exist, do columns match the schema, do foreign keys resolve, and are any of those FKs stale from a recent edit?

docs.title: Quick example
docs.text:
Validate the bundled Leavenworth fixture from the shell. Add --json to any netstead (or corral) CLI command and the output becomes a single machine-readable JSON document on stdout — pipe into jq, save to a file, feed to a script or AI agent. Default output is human-readable rich panels.

netstead validate --json packages/netstead/netstead/fixtures/leavenworth/csv

Expected — the command exits 0 because Leavenworth has no ERRORs. The issue list holds 16 INFO entries (structural.missing_optional_resource, one per optional GMNS table the fixture doesn’t ship) and nothing else. (node declares a foreign key into zone, but the fixture has no node.zone_id column, so there is nothing to verify and no finding is raised.)

{"header": "validation report: ...", "issues": [{"severity": "info", "code": "structural.missing_optional_resource", ...}, ...]}

The same call from Python returns a ValidationReport dataclass:

from netstead import Network
from netstead.fixtures import leavenworth

net = Network.from_source(leavenworth.csv_dir())
report = net.validate()
print(f"is_clean={report.is_clean}  issues={len(report.issues)}")

Expected:

is_clean=True  issues=16

is_clean is True because no ERROR or WARNING fired; the INFO findings don’t break it. report.has_errors is False.

The CLI exits non-zero if any ERROR-severity finding fires, so it drops straight into a CI gate.

Validation report card. Zero ERRORs, zero WARNINGs, and 16 INFO findings for the optional tables the fixture doesn’t ship. Data-quality rules are a separate pass (netstead quality) and don’t appear here.

docs.title: 1. Run validation
docs.text:
net.validate() runs all four passes — structural, schema, FK, sync-state — and returns a ValidationReport. Toggle individual passes with boolean kwargs:

report = net.validate()                                                  # all four passes
report = net.validate(structural=False, sync_state=False)                # schema + FK only

The same operation is available from the shell, with three output formats:

netstead validate <source>                       # human-readable summary
netstead validate <source> --all                 # ...one row per finding, nothing folded
netstead validate <source> --json                # machine-readable
netstead validate <source> --html report.html    # standalone HTML report

The human-readable table opens with a severity summary line (0 errors · 1 warning · 16 info) and names the source once. Structural findings that differ only by resource — the sixteen structural.missing_optional_resource lines above — fold into one row whose table column reads 16 tables and whose message lists the absent resources; --all expands them to a row each. --json is never folded.

docs.title: 2. Read the report shape
docs.text:
ValidationReport is a dataclass with five fields and properties you’ll touch:

Field / property Type Description report.is_clean bool True iff no ERROR and no WARNING fired. INFO findings don’t break it. report.has_errors bool True iff ≥1 ERROR-severity issue fired. CI gates usually want if report.has_errors:. report.has_warnings bool True iff ≥1 WARNING-severity issue fired. report.spec_version str The GMNS spec version the validator ran against. report.issues list[Issue] One entry per finding.

Each Issue is a small dataclass carrying severity, category, a stable code, a human-readable message, and the offending row coordinates when known:

@dataclass
class Issue:
    severity: Severity      # ERROR | WARNING | INFO
    category: Category      # SCHEMA | STRUCTURAL | FOREIGN_KEY | SYNC_STATE | DATA_QUALITY
    code: str               # stable identifier, e.g. "schema.required"
    message: str            # human-readable
    table: str | None       # table the finding is about
    column: str | None      # column, if applicable
    row: int | None         # row index, if applicable
    fix_hint: str | None    # what to do about it
    extra: dict             # adapter-specific payload (FK target, coordinates, ...)

docs.title: 3. Filter by severity
docs.text:
Most CI gates want if errors: sys.exit(1). The CLI does this for you; from Python it’s a one-liner:

from corral.validation import Severity

errors = [i for i in report.issues if i.severity is Severity.ERROR]
warnings = [i for i in report.issues if i.severity is Severity.WARNING]

docs.title: 4. Filter by category
docs.text:
Categories group findings by which validation pass produced them:

from corral.validation import Category

schema_problems = [i for i in report.issues if i.category is Category.SCHEMA]
fk_problems = [i for i in report.issues if i.category is Category.FOREIGN_KEY]
  • SCHEMA — field-level type / enum / required-column violations.
  • STRUCTURAL — package-level shape problems (missing required table, missing required file).
  • FOREIGN_KEY — cross-table integrity (link.from_node_id points at a node that doesn’t exist).
  • SYNC_STATE — FKs that resolved on disk but were invalidated by an in-memory edit (see edit-with-rollback).
  • DATA_QUALITY — rule-pack findings (high-speed-residential, lane-count-mismatch, etc.). Always WARNING / INFO; see customize the quality pack.

docs.title: 5. Common codes you’ll see
docs.text:
Stable identifier strings let you script around specific findings without parsing free-text messages. Codes live inline at the top of each validator module (see corral.validation.structural, schema_check, foreign_keys, sync_state). The most common ones:

Code Category Severity What it means schema.required SCHEMA ERROR A required column is missing or null on a row. schema.enum SCHEMA ERROR A column value isn’t in the spec-defined enum set. schema.type SCHEMA ERROR A value doesn’t parse as the declared type. structural.missing_required_resource STRUCTURAL ERROR A required table (link, node) isn’t in the package. structural.missing_optional_resource STRUCTURAL INFO An optional spec table isn’t in the package. Leavenworth reports 16 of these. structural.missing_file STRUCTURAL ERROR A table is declared in the package descriptor but the file isn’t there. fk.missing_target FOREIGN_KEY ERROR FK points at a row that doesn’t exist in the parent table. fk.null_in_required_fk FOREIGN_KEY ERROR A required FK column is null on a row. fk.unverifiable FOREIGN_KEY WARNING The FK’s target table isn’t in the package, so it can’t be checked and the source column holds at least one value. An absent or all-null source column raises nothing. sync.fk_stale SYNC_STATE ERROR An edit invalidated an FK and no recompute ran. quality.high_speed_residential DATA_QUALITY WARNING Residential link with speed limit above the configured threshold.

docs.title: Common variations
docs.text:
Default — full validation, rich console output

The most common path: run all four passes and read the panel.

netstead validate <source>
JSON for scripts and AI agents

--json emits one parseable document on stdout — exits non-zero on ERROR.

netstead validate <source> --json | jq '.issues[] | select(.severity=="error")'
Interactive map+table HTML report (--html)

Self-contained file you can email or upload to a docs site. The map pane on top plots each finding on the actual network geometry (Leaflet, vendored — no network calls when the report is opened); the filterable table below shows the same findings with severity, code, message, and fix hint. A “Resources” table above the findings lists every spec table with required / optional, present ✓ / ✗ and its row count, and the “Unlocated findings” block (collapsed by default) folds repeated structural findings into one line. For networks imported from OpenStreetMap, each finding’s popup carries a one-click “Edit in OSM” deep link to the iD editor.

netstead validate <source> --html report.html

Or programmatically:

from netstead.map import render_validation_html
open("report.html", "w").write(render_validation_html(net, report))

Requires pip install 'netstead[reports]'. When that extra is not installed, --html still writes a file — the older corral table-only HTML — and prints a stderr note pointing at the install command.

Findings spreadsheet (--csv / --xlsx)

Flat one-row-per-finding spreadsheet — the right shape for triage in Excel, Google Sheets, or jq.

netstead validate <source> --csv findings.csv --xlsx findings.xlsx

Columns: severity, category, code, table, column, row, message, fix_hint, extra. The extra column is a JSON blob carrying adapter-specific payload (FK target, OSM provenance, …). --xlsx needs [reports]; --csv works on the lean install.

Just the failing tables

Useful for triaging which datasets need attention first.

from corral.reports import Severity
failing = {i.table for i in report.issues if i.severity is Severity.ERROR}
Embed in a CI step

Non-zero exit code on ERROR — no extra wiring needed.

netstead validate ./data || exit 1
Pretty-print in a notebook

ValidationReport ships a _repr_html_; just leave it as the last cell expression.

report  # renders an HTML summary in Jupyter

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• WARNING-level findings don’t fail CI. That’s intentional — data-quality findings are advisory. If you want them to be blocking, post-process: if any(i.code.startswith("quality.") for i in report.issues): sys.exit(1).
  • Data-quality thresholds are configurable. A WARNING firing on your network may just mean the default threshold doesn’t match your context (e.g. metric vs imperial speed). See the customize the quality pack recipe.
  • sync.fk_stale only fires after an edit. A freshly-loaded package can’t be out of sync with itself. If you see this in CI, an upstream step in the same process mutated the network.
  • The validator runs against the spec version embedded in the package. Override with Network.from_source(path, spec_version="0.96") if the package is mislabeled.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Architecture — the four-pass validator design.
  • Edit with rollback — sync.fk_stale is produced by edits without a recompute_fks.
  • API reference — ValidationReport, Issue, Severity, Category.

docs.title: View a network on a map (with or without findings)
View a network on a map
When to use this
docs.text:
You want a one-file, send-it-to-a-colleague visual of a GMNS network — without having to spin up a Jupyter notebook, a geopandas plot, or a folium map. Maybe to confirm an OSM build covered the right area, demo the result of an edit, attach to a bug report, or check that quality-rule findings cluster where you expect them.

The renderer is the same one netstead validate --html uses. Calling it directly lets you pass any list of Issue objects (validation, quality, graph topology, custom) as overlays — or none at all.

docs.title: Quick example
docs.text:
Render the bundled Leavenworth fixture to a single HTML file. The renderer lives in netstead.map; nothing is overlaid because no issues are passed:

from netstead import Network
from netstead.fixtures import leavenworth
from netstead.map import render_network_html

net = Network.from_source(leavenworth.csv_dir())
open("net.html", "w").write(render_network_html(net, title="Leavenworth"))

Open net.html in any browser. You’ll see the link geometry as a thin underlay on a Leaflet base map. No overlay markers because no issues were passed.

docs.title: 1. Overlay validation findings
docs.text:
render_validation_html takes the network and a ValidationReport and composes the map with the findings table — it is what netstead validate --html writes:

from netstead.map import render_validation_html

report = net.validate()
open("net.html", "w").write(render_validation_html(net, report))

Each finding becomes a clickable marker, color-coded by severity. A Resources table above the findings lists every spec resource (required/optional, present, row count). Cross-cutting findings (no row, no coords) sit in a collapsed “Unlocated findings” <details> block, with its count in the summary — still clickable for the row-sync when expanded. Findings that share a code and differ only by resource (such as the sixteen structural.missing_optional_resource lines a partial GMNS package produces) are grouped into one line there.

docs.title: 2. Overlay anything else
docs.text:
The renderer accepts a flat list[Issue], so any Issue source plugs in without renderer changes:

from corral.reports import Category, Issue, Severity

custom = [
    Issue(
        severity=Severity.WARNING,
        category=Category.DATA_QUALITY,
        code="quality.signage_missing",
        message="no stop sign at intersection 42",
        extra={"lon": -120.66, "lat": 47.59},
    ),
]
open("net.html", "w").write(render_network_html(net, custom))

GMNS-specific data-quality rules (netstead.quality.*) already produce Issue objects in this shape, so run_quality(net).issues drops straight in.

docs.title: 3. OpenStreetMap deep links
docs.text: When the network has osm_way_id (and optionally osm_node_id) columns — as produced by netstead build, the OSM importer — each marker’s popup carries an “Edit in OSM” link straight to the iD editor at openstreetmap.org/edit?editor=id&way=<id>. Pass osm_editor="josm" to target the desktop JOSM editor instead (via its localhost RemoteControl plugin).

docs.title: Common variations
docs.text:
Different base map 
render_network_html(net, tile_provider="openstreetmap")  # default is "esri", a keyless light grey
Embed in a Jupyter notebook 
from IPython.display import IFrame
open("/tmp/net.html", "w").write(render_network_html(net, report.issues))
IFrame("/tmp/net.html", 900, 600)
From the CLI

netstead validate --html writes this same page with the findings overlaid:

netstead validate <source> --html report.html  # findings overlay

For interactive viewing — linked map and table, validation, editing — open the network in the Workbench instead; this renderer is for a self-contained, offline HTML file you can send to someone:

netstead app <source>

See Explore in the Workbench.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• Requires the [reports] extra. pip install 'netstead[reports]' (pulls in jinja2, openpyxl and pyyaml). Leaflet itself is vendored — no internet required when the report is opened.
  • No marker clustering yet. Past a few thousand findings the Leaflet canvas slows down. Filter the issue list before passing it in.
  • title= controls the <title> tag. It does not override how the network’s spec version / link / node counts appear in the subtitle.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Validate a network — --html / --csv / --xlsx CLI flags wrap the same renderer.
  • Build from OSM — produces a network with osm_way_id columns so the “Edit in OSM” links light up.
  • Customize quality — quality rules feed the same Issue overlay path.

docs.title: When to use this
docs.text:
You want the Workbench to do something it doesn’t do yet, such as authoring project cards, managing a scenario catalog or running a domain check, and you don’t want to fork netstead to get it. A plugin is a separate pip package. Install it next to netstead and netstead app picks it up.

For a full plugin built on this API (Actions with undo, routes, a dock panel, schema forms, a preview on a derived network), read the netstead-project-cards package in plugins/project-cards.

The plugin API is provisional until netstead v1.0 (see Versioning).

docs.title: What a plugin is
docs.text:
A plugin is a Python package that declares an entry point in the netstead.workbench.plugins group. The entry-point name must equal the plugin id, and it points at a zero-argument factory that returns a netstead.workbench.plugins.WorkbenchPlugin:

[project.entry-points."netstead.workbench.plugins"]
hello = "netstead_hello:plugin"

At startup each netstead app session discovers the installed entry points, checks each plugin, and installs the ones that pass. A plugin that fails is recorded with its reason and skipped. It never stops the app (see Startup outcomes).

docs.title: Trust model
docs.text:
Plugins are full-trust code running inside the Workbench process, the same as pytest plugins. Nothing sandboxes them. A plugin can do anything your user account can do: read and write any file, call the network, and read the OS keyring. The Host API is the supported surface, not a security boundary. The io.allowed_roots sandbox that host.writable applies only helps plugins that choose to use it. Install only plugins you would also run as a script.

The --host 0.0.0.0 warning from Explore in the Workbench applies with more force here. An exposed bind has no authentication, and every loaded plugin’s routes (/api/plugins/<id>/...) and Actions (POST /api/actions) are exposed with it. While the server binds to a loopback address, plugin routes sit behind the same Host-header and cross-origin write guards as every core route. Those guards do not run on an exposed bind.

docs.title: The UX contract
docs.text:
The Workbench stays coherent only if every plugin follows the same rules. These are condensed from the design. Core enforces some of them and plugins are expected to follow the rest.

  1. Core owns the shared network nouns; plugins may own domain nouns. Core owns networks (including derived networks and their lineage), the one shared selection, the map and tables, jobs, history and settings. A plugin never forks the selection or brings a second map. A plugin may add domain nouns of its own (a card, a scenario), and these follow three rules:

    • Namespaced and exposed. They live in plugin state (plugins.<id>.* in /api/state) and change only through that plugin’s namespaced Actions, so other plugins, Python and NL can see and act on them.
    • Projected onto core nouns, never duplicating them. A card resolves to a core selection (highlighting it is an ordinary Select). A scenario materializes as a core derived network, so the map, tables and validation work on it unchanged.
    • Referenceable by a stable id of the form {plugin}:{kind}/{id}, for example catalog:card/I80-hov-2035, so history and “copy as Python” stay replayable.

    Cross-plugin interaction is by Action. Check for the other plugin’s Action with host.has_action("catalog.add_card") and dispatch it, or fall back. That is a soft dependency, and core has no service registry. If you need another plugin’s Python API, declare a normal pip dependency on it. 2. Selection → verb → form → preview → commit. The user selects, picks a verb, fills a form prefilled from the selection, sees a preview on the map, and commits. Present your workflows in this shape. 3. Nothing mutates silently. Previews and scenarios are derived networks (host.derive) and leave the base untouched. Make in-place changes (host.mutate) inside an Action handler: the Action is recorded in history and replays in “copy as Python”, and if the handler fails the change is undone. A mutate from anywhere else (a submit_job function, a plugin route) still appears in history, as a <id>.mutate entry, but it can’t be replayed: the copied script shows it only as a comment. 4. Everything is an Action, plugins included. Plugin Action types are namespaced (<id>.<name>) and get the same history, “copy as Python”, replay and HTTP dispatch as core Actions. 5. Schema-driven forms. Plugin Actions render from their JSON Schema through one core form component (wb.schemaForm); every plugin Action also gets a generated form in the command palette. 6. Workspaces as tabs, with predictable placement. Plugins contribute workspaces, dock panels, commands (palette and context menus; and, once opted in, the NL assistant: see below) and map layers. They don’t add ad-hoc UI. 7. Dirty state is always visible. Unsaved drafts, uncommitted cards and derived networks are badged in the network switcher and on workspace tabs. 8. Plugins are accountable. Every installed plugin reports its id, version, required API and load error. A broken plugin degrades to “not loaded, with this error” and never takes down the app.

docs.title: Walk through the hello example
docs.text:
examples/workbench-plugin-hello is a complete plugin. Copy it as a starting point:

uv pip install -e examples/workbench-plugin-hello   # needs the `server` extra, as `netstead app` does
uv run netstead app

docs.title: Actions
docs.text:
An Action is a module-level subclass of netstead.workbench.plugins.BaseAction. Its type field is a single-value Literal named "<plugin id>.<name>":

from typing import Literal

from netstead.workbench.plugins import BaseAction


class Greet(BaseAction):
    type: Literal["hello.greet"] = "hello.greet"
    name: str

Each Action is paired with its handler in a netstead.workbench.plugins.ActionSpec. The handler signature is handler(host, action) -> result. It runs under the session lock. Its return value is what session.dispatch returns, and over HTTP it is the result field of the POST /api/actions response, next to ok, error and the recorded history entry. Raise netstead.workbench.plugins.ActionError("…") to refuse: the message is shown to the user and the Action is recorded as failed (NotSupportedYet for “not in this version”). Any other exception is recorded as an internal error (InternalError), with secrets scrubbed from its message. Set mutates: ClassVar[bool] = True on an Action that changes a network in place, so the assistant drafts it for the user to confirm instead of applying it. Plugin Actions can’t be runs_as_job. For slow work, call host.submit_job from the handler.

Two rules keep “copy session as Python” working:

  • The class must be importable. Define it at the top level of a module (not in a function and not in __main__), and give it a class name no core Action or other plugin uses. The copied script imports it as from <its module> import <Class>. For the example that is from netstead_hello import Greet.
  • Field values must round-trip through repr. The replay line is app.do(Greet(name='Ada')), built from repr(value) of each field. Use str, numbers, bools, None, lists, dicts and tuples of those, or nested pydantic models. A value whose repr isn’t valid Python (a numpy array, a datetime without an import, an open file) makes the copied script fail.

Two optional class variables shape the replay line:

  • replay_omits: ClassVar[frozenset[str]] names fields the replay line leaves out. Use it for a guard that only means something in the live session, such as expected_version: a version planned in the browser is stale in a script run later, so the replay plans again. Core DeleteRows omits its expected_version this way. A name that isn’t one of the Action’s fields is refused at install.
  • replay_overrides: ClassVar[dict[str, Any]] forces field values in the replay line, applied after the defaults are dropped. Core BuildNetwork sets {"approved": True}, so a replayed build doesn’t stop to ask for the approval the user already gave.

The startup checks enforce the namespacing, the single Literal, importability, unique class names and replay_omits field names. The repr rule is yours to keep.

docs.title: The plugin object
docs.text:
from pathlib import Path

from netstead.workbench.plugins import HOST_API, ActionSpec, Host, WorkbenchPlugin
from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict


class HelloSettings(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(extra="forbid")
    prefix: str = "Hello"


def plugin() -> WorkbenchPlugin:
    greeted = {"count": 0}  # per-session state lives in the factory's closure

    def greet(host: Host, action: Greet) -> str:
        greeted["count"] += 1
        host.publish("greeted", {"name": action.name})
        return f"{host.settings.prefix}, {action.name}!"

    return WorkbenchPlugin(
        id="hello",
        name="Hello",
        version="0.1.0",
        requires_api=HOST_API,
        actions=(ActionSpec(Greet, greet),),
        router=router,  # see below
        static_dir=Path(__file__).parent / "static",
        settings_model=HelloSettings,
        state=lambda host: {"greeted": greeted["count"]},
    )
Field What it does id The namespace for Action types, routes, state, settings and static files. Must match [a-z][a-z0-9_]* and equal the entry-point name. requires_api The plugin API version you wrote against. Pass HOST_API from the netstead you develop with. actions A tuple of ActionSpec(model, handler). settings_model A pydantic model that validates the [plugins.<id>] table. Read the result as host.settings. state(host) Returns a JSON-safe dict merged into /api/state under plugins.<id>. Keep it cheap, because it runs on every state push. router(host) Returns a FastAPI APIRouter, mounted at /api/plugins/<id>. Called once, at install. static_dir / frontend A directory served at /plugins/<id>/, and the ES module in it the browser loads (default main.js). on_load(host) Runs once at install, before the router is built and the Actions register. If it raises, the plugin isn’t installed, but whatever it did before raising (files written, threads started) is not undone. The same holds if the router or static dir then fails.

The factory runs once per session, so state kept in its closure belongs to that session.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Settings come from the same layers as every other setting (user config, project netstead.toml, env, session):

# ./netstead.toml
[plugins.hello]
prefix = "Howdy"

Bad values mark the plugin error at startup. Through the Workbench’s settings API they are refused before anything is written. Credentials are never settings. A secret-named key (api_key, token, password and so on), a value shaped like an API key, or a URL carrying a password under [plugins.<id>] is refused in every layer, and the settings fail to load. Read keys from the OS keyring or the environment in your own code instead.

docs.title: Routes and front end
docs.text:
from fastapi import APIRouter


def router(host: Host) -> APIRouter:
    api = APIRouter()

    @api.get("/count")  # served at GET /api/plugins/hello/count
    def count() -> dict:
        return {"greeted": greeted["count"]}

    return api

static_dir is served at /plugins/<id>/. Requests can’t escape it (.. and its encoded forms get a 404). At startup the Workbench imports frontend and calls its activate(wb) (see The front end). If the module fails to import, has no activate, activate throws, or importing the module and running activate take more than 5 seconds together, everything it registered is removed and Settings → Plugins shows the error. The rest of the Workbench carries on. router(host) is called once, when the session installs the plugin. If it raises or returns something other than an APIRouter, or static_dir isn’t a directory, the plugin isn’t installed: it is marked error, none of its Actions register, its state isn’t merged, and nothing of it is mounted.

docs.title: The Host reference
docs.text:
A plugin never sees the Session. Every handler, router, state and on_load gets a netstead.workbench.plugins.Host bound to that plugin’s id.

Member What it gives you host.plugin_id This plugin’s id. host.settings The validated [plugins.<id>] model, or None if there is no settings_model. Re-read on each access, so it reflects setting changes. host.active The active network’s id, or None. host.selection A copy of the shared selection payload (the dict /api/state carries), or None. It adds projectcard: a resolved selection’s ProjectCard facility forms (picked, resolved, query; and, added to 1.8 without a version bump, the Find tab’s strict forms segment and link_list, each a {id system: facility} map for gmns and osm, with segment_problem, id_systems ({system: None or why not}) and id_captions), else None. anchors are the from/to nodes with lon/lat; anchors_unplaced (API 1.2) are those whose node has no coordinates. host.saved_selections() A summary of each saved selection: name, net_id, status, links (a count), utterance, by (query or ids) and stale (it was saved with a stale pin). API 1.3. host.saved_selection(name) A copy of the selection saved as name, or None: net_id, source (a locator: no query string), version, status, utterance, intent (with any pins), parsed_by, link_ids, the anchors’ nodes and stale_pins, plus projectcard (its facility forms, as for host.selection) and warnings (a stale pin, in words). It is the selection as saved; UseSelection resolves it again on the network as it is now. API 1.3. host.network(net_id=None) The network handle (default: the active one). Read it, but change it only through mutate. host.mutate(net_id, edits, note=..., expected_version=None) Applies corral.editing.Edits to a network’s roadway all or nothing. The edits run on a draft, so a failing edit leaves the network (and its caches) untouched and re-raises. If storage refuses an edit while it is applied to the draft (corral’s EditingError, or an Arrow, ibis or DuckDB error), it raises ActionError (“the edit failed: : “, with URL credentials and key-shaped tokens scrubbed; the original is logged), so the user sees why (API 1.6; before, a plugin’s handler failed with “internal error”). Any other exception re-raises as it is, and so does a failure after the edit was applied: it is not reported as a failed edit. On success it bumps the version, appends "<id>: <note>" to the lineage and pushes state. It returns a Mutation, a frozen dataclass: results (a tuple of the EditResults, the rollback data) and seq, the pending edit’s id (API 1.6; None for an empty list of edits). Before 1.6 it returned the list of results itself. Inside a handler, the change is undone if the handler fails. Outside one (a job, a route), it is recorded as a non-replayable <id>.mutate history entry. With expected_version (a plan’s version, API 1.2) it refuses with ActionError, changing nothing, if the network’s version moved since. host.undo(net_id=None) Reverts this plugin’s newest mutation of a network, if it is that network’s newest change, and returns the undone entry (seq, source, note, version, rows, saved); seq is the id host.mutate returned for it. Raises ActionError when there is nothing to undo or the newest change came from core, Python or another plugin, and (API 1.6) when storage refuses the reverse (“the undo failed: …”, scrubbed as for mutate). API 1.2. host.pending_edits(net_id=None) A PendingEdits (frozen), read in one moment under the session lock: edits, the network’s pending edits from every source, oldest first, each as host.undo returns it (seq, source, note, version, rows, saved); and issued, the newest seq handed out at that moment. Check your own edits against it rather than the network’s lineage. Raises ActionError if the network is not open. API 1.6. host.on_rollback(fn) From a handler: call fn() if this Action is rolled back, either because it fails or because an Action it is nested in fails after it succeeded. Use it to put back your own state and files, which core does not roll back. See Rolling back your own state. Raises RuntimeError outside a handler, and from inside a rollback callback. API 1.6. host.edit_warnings(net_id=None) The live edit warnings on a network now, from every source (dicts with code, table, key, column, value, message). API 1.2. host.plan_update(net_id, table, ids, values), host.plan_delete(net_id, table, ids), host.plan_add(net_id, table, rows) Core’s edit plans (EditPlan: edits, summary, rows per table, keys, and the version it planned on), refusing what storage cannot hold with EditRefused. Apply one with host.mutate. API 1.2. host.derive(net_id, label=..., note=...) Registers a copy-on-write copy of a network (a preview or scenario) and returns its id. Edits to the copy never touch the base. The copy records derived_from and inherits the lineage. Inside a handler that fails, the copy is unregistered again. host.has_action(type) Whether core or any loaded plugin registered that Action type. Use it for soft cross-plugin dependencies. host.dispatch(action) Dispatches any Action (a model or a dict). Called from a handler, it is recorded in history as nested in that handler’s Action (parent_seq): “copy as Python” shows it as a comment, since replaying the outer Action runs it again, and it is undone if the outer handler fails. Job Actions (open_network, build_network, run_validation, save_network) can’t be dispatched from a handler, because waiting for them would deadlock. Use host.submit_job for slow work instead. host.publish(name, payload) Sends the browser a {"type": "plugin", "plugin": <id>, "name": ..., "payload": ...} event over the session’s event stream; wb.on(name) hears it. name is lowercase letters, digits and underscores, starting with a letter ([a-z][a-z0-9_]*), since a dot in wb.on names another plugin; anything else raises ValueError. host.submit_job(label, fn) Runs fn(ctx) on a background job, with progress and cancel in the jobs panel, and returns the job id. mutate and derive are safe to call from it. host.writable(path) Resolves a path for writing inside io.allowed_roots. Raises PathNotAllowed outside it. host.readable(path) Resolves a path for reading inside io.allowed_roots: a file or a folder that exists. Raises PathNotAllowed outside the roots (before touching the disk) and ActionError when nothing is there. API 1.7. host.list_dir(path) The entries of a folder inside io.allowed_roots, folders first, hidden entries skipped, each {name, path, kind, is_dir} (kind is what core’s file browser can open it as, else None). Reads no file. Raises PathNotAllowed outside the roots and ActionError when the folder is missing or is a file. API 1.7. host.history(prefix=None) The session’s history (the entries GET /api/history returns: seq, action, python, ok, error, ts, via, …), oldest first, as copies; with prefix (say "my_plugin."), only the Actions whose type starts with it. Read-only; the Action now running is not in it yet. API 1.7. host.register_table(name, title, rows_fn, *, primary_key, columns=None) Publishes a read-only table to the table view, listed under “Plugins” in its rail. rows_fn() returns the rows (dicts, or a pandas frame), each with a unique, non-null primary_key; core builds them into a frame when the table is read and keeps it until you host.publish anything or the network changes. It is served by the table routes (/api/n/<net>/roadway/table/<name>/rows, schema, distinct), so sorting and the column filters work as on a network table (a comma-separated text column takes any_of); a yes/no column with gaps is a nullable boolean. Never edited, never linked to the map. name is [a-z][a-z0-9_]*, not a network table’s (link, node, …) nor another plugin’s. Goes when the plugin is unloaded. API 1.8. host.unregister_table(name) Takes your table out of the table view; False when you have none by that name. API 1.8.

A preview, following “nothing mutates silently”:

from corral.editing import Edit


def widen(host: Host, action: Widen) -> str:
    preview = host.derive(None, label="Preview: widen", note="preview")
    payload = {"predicate": lambda t: t.link_id == action.link_id, "set": {"lanes": action.lanes}}
    host.mutate(preview, [Edit(op="update_rows", table="link", payload=payload)], note=f"widen {action.link_id}")
    return preview  # the base network is untouched

docs.title: Editing networks (API 1.2)
docs.text:
Plan a change with core’s rules, apply it, check it, and undo it yourself if you need to:

from netstead.workbench.plugins import ActionError, EditRefused


def retag(host: Host, action: Retag) -> list[dict]:
    try:
        plan = host.plan_update(None, "link", [action.link_id], {"name": action.name})
    except EditRefused as exc:  # a value the column cannot hold, a key column, a missing row...
        raise ActionError(str(exc)) from exc
    host.mutate(None, plan.edits, note=plan.summary, expected_version=plan.version)
    return host.edit_warnings()  # read these before committing anything to disk
  • A plan reads the network as it is now and records that version as plan.version. Pass it to host.mutate(..., expected_version=plan.version): if anything changed the network in between, the mutation is refused with ActionError and nothing changes, so plan again. Inside a handler nothing can come between them (handlers run under the session lock). From a job or a route, another edit can land between the two calls even when they run back to back, so always pass expected_version there.
  • host.plan_delete cascades through the spec’s foreign keys (a link takes its lanes with it) and refuses to delete a node a link still uses; plan.rows says what would go.
  • What the spec says about the new values (required, enum, type, foreign keys, duplicate keys) is never a refusal: it comes back as a live warning from host.edit_warnings().
  • Every host.mutate is a pending edit whose source is your plugin id. Core lists it in its Edit tab with that id and never undoes it.
  • Undo is strict last-in, first-out across sources. host.undo() reverts your newest change only when it is the network’s newest change; core’s Undo and host.undo each refuse the other’s change, naming who made it.
  • A plugin that uses these declares requires_api="1.2" (or HOST_API).

docs.title: Edit ids (API 1.6)
docs.text:
host.mutate returns a Mutation(results, seq): seq is the pending edit’s id. host.pending_edits(net_id) returns a PendingEdits(issued, edits), and host.undo() returns the seq it reversed, so a plugin that keeps a record of its own edits can check it against the ledger:

done = host.mutate(None, plan.edits, note=plan.summary, expected_version=plan.version)
my_edits.append(done.seq)
...
pending = host.pending_edits()
mine = {e["seq"] for e in pending.edits if e["source"] == host.plugin_id}
gone = [seq for seq in my_edits if seq <= pending.issued and seq not in mine]
  • A network id’s seqs are unique for the whole session: a seq is never handed out twice, not after a rolled-back Action spent it, and not after the network is closed and opened again under the same id (numbering goes on). So an edit a rollback took away never comes back under the same id. (The handle still changes when a network is reopened; checking it too costs nothing.)
  • Because rolled-back edits keep their seqs, the seqs in the Edit tab can have gaps.
  • issued is the newest seq handed out when the edits were read. An edit you hold with a seq above it was made after the read, so the read says nothing about it: don’t drop it. This matters when you read outside an Action handler (a route), where an Action can land between your read and what you do with it.

docs.title: Rolling back your own state (API 1.6)
docs.text:
When an Action fails, core rolls back what it changed: the networks’ tables, versions, lineage and pending edits, the networks it derived, and the active network, selection, style, saved selections and filters. It does not know about your plugin’s own state (a draft kept in your factory’s closure) or the files your handler wrote. A handler nested in another Action (host.dispatch) can succeed and still be rolled back when the outer Action fails later.

Register a callback that puts your state back, after the change it undoes:

def commit(host: Host, action: Commit) -> dict:
    written = write_file(path, text)  # your own helper
    old = state.take_draft(net)
    host.on_rollback(lambda: (remove_or_restore(written), state.put_draft(net, old)))
    return {"path": str(path)}
  • It runs if this Action fails, or if it succeeds and an Action it is nested in fails afterwards. Once the outermost Action succeeds, it is dropped.
  • Rollback runs newest first, in one stack with core’s own undo records: when your callback runs, the network changes made after you registered it are already undone, and the ones made before it are not yet.
  • It runs under the session lock. Put back your own state and files there, and call no Host method: host.mutate, host.derive, host.undo, host.dispatch and host.on_rollback raise RuntimeError("... cannot be called from a rollback callback").
  • Lock order is the session lock, then your plugin’s own lock. Take your lock inside the callback if you need it, and never call Host while holding your own lock: a handler holds the session lock and then takes yours, so the other order can deadlock.
  • An exception in it is logged and the rest of the rollback still runs. A BaseException (KeyboardInterrupt) lets the rollback finish, then propagates. Handle your own failures (a file that can’t be restored) inside it.

docs.title: Your Actions in the assistant
docs.text:
A plugin’s Actions are offered to the natural-language assistant only when the user turns the plugin on in Settings → Assistant: actions & plugins (assistant.plugins = ["<your id>"]). Then each of your Actions is a tool, named <id>__<name> (a dot is not allowed in a tool name), with its JSON schema, and the first paragraph of its docstring as the description: write it for a model as well as a person. Actions with mutates = True are drafted for the user to approve; the others run at once, recorded with via: "assistant".

To keep an Action out even when the plugin is on (it needs a file path, or it only makes sense from your panel):

class Rebuild(BaseAction):
    type: Literal["cards.rebuild"] = "cards.rebuild"
    assistant: ClassVar[bool] = False

assistant needs Host API 1.4. Your browser commands are not offered to the assistant.

With a model on this machine (assistant.compact_tools = "auto", the default, or "on") the assistant gets a compact tool set: the read-only Actions that apply now, and only those mutates Actions marked assistant_compact. Core marks its everyday edits (edit_cells, delete_rows, undo_edit). Mark yours when a small model can fill in its fields reliably (no file path, no judgement call):

class AddChange(BaseAction):
    type: Literal["cards.add_change"] = "cards.add_change"
    mutates: ClassVar[bool] = True
    assistant_compact: ClassVar[bool] = True  # offered to a local model too

assistant_compact needs Host API 1.6 (GET /api/actions entries carry it). Before it, a plugin’s mutating Actions were offered only with assistant.compact_tools = "off".

Declare mutates honestly. An Action the assistant runs at once (one without mutates = True) can’t change a network: if its handler dispatches a mutating Action through host.dispatch, or calls host.mutate, host.undo (which reverts through the same path) or host.derive, the Action fails with an ActionError (“ran from the assistant without approval”) and everything it did is rolled back. The same Action dispatched by the user, Python or a script is unaffected. host.submit_job is not checked this way: a job runs after the handler has returned, so a plugin that starts one from a read-only Action is trusted not to change a network in it.

The tools are built from the session’s registry (session.actions), which holds the core Actions plus every loaded plugin’s. The module-level netstead.workbench.actions.action_json_schema covers core Actions only.

docs.title: The front end: activate(wb)
docs.text:
A plugin’s front end is one native ES module (no build step), served from static_dir as /plugins/<id>/<frontend>. After core has drawn the map, the Workbench imports every loaded plugin’s module at once and calls each one’s activate(wb). A slow plugin never delays the map or another plugin. Tabs, panels, commands and layers sort by order; between two plugins’ entries with the same order, which comes first depends on which plugin finished loading first, so set order when placement matters. wb is the only way in: don’t import core’s modules or reach into its DOM.

The hello example’s main.js, annotated:

export function activate(wb) {
  let greeted = 0;

  // A dock panel in the Inspect workspace. render(el) runs the first time the panel shows.
  const panel = wb.registerPanel({
    workspace: "inspect",
    id: "hello.panel",                 // every id starts with "<plugin id>."
    title: "Hello",
    order: 50,                         // after core's Details (0)
    badge: () => greeted || null,      // a count on the tab; {dirty: true, title: "…"} for unsaved work
    render(el) {
      el.innerHTML =
        '<p class="muted">Greet someone. Each greeting is a recorded Action: see the history strip.</p>' +
        '<div></div><button class="mini">Greet</button> <span class="muted" role="status"></span>';
      const [, slot, button, status] = el.children;
      // A form generated from the Action's JSON Schema (from GET /api/actions).
      const form = wb.schemaForm(slot, wb.actionSchema("hello.greet"), { name: "world" });
      button.onclick = async () => {
        const errors = form.errors();  // required fields, bounds, entries that didn't parse
        if (errors.length) { status.textContent = errors.join("; "); return; }
        try {
          // Every change is an Action: recorded in history, replayable in "Copy as Python".
          status.textContent = await wb.api.dispatch({ ...form.value(), type: "hello.greet" });
        } catch (e) {
          status.textContent = e.message;  // text, never markup
        }
      };
    },
  });

  // The count comes from the plugin's own route; host.publish("greeted") says when to re-read it.
  const refresh = async () => {
    greeted = (await wb.api.get("/count")).greeted;  // GET /api/plugins/hello/count
    panel.refreshBadge();
  };
  wb.on("greeted", () => refresh());
  refresh().catch(e => wb.toast(e.message));

  // Commands: one in the palette, one on a right-clicked map feature or table row, one for the selection.
  wb.registerCommand({
    id: "hello.greet", title: "Say hello", contexts: ["palette"],
    run: () => wb.api.dispatch({ type: "hello.greet", name: "world" }),
  });
  wb.registerCommand({
    id: "hello.greet_record", title: "Say hello to this record", contexts: ["feature", "row"],
    run: ctx => wb.api.dispatch({ type: "hello.greet", name: `${ctx.target.table} ${ctx.target.id}` }),
  });
  wb.registerCommand({
    id: "hello.greet_selection", title: "Say hello to the selection", contexts: ["selection"],
    when: ctx => ctx.selectionCount > 0,
    run: ctx => wb.api.dispatch({ type: "hello.greet", name: `${ctx.selectionCount} selected links` }),
  });
}

docs.title: The wb reference
docs.text:
Member What it gives you wb.id, wb.hostApi This plugin’s id, and the plugin API this netstead provides ("1.8"). wb.api.fetch(path, init), wb.api.get(path), wb.api.post(path, body) fetch, and JSON helpers, scoped to your router: "/count" is /api/plugins/<id>/count. A path must start with / and, once resolved (%2e%2e and \ count as .. and /), stay under that prefix; other hosts are refused. wb.api.dispatch(action) Posts any Action (yours, another plugin’s, core’s) to POST /api/actions and resolves to its result. wb.store.get(), wb.store.subscribe(keys, fn) The server state (/api/state), and a listener that fires when any of keys changes. Keys may be dotted ("plugins.hello"). get() and the listener’s argument are a frozen copy: changing it throws (changes go through Actions). Returns an unsubscribe function. wb.selection.get(), wb.selection.subscribe(fn) The active network’s shared selection (or null), as a frozen copy, and a listener for its changes. Returns an unsubscribe function. wb.registerWorkspace({id, title, layout?, badge?, order?}) A workspace tab. layout: {view: "map" \| "split" \| "table"} is its first-visit view; after that it opens in the view the user left it in. Returns an unregister function. wb.registerPanel({workspace, id, title, render?, badge?, onShow?, order?}) A dock panel. workspace is an id, a list, or "*" (every workspace). render(el) runs once, the first time it shows; onShow() each time it is shown. Returns {refreshBadge(), dispose()}. wb.registerCommand({id, title, run, contexts?, when?, group?, order?}) A command. contexts defaults to ["palette"] (see Commands). Returns an unregister function. wb.registerLayer(component, id, factory, {order?, title?}) A map layer (see Map layers). Returns an unregister function. wb.schemaForm(el, schema, value, {onChange?, omit?}) Renders a form for a JSON Schema into el (see Forms). Returns {value(), errors(), set(value), focus()}. wb.actionSchema(type), wb.hasAction(type) An Action’s JSON Schema (or null), and whether it is registered: for soft dependencies on another plugin, as host.has_action is in Python. Read from GET /api/actions before activation. wb.on(event, fn) Your own host.publish(event, payload) events ("greeted"), another plugin’s ("catalog.added"), or core’s ("core.history", "core.job"; "core.table_row" {plugin, table, id} when a row of a plugin table is clicked, "core.table_changed" {plugin, tables} when a plugin’s tables were rebuilt). They arrive over the page’s one event stream: never open your own EventSource. Returns an unsubscribe function. wb.showPanel(id) Shows a panel, switching workspace when the current one doesn’t have it. wb.showTable(name) Shows a table in the table pane (one you registered with host.register_table), opening the pane beside the map when only the map shows. Resolves once its rows show; rejects when no network is open or there is no such table. API 1.8. wb.toast(message) A short notice, prefixed with your plugin id. wb.highlight({links}) Replaces the page’s highlighted links (the highlight tool’s cyan links, listed in the Find panel) with links; wb.highlight() clears them. Nodes are not highlighted by core yet (nodes is accepted and ignored).

GET /api/actions lists every registered Action: type, class name, description (its docstring’s first line), owning plugin (null for core), mutates, assistant (whether the NL assistant may ever offer it), and its JSON schema.

Ids. Every id a plugin registers (workspace, panel, command, layer, and the id of each deck.gl layer a factory returns) starts with "<plugin id>.". Core’s ids are bare (inspect, details, links), and the plugin id core is reserved.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
run(ctx) and when(ctx) get one context:

Key What it is network {id, version, derived_from} of the active network, or null. selection, selectionCount The active network’s shared selection ({net_id, link_ids, …}) and its number of links. A selection with no links counts as none. focus The record last clicked, {table, id}, or null. highlights The highlighted link ids (an array). workspace The active workspace’s id. target The right-clicked record, {table, id}: a map feature or grid row, or the focused record in the palette’s “For …” group. null otherwise. state The server state.

Everything in ctx is a frozen copy: changing it throws, and the page’s own state is untouched. Changes go through Actions. A panel’s or workspace’s badge(ctx) gets the same context.

Where each context shows:

contexts entry Where "palette" The command palette (Ctrl+K, ⌘K on a Mac, or Commands… in the header). "feature" Right-click on a link or node on the map. "row" Right-click on a table row. "selection" Selection actions ▾ in the Selection panel, a “Selection (n links)” section in the map and row menus, and in the palette.

The palette is also the keyboard way to a context menu: with a record focused it lists that record’s feature and row commands under “For ‹table› ‹id›”, and the selection’s under “Selection (n links)”. A command’s group shows as “Group ▸ Title” in menus and the palette. A menu opens only when a command applies; with none, the map keeps its right-drag rotate and a table row the browser’s own menu.

Declarative first. Every plugin Action also gets a generated palette command, “‹Plugin›: ‹Action›…” (for hello, “Hello: Greet…”). It opens a dialog with the Action’s schema form and a Run button, so a plugin that ships no JavaScript is still usable.

docs.title: Badges
docs.text: badge(ctx) returns a count, a string, or {text, dirty, title}, or nothing for no badge. It is re-evaluated on every server-state change, and when you call panel.refreshBadge(). dirty: true shows a dot on the panel’s tab and on its workspace tab, so unsaved work is visible from anywhere.

docs.title: Map layers
docs.text:
wb.registerLayer("roadway", "hello.pins", ctx =>
  ctx.focus && ctx.focus.table === "node"
    ? new ctx.deck.ScatterplotLayer({ id: "hello.pins", data: [/* … */], getPosition: d => d.xy, getRadius: 8 })
    : null,
  { title: "Hello pins", order: 350 });
  • factory(ctx) returns a deck.gl layer, a list of them, or nothing, on every map redraw. Anything that isn’t a deck.gl layer, or a layer whose id doesn’t start with "<plugin id>.", is left out and reported (core’s ids drive picking, tooltips and box-select).
  • ctx has deck (the page’s deck.gl), server, style, selection, focus, highlights (a Set), related, marker, zoom, net and attrs. server, selection, focus, related and marker are frozen copies and highlights is a copy. net and attrs (the decoded network and its attributes) are too big to copy on each redraw, so they are the page’s own: read them, never change them.
  • Core’s layers, bottom to top: base 100, selection 200, related 300, highlighted 400, focus 500, marker 600. A plugin layer defaults to 350: above related records, under the user’s highlights, focus and marker.
  • A title lists the layer under the View tab, with a show/hide switch (per browser tab, not recorded).
  • "transit" is accepted as a component and not drawn yet.

docs.title: Forms
docs.text: wb.schemaForm(el, schema, value, {onChange, omit}) is the Settings dialog’s field renderer, made general: text, numbers (with their bounds), checkboxes, menus for enums and Literals, lists, one level of nested object as a group, and JSON for anything else. A const property (an Action’s type) gets no field, and omit drops others by name. value() is what the form shows: a checkbox’s or menu’s shown value is included, a field left blank is left out, and a required field that may be None sends null (its blank choice reads “None”). errors() lists required fields left empty, numbers out of bounds, and entries that didn’t parse. The server validates again.

docs.title: Styling
docs.text: Use core’s classes (mini, ghost, muted, pcount, row, sw) so your panel looks like the rest of the Workbench. Scope your own CSS under [data-panel="<your panel id>"], the panel’s container. If you ship a stylesheet, add a <link> for it from activate.

docs.title: When plugin code fails
docs.text:
Every call into plugin code is contained, so one plugin’s bug never breaks core or another plugin:

Call When it throws (or its promise rejects) activate(wb) (or the module import, or no activate, or the import and activate taking more than 5 s together) Everything it registered is removed, and later registrations and listeners (wb.on, subscribe) through that wb are refused. A panel’s render The panel shows “This panel failed to load: …”. A badge No badge. onShow, a wb.on or wb.store / wb.selection listener Skipped for that call. A command’s when The command doesn’t apply. A command’s run Nothing else happens. A layer factory That layer isn’t drawn.

Each failure is logged to the browser console, shown in a notice (“Plugin hello: …”), and listed under the plugin in Settings → Plugins. A failure that would repeat on every redraw (a badge, a layer, a when, a listener) is reported once per message. A command’s run is reported every time the user runs it, so they always see why nothing happened, but it is listed once.

Only calls core makes into your code are contained this way. An error thrown from your own timer (setTimeout, setInterval), an event handler you attached yourself, or a promise you don’t return to core reaches the browser console but isn’t attributed to your plugin or listed in Settings → Plugins. Catch those yourself (and wb.toast if the user should know).

Every string a plugin hands core (titles, badges, menu labels, schema text) is shown as text, never as markup. Markup you write into your own panel’s el is yours to escape.

docs.title: Test a plugin
docs.text:
