  • projectcard: the ProjectCard schema and validator.

docs.title: Explore networks in the Netstead Workbench
Explore networks in the Netstead Workbench
When to use this
docs.text: You want to look around a network interactively. That means panning the map, browsing tables, checking what a selection phrase resolves to, and copying the exact Python that reproduces what you did. For a single self-contained HTML file to send someone, see View a network on a map.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
New to the Workbench? Quickstart: the Workbench walks through open, select, validate, fix, replay and save on the bundled Leavenworth network in ten minutes.

uv run netstead app ./my-network

Open http://127.0.0.1:8850. Open more networks with the Open (folder) icon in the header: it opens a menu with up to three recent networks, then Browse / import… for the full wizard (see below). Switch between open networks with the network picker. netstead viz and netstead select-serve are aliases of netstead app (the old standalone apps they used to start are gone).

uv run netstead app ./base ./build --port 8900 --basemap esri --provider anthropic

The server binds 127.0.0.1 by default. While bound to a local host (127.0.0.1, localhost, or [::1]), it only accepts requests whose Host header names that same local address, and it rejects any cross-origin write (a POST from a page with a different origin, or flagged Sec-Fetch-Site: cross-site). --host 0.0.0.0 exposes it to the rest of the network — there’s no authentication in front of it, so don’t do that on a shared network.

Exposing the Workbench needs explicit roots. netstead app refuses a non-loopback host (from --host, NETSTEAD_APP__HOST or a config file) while io.allowed_roots is empty, because empty means your home folder and the server-side file browser described below would show it to anyone on the network. It exits with code 2 and says how to fix it. List the folders you want to share first, in ./netstead.toml or your user config.toml (see Which folders the app can read and write), or for one run with NETSTEAD_IO__ALLOWED_ROOTS='["/data/networks"]'. Paths you name on the command line are allowed for that session, but they don’t count as explicit roots. Blank entries such as [""] are rejected (a blank path would mean the current folder). Other loopback spellings, such as 127.0.0.2 or LOCALHOST, are refused too while the roots are empty: the Host-header check above only covers 127.0.0.1, localhost and ::1, so use one of those.

Plugins. Installed Workbench plugins are full-trust Python running inside this server, and an exposed bind exposes their routes and Actions too. Install only plugins you trust, and turn one off with [app] disabled_plugins = ["<id>"].

docs.title: Open or import a network
docs.text:
Open → Browse / import… opens a wizard with four sources:

  • GMNS on this machine: a server-side file browser. Entries are tagged (GMNS folder, .zip, .duckdb, datapackage.json); pick one and it opens in place. Nothing is uploaded.
  • GMNS at a URL (s3://, gs://, az://, https://): Check says whether the URL is reachable, which credential source would be used (env, keyring, netrc, or none; never the secret), and which tables it found.
  • Build from OpenStreetMap or Build from Overture: choose an area by drawing a rectangle (drag its corners to adjust), typing W,S,E,N or a point plus a buffer, or searching for a place and picking one of the outlines. You can instead pick a local file: a .osm XML file or an Overpass JSON export for OSM, or an Overture snapshot folder holding segment.parquet + connector.parquet (see netstead.overture.layout).

Below the four sources, Included examples lists the networks that ship with netstead (Leavenworth, WA and an RDU I-40 interchange stretch), each with its link and node counts. One click opens it, with no path to look up and no need for it to sit under io.allowed_roots. Once you pick a source, the ‹ (Back) button at the top-left of the dialog returns to this list; Esc closes the dialog.

A build always writes to the output folder and format you choose (Parquet, CSV, DuckDB, or Zip) and then opens the result from disk, so what you see is what was saved. It never overwrites an existing output; a leftover hidden .partial-* staging folder from a crashed build is cleaned up automatically once it’s more than 24 hours old. The output name must be a plain file name — no path separators, no trailing dot — and if it ends in a format suffix (.zip, .duckdb, .csv, .parquet), that suffix must match the format you chose.

Before a build runs, the wizard shows an estimate of its time and size, from a quick count (Overpass out count, or a DuckDB COUNT(*) over Overture) and a simple cost model. When the estimate is over app.approve_above_s (90 s by default), or when the count fails, the button changes to Run (~N min) or Run anyway, and the build only starts when you click it. The cost model’s numbers are in netstead/workbench/data/build_cost.toml; they are rough, so treat the estimate as a guide.

Opens and builds run as background jobs. The Jobs button in the header shows their stage and progress and lets you cancel one; a cancel takes effect when the job reaches its next stage.

docs.title: Which folders the app can read and write
docs.text:
The file browser, opening a local path, and build input and output folders are all limited to io.allowed_roots. When that list is empty (the default) it means your home folder. Paths given to netstead app on the command line are always allowed for that session.

A remote source must look like scheme://host/... (for example s3://bucket/net) and must not contain any .. path segments. file:// and duckdb:// sources are treated as local paths in disguise and are checked against io.allowed_roots like any other local path.

Credentials never go in the URL: a source with user:password@ in it is refused. Put them where the credential cascade looks instead (environment variables, the system keyring, or ~/.netrc). A presigned URL’s query string (?X-Amz-Signature=…, an Azure SAS token) is accepted and kept in the session history, because the replay script needs it to open the same object; it is stripped from error messages, job labels, the network summary, and the Open menu’s recents list. Treat a copied Session as Python script that opened a signed URL as holding that (expiring) signature.

# ./netstead.toml
[io]
allowed_roots = ["~/networks", "/data/gmns"]

[app]
approve_above_s = 120

docs.title: The same thing from Python
docs.text:
A build is an ordinary action, so the history strip shows it as Python you can replay. The replayed call always passes approved=True, because re-running a build you already approved counts as approval.

from netstead.workbench import BuildNetwork, Session

app = Session()
app.do(
    BuildNetwork(
        source="osm",
        area={"kind": "bbox", "bbox": (-78.91, 35.98, -78.88, 36.01)},
        output_dir="/home/me/networks",
        output_format="parquet",
        name="durham-core",
        approved=True,
    )
)

Without approved=True, a build over the threshold raises netstead.workbench.ApprovalRequired, and its .estimate holds the estimate.

Three things to know before replaying a session’s script:

  • Folders trusted on the command line are not in the history. netstead app /data/net allows /data/net for that session only, without recording an action. A replay in a new Session() only gets your configured io.allowed_roots, so an open or build under such a folder fails with PathNotAllowed. Add the folder to io.allowed_roots (config file or NETSTEAD_IO__ALLOWED_ROOTS), or pass it as an override: Session(overrides={"io.allowed_roots": ["/data/net"]}).
  • Builds never overwrite. Replaying a BuildNetwork whose output already exists fails with … already exists. Point the replay at a fresh output_dir, or move the earlier output away first.
  • Saves never overwrite either. A replayed SaveNetwork writes its copy again, so it fails with … already exists while the earlier copy is still there; a second replay of the same script always does. Its accept_warnings=True accepts the edit warnings the network has when the replay runs, which need not be the ones you reviewed when you saved.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Every section, key, type and default is listed in the Settings reference.

The workbench reads layered settings. From lowest to highest precedence:

  1. built-in defaults
  2. ~/.config/netstead/config.toml
  3. ./netstead.toml
  4. NETSTEAD_<SECTION>__<FIELD> environment variables
  5. command-line flags
# ./netstead.toml
[app]
port = 8900

[viz]
basemap = "esri"

[select]
provider = "anthropic"

docs.title: The Settings dialog
docs.text:
The gear icon in the header (tooltip “Settings”) opens a form built from the same settings model. Each field has a badge showing where its current value comes from: default, user, project, env or session.

  • Save to chooses the layer a change is written to: User (all projects) (your user file, the default), This project (./netstead.toml), or This session only (nothing is written to disk). Every change is a SetSetting action, so it appears in the history and replays from Python.
  • Reset removes the value from the layer it comes from. Emptying a field does the same in the Save to layer. If the value comes from another layer, the dialog points you to Reset instead. A number the browser can’t read, such as 1e, is never saved: the dialog says so and keeps the saved value.
  • A value set by a NETSTEAD_* environment variable outranks both files. The form says so when a saved value would not take effect.
  • Keys read only at launch, such as the app server’s port, are tagged applies on next launch. A session value has no effect on them.
  • io.allowed_roots is read-only here. The folders the app may read and write can only be widened in a config file, an environment variable, or on the command line.
  • A basemap change applies at once, without reloading the page.
  • Language models is a section of the same dialog. Models…, in the model picker (the robot icon in the header), opens it too.
  • The dialog is keyboard-friendly: focus starts in it, Tab stays inside it, and Esc closes it and returns focus to where you were.

docs.title: Linked map and table
docs.text:
The map and the table are linked both ways. Three sets drive what you see:

  • the selection, which is recorded: a natural-language select, or Set as selection;
  • the highlights, links you click or shift-drag a box over in Highlight mode; these are not recorded;
  • the focus, the one record you last clicked on the map or in the table. It is not recorded either.

Focus is a view. Clicking never changes the selection.

  • Focus. Click a link or node on the map: its details show and, when the table shows that table, its row is outlined and scrolled into view (on whichever page it sits). Click a row: it is focused, and the map flies to it.
  • Show in the table bar picks the rows:
  • All rows;
  • Selection: the selected links, or the rows of another table that point at them (for example their lanes);
  • Highlighted: the same for the highlighted links. A shift-drag box in Highlight mode switches to it.
  • Related: the records related to the highlighted links. A focused record only tints rows; it does not change this list. So clicking a row here focuses it without changing the list.
  • Foreign keys. A key column such as from_node_id is a link. Click it to open the node table at that row; the map marks the node and flies to it.
  • Related records. Rows a foreign key away from what is focused or highlighted are tinted in every table and on the map. Examples are the lanes of a link, a link’s end nodes, and the links at a node.
  • The keys come from the GMNS spec, not a hard-coded list.
  • The table list shows how many records are related in each table (N related; a + means the count stopped early). Hover a tinted row to see which key relates it, for example related via lane.link_id → link.
  • With Show → Related, the Related control chooses how far to follow keys: 1 step (direct references, such as the links at a node) or 2 steps (references of references, such as then their lanes). It shows only for that scope. The i button beside it explains Related with an example, using the real record counts when something is highlighted or focused. 2 steps reaches new tables only; it never loops back to one already reached.
  • Related records are a read-only view. Nothing is recorded.

docs.title: Workspaces, panels and commands
docs.text:
• Command palette. Press Ctrl+K (⌘K on a Mac), or click the >_ terminal icon in the header (tooltip “Commands (⌘K / Ctrl+K)”) when it shows, to search every command: open a network, Settings, zoom, the view modes. With a record focused it also lists that record’s commands (“For link 123”), and the selection’s (“Selection (3 links)”). Arrow keys pick, Enter runs, Escape closes.
  • Right-click a link or node on the map, or a table row, for its commands. Core puts one command there: Fix…, on a record that has an issue or an edit warning (see Validate and fix). Edit and Delete are in the palette (Edit record…, Delete record…) and in Inspect, not in the menu. With no command for a record (no issue, and no plugin command), right-click opens no menu: the map keeps its right-drag rotate and the row the browser’s own menu.
  • Workspaces and the dock. When a plugin adds a workspace, tabs for each appear in the header; each keeps the map / split / table view you left it in. The right drawer is a dock, with a tab per panel at its top, in order: The tabs are icons (hover for the name; counts stay as a badge on the icon): Find (magnifier; the selection form or box, anchors, diagnostics, export, saved selections and highlighted links), View (sliders; the layers, color and width, direction and filter controls), Inspect (info; the focused record; comes forward automatically when you click a map feature or a table row), Edit (pencil; the edit list, undo/redo, edit warnings and “Save selection as card…”), Cards (stacked cards; the project-cards plugin’s panel, when it’s installed) and Validate (shield with a check; run / export, status, facets and the grouped findings list), then Assistant (chat bubble), then any panel another plugin adds. The map itself keeps only its zoom/highlight/fit buttons and the legend; the old Layers and Map display popovers are gone, and their controls live in the View tab. A tab’s badge is one pill at its icon’s corner (orange while edits are unsaved) and the tooltip says what it counts. The Edit tab’s help paragraph hides behind its ×; the ⓘ beside the heading brings it back. Draggable handles between the map and the table, and between the map/table and the side panel, resize them (double-click a handle to reset; sizes are remembered per browser).
  • Settings → Plugins lists the installed Workbench plugins: version, the plugin API each needs and whether it fits, and any error loading it. Its switch turns a plugin on or off; that applies the next time netstead app starts.

docs.title: Validate and fix
docs.text:
• Run validation: the play icon in the Validate tab (tooltip “Run validation”), or in the command palette, Ctrl+K / ⌘K, checks the spec, the keys and the quality rules as a background job; the Jobs badge counts it while it runs. The quality rules read Settings → Validation (validation.rules, keyed by rule code, such as quality.high_speed_residential).
  • When it finishes, the panel reads Validated v0: 271 warnings, 16 info (for the Leavenworth fixture), the header’s validity light turns green / amber / red with the counts on hover, and each located issue is a dot on the map. The Validate tab badge counts what needs attention: a red pill with the number of errors when there are any, else an amber pill with the number of warnings (open edit warnings included), else no pill. Info findings are never counted; hover for the whole breakdown (“Validate — 3 errors, 1 warning, 16 info”, “Validate — clean”, “Validate — not run yet”).
  • Click an issue: its record is focused, the map flies to it, and when the table shows that table its row is scrolled into view and marked. Click a dot on the map: the Validate panel opens on This record, that record’s issues. Rows with issues carry a mark in the table. A located finding also carries a crosshair “zoom to” icon as an explicit affordance.
  • Findings are grouped by type. One collapsible row per rule code and severity (“▸ quality.high_speed_residential warning 271”), with the rule’s fix hint shown once, ordered errors first, then warnings, then info, largest group first. Open a group to see its findings (50 at a time, with Show more), each with its crosshair “zoom to” and Fix. Groups are built from every finding, not from one page. For structural findings (such as the sixteen structural.missing_optional_resource lines a partial GMNS package produces) the row names the resources instead of a hint.
  • Filter with the Severity, Table and Type menus (each starts with an “All …” choice; Type lists the finding types with their counts). This record lists only the focused record’s issues, with its groups already open. Issues with no place on the map (a table-level check, a row whose node has no coordinates) are also listed under Unlocated, where repeated structural findings fold into one row.
  • Fix on an issue opens the record editor on that issue’s record, on the column the issue names (or the whole record when it names none), prefilled with the current value and with the issue as the note. Apply sends one edit with only the values you changed.
  • Stale results. An edit makes the stored validation stale: the panel says the network changed since: re-run, the button’s tooltip becomes Re-run validation, and the validity light turns amber-outlined. The list and the dots stay until you re-run, so you can work down them. If two runs overlap, the newer one wins; the older one finishing later says so and leaves the panel alone.
  • Export report: the download icon next to the run icon (tooltip “Export report (HTML)”) downloads the offline HTML validation report (<network>-validation.html) for a current (not stale) validation. It needs the reports extra. The report itself opens with a severity summary line, the source path once, a Resources table of every spec resource (required/optional, present, row count), and the grouped structural findings collapsed under Unlocated findings.

The same from Python:

from netstead.workbench import RunValidation

app.do(RunValidation())  # a job; the result has counts, version, stale and superseded

docs.title: Edit tables
docs.text:
Edits change the network you opened in memory. Nothing is written to disk until you save a copy, and the source is never overwritten.

  • A cell. Click a row to focus it, then click one of its cells, type, and press Enter (Escape cancels and discards; an empty value clears the cell). Leaving the cell — clicking elsewhere, tabbing away — applies the edit too, as in a spreadsheet. A text column completes from the spec’s allowed values plus the column’s existing values (a <datalist> under the cell); a comma-list column such as allowed_uses completes one token at a time and says “comma-separated”. The key column and geometry are not edited in place. A value the column cannot hold (1.5 lanes) is refused with a toast, and nothing changes; a value outside the spec’s allowed list (an out-of-enum categorical, such as facility_type = "boulevard") is kept, not dropped, and the cell is outlined in red with a warning icon, the reason as its tooltip.
  • A record. Edit… in Inspect, or Edit record… in the palette for the focused record, opens a form for every editable column. When the record is a link in a multi-link selection, a checkbox applies the same values to every selected link. The note you type is kept with the edit.
  • Fix… opens the same editor from an issue, or from right-clicking a record that has one.
  • Delete… (Inspect, the record editor, or Delete record… in the palette) first runs a dry run and says what goes with the record: a link takes its lanes and time-of-day rows (Delete 1 link row? This also deletes 2 lane rows, 1 link_tod row. Undo is in the Edit tab.). Confirm to delete. A node a link still uses cannot be deleted: the refusal names the links. The delete runs against the network version the dry run planned on: if another Workbench action (or a plugin’s or your Python’s mutate) changed the network in between, it is refused and you confirm again. A replayed delete has no dry run: it deletes the ids and whatever depends on them in the network it runs against.
  • Adding rows is Python or the API only: app.do(AddRows(table="node", rows=[{...}])).
  • Each edit is one action in the session history (so “copy as Python” replays it), bumps the network’s version, and is listed in the Edit tab with what it changed.

docs.title: Undo and redo
docs.text:
The undo icon in the Edit tab (tooltip “Undo last edit”; also in Inspect, or Undo last edit in the palette) reverses your newest edit. Undo is last-in, first-out across everything that changed the network, and the Workbench only undoes its own edits:

  • If the newest change came from Python (session.mutate(...) outside an action), Undo is unavailable and says The last change was made from Python; undo it there. Undo it with session.undo_last(net_id, source="python").
  • If a plugin made it, Undo names the plugin: undo it in that plugin.
  • Undo puts the rows it restores at the end of their table, not where they were: a deleted row, and also the earlier version of a row you changed. Row order carries no meaning in GMNS, but an unsorted table shows those rows last. (An edit itself keeps the row where it is.)

The redo icon next to it (tooltip “Redo”) re-applies the edit undo_edit most recently took back — app.do(RedoEdit()) — and is disabled (“nothing to redo”) until there is an undone edit waiting, or whenever any other change to the network clears it.

docs.title: Live warnings
docs.text: An edit the spec disagrees with is still applied, and warned about at once: a foreign key that is not in the referenced table, a required field left empty, a value of the wrong type or outside the allowed list, or a duplicate key. The cell is outlined (hover for why), the row is marked, and the warning is listed under Edit warnings in the Edit tab, with Fix. A later edit that puts it right clears the warning. The live check covers the rows an edit touched; after a very large edit it stops early and says so, and Run validation checks everything.

docs.title: What the selection does after an edit
docs.text:
A selection follows an edit of links or nodes:

  • one made by a query (a natural-language select) is resolved again against the edited network, so it may gain or lose links;
  • one made by clicking or by ids keeps its links, minus any you deleted (and is cleared when none is left).

An edit of lanes or time-of-day rows leaves the selection alone. Undo restores the links, but an id selection does not take back a link it lost.

A query selection with a pinned anchor whose node the edit takes off the facility is not lost: it keeps the links it had (minus any you deleted) and its resolved status, and keeps the pin. The Find tab says Stale pin at its top: those links are no longer what the query gives. Re-pin the anchor, or Unpin it.

docs.title: Save a copy
docs.text:
The Save icon in the header (tooltip “Save a copy…”; or Save a copy… in the palette) opens the save dialog: name the copy, pick a format, then Choose folder… inside your allowed folders, and Save. The save runs as a job and writes a new folder or file; the network you opened, local or remote, is never written to, and a copy inside the source folder is refused.

  • It never overwrites. If the name already exists in that folder, the save fails with … already exists.
  • Warnings are confirmed. With edit warnings open, the dialog lists them and a checkbox asks whether to save anyway. If the live check failed or stopped early, it says that instead (the warning count may be 0, and proves nothing) and asks the same. Saving anyway is recorded as SaveNetwork(..., accept_warnings=True). The server checks again when the job runs, and asks again if something changed.
  • When the job ends, a toast says where the copy went and which tables differ from the source. The badge on the Edit tab and in the network switcher (• 1 unsaved) counts edits no saved copy holds yet, and clears. If the network was edited while saving, the copy holds the version the save started from and the later edits stay unsaved; if it was closed while saving, nothing is marked saved.
  • Replay. A replayed SaveNetwork writes the copy again (and fails if it is still there), and its accept_warnings=True accepts whatever warnings the network has when the replay runs. See Every action is replayable.

docs.title: Find: the offline form and the language-model box
docs.text:
For everything you can type, which requests need a language model, and how fast each is, see Find links by describing them.

With Offline (pattern) chosen, the Find tab is a form, so you never have to guess the phrasing:

Pattern Blanks Sentence sent to Select Street Street Pine Street Street between two cross streets Street, From cross street, To cross street Pine Street between Orchard Street and Central Avenue All links of a type Facility type All residential links Link ids Ids Links 59, 60

Street and cross-street fields suggest the open network’s street names; after you pick a Street, the cross streets are narrowed to the streets that meet it. The assembled sentence shows under the form, and Select sends exactly that sentence (so the history and the replay script read as they always have). A blank that is still empty blocks Select and is named under the form. Ask keeps its own behavior; offline it understands only a few fixed requests (see Ask the assistant), which its tooltip says.

Choose a language model in the header and the free-text box comes back, prefilled with the last sentence; choosing Offline again restores the form. The offline parser also reads <street> from <A> to <B>, with the same cross-street names the resolver uses for between.

docs.title: Verify a selection
docs.text:
• The Find tab shows the selection’s status, its anchors and diagnostics.
  • An ambiguous selection lists the other nodes each anchor could be, also drawn on the map as rings (the anchor-candidates overlay draws automatically; there is no separate toggle). To pin the anchor to one, click one in the Find tab, or Pin node N to keep the resolver’s own choice; the selection is resolved again. Unpin goes back to the resolver’s choice. In Python: app.do(PinAnchor(role="to", node_id=60)).
  • A pin that resolves nothing (a node off the facility, or one with no path to the other anchor) is refused, and the selection you were checking stays as it was.
  • A pin is part of the selection’s query, so it survives an edit and a saved selection’s reuse. When an edit takes the pinned node off the facility, see What the selection does after an edit.
  • Export shows a resolved selection in the Fragment box, as a GMNS fragment (checked against the selection schema) or a ProjectCard facility object, one form at a time: Segment (the facility’s name plus the from/to anchors, which a tool can resolve again on another version of the network) or Link list (only the resolved link ids). The box changes as soon as you change an option; the utterance is a caption under it, not part of the fragment. IDs picks the id system: GMNS (link_id, node_id), OpenStreetMap (osm_way_id, osm_node_id) or Overture GERS (overture_segment_id, overture_connector_id). A system the network has no columns for is disabled, with the reason as its tooltip (the Leavenworth example has OSM ids, not GERS). Several links can share one OSM way, so the list is deduplicated and a caption says so (“3 links share OSM way 5847010”), and when a way also covers links outside the selection (“OSM way 5846369 also covers 11 links outside this selection”). ProjectCard has no key for GERS ids, so that choice is disabled for ProjectCard objects. A selection made by clicking links has no named segment: Segment is disabled, with the tooltip “This selection has no named segment; use Link list”. The copy button at the top right of the box copies the fragment to the clipboard. A saved selection’s Export still downloads a file, in the form and ID system chosen here. With a stale pin, Segment is refused (the query no longer gives those links), and Link list exports with a warning.
  • Save selection… keeps the selection under a name; Use brings it back, resolved on the network as it is now. app.do(SaveSelection(name="ski hill")), app.do(UseSelection(name="ski hill")). Export on a saved selection resolves it the same way without making it current, and warns when its network is not open (it then exports it as saved). Saved selections last for the session, up to 50 (a replayed history saves them again).
  • A save belongs to the network it was made on: its id and its source’s location (scheme, host and path, never a URL’s query string, so a re-signed link to the same file still matches). Networks added from Python all have the source <python>, so two of those under the same id are not told apart.

docs.title: Style, filter and navigate
docs.text:
The map’s style and link filter are set from the View tab (its layer toggles, color and width pickers, direction controls and Filter links replace the old map popovers). Nodes colored by ctrl_type use a fixed style where size carries meaning too (signals large and red, stop signs orange or amber, yield yellow, uncontrolled nodes small and grey) and signals draw on top; other columns use the generic palette.

  • Color links by / Color nodes by pick a categorical or numeric column for links and nodes independently (app.do(Style(color_by="facility_type")), app.do(Style(node_color_by="ctrl_type"))). A fresh network defaults to coloring links by facility_type and nodes by ctrl_type when those columns exist, falling back to a single color otherwise.
  • The color swatches beside Links, Nodes and Selection set a single color. Picking the Links or Nodes swatch while that layer is colored by a column turns Color links by / Color nodes by off in the same recorded action (Style(colors=..., node_color_by="none")), since a column coloring would hide the swatch.
  • Each section of the View tab (Layers, Overlays, Color, Width, Direction, Show only links where…) folds open and closed; the tab remembers which are folded in this browser. Overlays lists a plugin’s or core’s map layers (issue markers, anchor candidates) with a switch and an info tooltip saying what each draws.
  • On the map, a click, right-click or hover picks only layers that are switched on, and when a node and a link are both under the pointer the node wins (so nodes can be inspected where links run through them).
  • Width by sizes links by a numeric column (app.do(Style(width_by="lanes"))).
  • Show only links where… (the View tab’s filter; it hides the other links on the map and in the table’s Filtered view and never changes the data) dims every link that doesn’t match (app.do(Filter(where=[{"col": "lanes", "op": "gte", "val": 2}]))); the table’s Filtered scope lists the matching links (the filter applies to links: on the node table it lists every node). Filter(where=None) clears it. Filters are fields and operators only, never free text or SQL: contains matches a plain substring, between takes an inclusive [low, high] range, and any_of / all_of / none_of match a list of values against a comma-separated cell such as allowed_uses (so “auto” matches “auto,truck,walk”); each value is read as its column’s type ("2" on lanes is 2; a value the column can’t hold is refused). The in operator (a list of values) is available from Python and the API only.
  • app.do(Navigate(record={"table": "link", "id": 170})) flies the map to one link or node.

docs.title: Column filters in the table
docs.text:
Each table column header carries a funnel icon instead of a text box. Click it to open a popover whose body depends on the column’s kind:

  • a numeric column offers = ≠ < ≤ > ≥ between is empty is not empty, with one or two number inputs;
  • a text or boolean column offers a checklist of its distinct values (searchable past 12), under any of / all of / none of (all of only for a comma-list column such as allowed_uses), plus a contains text tab and is empty / is not empty.

Apply turns the popover into a removable chip in the strip above the grid (for example free_speed > 40 or allowed_uses any of auto, truck); a Clear all chip appears once two or more are active. The strip is hidden when there are no filters, so it takes no space. Column filters and the Filter links map filter are independent: the grid’s filters only narrow what the table shows.

docs.title: Ask the assistant
docs.text:
• Type a request in the Find tab’s box and press Ask (or Ctrl+Enter / ⌘Enter); Enter alone still selects. The Assistant panel (every workspace, or Ask the assistant… in the palette) keeps the conversation, for this session only: Clear empties it, and it is gone when the Workbench stops.
  • It uses the provider and model chosen next to the Find tab’s selection box (hover the model to see its full name when it’s truncated). With Offline (pattern) it understands a few fixed commands (color by lanes, width by lanes, filter lanes >= 2, clear the filter, zoom to the selection, zoom to link 170, select <street>, save the selection as <name>, set lanes to 3 on the selection).
  • Steps that only change the view or the selection run at once, and each is listed with its app.do(...) line. Steps that change a network or something you made (edits, deletions, undo, saving a copy, and, once you allow them, changing a setting, building a network or deleting a saved selection) wait in one draft: Approve runs them all in order and stops at the first failure, Reject drops them, and a step’s Edit… opens its form prefilled (running it from there is an ordinary action; the draft stays pending). A draft is refused once a network it touches has changed, and a new question replaces it.
  • Everything it runs is in the session history (the strip shows #12 · assistant) and in “Session as Python”, which replays it with no model.
  • What it sends is listed at the top of the panel. To a remote provider: your question, the recent conversation (your words, and its steps as action names and counts), the tool schemas, the networks’ names and sizes, column names and what the GMNS spec says they mean, the selection’s status and size, how many selections are saved, the filter’s size, the map style’s columns, the number of pending edits, whether validation is out of date, and validation counts, plus the shipped guide. Street names, the selection’s utterance, selected ids, saved selection names, issue counts by rule, column values and project notes go only to a local model unless you opt in (llm.quality.grounding, project_context). Network tables and what actions return are never sent, and a local model’s answer that used them is not passed on to a remote one.
  • Small local models get help, and the panel says so. A read-only step with a field its tool doesn’t have (or, for a style, a malformed one) runs without it, and the answer lists what was left out (“Left out: …”); a step that changes a network is never changed this way, it is asked for again. A field that belongs to another read-only tool becomes a step of its own: “select Ski Hill Drive and color by lanes” folded into one select is run as a select and a style (“Split: …”); if the field could belong to more than one tool, or to one that changes a network, the model is asked again. The model sees what each GMNS column means (free_speed is the speed limit). With assistant.compact_tools = "auto" (the default) a model on this machine is offered fewer tools: the read-only ones that apply now (no network switch with one network open, no saved selection to reuse when none is saved) plus edit, delete, undo and the plugin Actions marked assistant_compact. "on" does this for any model, "off" never; it never offers more than assistant.actions / assistant.plugins allow. Measured with scripts/eval_nl_assistant.py on qwen2.5:7b (15 requests, 3 runs): 39/45 correct (87%), every answer valid. It still drops the second half of “select …, then save it as …”: ask in two steps.
  • Limits: assistant.remote_token_budget (200,000 tokens a session, shared by every remote provider and model; a local model is counted, never stopped), output_token_limit, context_max_chars, max_steps, history_turns (6 turns sent back to the model) and max_turns (50 kept). Settings → Assistant: actions & plugins shows the use so far, chooses which actions it may call and which plugins it may use (none by default), and lists names in those settings that this Workbench doesn’t know; the numbers are under Settings → Assistant.

docs.title: Language models (natural-language selection)
docs.text:
The utterance box can be read by:

  • an offline pattern parser (stub, the default — nothing leaves this machine);
  • a local model through Ollama, for example Qwen;
  • Anthropic, OpenAI or Gemini, with your own API key.

To set up a local model (install Ollama, pull qwen3:4b, troubleshoot), see Run language models locally with Ollama.

select.provider accepts anthropic, openai, gemini, ollama or stub. claude is still accepted as an alias for anthropic (existing config files keep working).

Pick a provider and model with the picker under the robot icon in the header. The choice is SetSetting(scope="session") — it applies to this session only; Make default saves the same pair with scope="user", and warns first if a project setting or a NETSTEAD_SELECT__* / NETSTEAD_SELECT__MODEL environment variable would still override it. Models… opens the Language models panel: set, replace, remove and test keys, point at another Ollama server, pull an Ollama model, tune quality and context, and browse the model catalog.

The robot itself shows whether the choice can answer, by color and by the shape of its small dot: green (circle) when the provider and model are ready (a configured key, or a reachable Ollama with the model pulled), yellow (diamond) when only the offline pattern parser is in use, and red (square) when the chosen provider is not available (missing key, Ollama not running, model not pulled). Hover for the state in words, for example “Language model: Ollama · qwen3:4b — ready” or “… — not available: Ollama is not running”, followed by what each selection sends; whether data leaves the machine is only ever said in that text, never by the color.

The defaults are each provider’s small, fast model — enough for one selection at a time — and are maintained in netstead/llm/models.toml:

Provider Default model anthropic Haiku 4.5 (claude-haiku-4-5-20251001) openai small/fast tier gemini small/fast tier ollama qwen3:4b, or an installed tool-capable model such as qwen2.5:7b when qwen3:4b isn’t installed

Pick a larger model from the picker if parses go wrong.

Requests the offline pattern parser can read with names the network has are answered without calling the model, in milliseconds instead of seconds (select.grammar_first, on by default). See When the model is called.

docs.title: Keys are write-only
docs.text:
• A key is looked up in an environment variable first (NETSTEAD_<PROVIDER>_API_KEY, or the provider’s own variable — ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, OPENAI_API_KEY, GEMINI_API_KEY), then in the OS keyring (macOS Keychain, Windows Credential Manager, or Secret Service on Linux). There is no plaintext file fallback.
  • Keys are never written to config.toml, shown in the browser, recorded in the session history, returned by any API response, or logged.
  • Set a key with uv run netstead llm set-key <provider> (a hidden prompt, or --stdin to pipe one in — never a command-line argument, so it never reaches shell history or ps), or from the Workbench’s Language models panel.
  • Keys are bound to their endpoint. If you point a provider at a different base_url (for example an OpenAI-compatible server), it needs a new key entered for that endpoint; an existing key is never sent there.
  • The Workbench’s key routes (/api/llm/keys/*, /api/llm/test, /api/llm/ollama/pull) are loopback-only (refused unless the server is bound to 127.0.0.1/localhost/[::1]) and every request must also carry an X-Netstead-Secrets: 1 header, which a cross-origin page cannot add without a CORS preflight this server never approves. When the Workbench is bound elsewhere, manage keys from a terminal with netstead llm set-key/remove-key instead, and pull models with netstead llm pull.
  • Known limitation: a key written by the CLI (or another process) while the Workbench is already running may take up to about 5 seconds to be seen by that running Workbench.

docs.title: Errors are explicit
docs.text: A missing or rejected key, a rate limit or a timeout shows as an error. The Workbench never quietly switches to another provider.

docs.title: What is sent, and quality settings
docs.text:
Every selection sends your utterance and the selection tool’s schema (GMNS field names such as lanes), never your network tables or files. The [llm.quality] settings add more, and the privacy note in the picker’s tooltip always lists exactly what the chosen provider receives. Every part of the prompt that is network- or project-sourced data (not an instruction) is fenced in its own tagged block (for example <network_vocabulary>…</network_vocabulary>) so a street name or project note can never be mistaken for a new instruction to the model.

"auto" means on for a model running on this machine (Ollama, or any loopback base_url) and off for a remote provider.

Setting Default What it does assistant_context true Sends the GMNS assistant guide that ships with netstead (data model, examples) assistant_context_max_chars 16000 Cap on that guide, in characters project_context "auto" Sends your project notes — see below — when allowed for the provider in use project_context_max_chars 4000 Cap on those notes, in characters grounding "auto" Sends the network’s most common street names and route numbers, so the model spells them as the network does grounding_max_names 200 Cap on those names few_shot false Shows the model this session’s earlier selections that resolved. Remembered only for this session, on this network — never persisted few_shot_max 3 How many of those earlier selections are shown match_retry "auto" If nothing matches, asks the model once more with the closest real names. "auto" is on for a local endpoint and off for a remote one match_candidates 5 How many close names that retry offers max_repairs 1 Re-prompts after an invalid reply temperature 0.0 Sampling temperature. A blank field restores the default; it cannot be unset from the dialog 
# ~/.config/netstead/config.toml: endpoints, choices and quality only, never keys
[select]
provider = "anthropic"
model = "claude-haiku-4-5-20251001"

[llm.ollama]
base_url = "http://localhost:11434"

[llm.quality]
grounding = "on"        # also send street names to remote providers
few_shot = true

docs.title: Project notes
docs.text:
A project’s notes are discovered next to the active network’s folder first, then in the project directory — never the process’s current working directory if neither of those applies. netstead looks, in order:

  1. A dedicated NETSTEAD.md, sent whole when found.
  2. Otherwise, AGENTS.md — and failing that, CLAUDE.md — but only its ## netstead section (any heading level ##-####, matched case-insensitively, up to the next heading at the same or a shallower level). A file without that section is treated as if it were absent: the rest of an AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md holds instructions for a coding agent, not notes for the network assistant, and is never read or sent.
  3. If neither is found, no project notes are sent.

Every candidate must resolve inside io.allowed_roots (symlinks included), so a notes file can’t be used to exfiltrate an arbitrary file on disk.

A NETSTEAD.md might read:

- "the Beltline" is I 440.
- SR-520 is the Evergreen Point Bridge.
- facility_type 7 means HOV lanes.

Or, inside an existing AGENTS.md:

## netstead
- "the Beltline" is I 440.
- SR-520 is the Evergreen Point Bridge.

docs.title: From a terminal
docs.text:
Also the way to manage keys when the Workbench is bound to a non-local address:

uv run netstead llm status
uv run netstead llm set-key anthropic
uv run netstead llm test anthropic
uv run netstead llm models ollama
uv run netstead llm pull qwen3:4b
uv run netstead select "I-40 EB between South Miami Boulevard and Airport Boulevard" ./my-network --provider ollama --model qwen3:4b

netstead select prints the selection fragment and exits 0 when the utterance resolves. Its other exit codes:

Exit code Meaning What it prints 1 Nothing matched, or the parser failed status and diagnostics 2 Invalid settings (an unknown provider, for example) the error 3 Ambiguous: an anchor could be more than one node status, the provisional link_ids, each anchor with its candidates, and diagnostics

An ambiguous selection is the same one the Workbench’s Find tab shows with its candidate rings (see Verify a selection); the CLI has no pin, so narrow the utterance or pin the anchor in the Workbench and export from there. --json puts the same fields on stdout as one JSON object.

docs.title: Every action is replayable
docs.text: Everything you do in the browser is a typed action: open, select, style, navigate, change a setting. The strip at the bottom shows the last action as Python. The code icon in the footer (tooltip “Copy session as Python”) shows the whole session as a script you can copy. Networks added from Python via Session.add_network aren’t recorded as actions and so aren’t replayed in that script. A replayed delete has no dry run: it deletes the ids and whatever depends on them in the network it runs against, which may be more (or fewer) rows than you confirmed in the browser.

docs.title: Other tools
docs.text: The Workbench is a network session, not a GIS: it owns the tables, the selection, validation and the edit history, and leaves cartography, context layers, printing and model runs to tools built for them. Save a copy as Parquet and the result opens directly in GeoLibre, QGIS or ArcGIS Pro, and feeds AequilibraE, DTALite and Path4GMNS. The Workbench and other tools says what each does best and how to move between them.

docs.title: Migrating from GMNSpy v0.3.x to Netstead v1.0
Migrating from GMNSpy v0.3.x to Netstead v1.0
docs.text:
Netstead v1.0 is the successor to GMNSpy — a ground-up rewrite published under a new name. The package name, public API, package layout, and runtime engine all changed. This guide walks GMNSpy v0.3.5 users through the breaking changes and shows the new equivalents.

If you need the old behavior, keep depending on gmnspy<1 — v0.3.5 is the last release of the old line and is no longer maintained. (An early gmnspy==1.0.0b1 preview of the rewrite was published under the old name before the rename; it has been yanked and is superseded by netstead.)

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• v1.0 is a clean rewrite — no automatic upgrade path, no compat shim, no DeprecationWarning bridges. You will edit your imports.
  • The codebase is split into two packages: corral (generic schema / validation / IO engine) and netstead (GMNS-specific bindings on top).
  • Old: import gmnspy; gmnspy.read_gmns_network(path) → New: from netstead import Network; Network.from_source(path).
  • Validation returns a single ValidationReport — multiple renderers (rich terminal / JSON / HTML) replace ad-hoc _check_* helpers.
  • Memory + performance are first-class: tables are lazy DuckDB expressions (driven through ibis). pandas / polars / Arrow are input and output formats, not engines — call .to_pandas() / .to_polars() only when you actually need the materialized frame.
  • New CLI: netstead validate, netstead info, netstead quality, and the inherited corral commands. Every data command supports --json for AI / scripting consumption.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
GMNSpy v0.3.x

pip install gmnspy

Netstead v1.0

pip install \
  "dbcorral @ git+https://github.com/e-lo/netstead.git@main#subdirectory=packages/corral" \
  "netstead @ git+https://github.com/e-lo/netstead.git@main#subdirectory=packages/netstead"

netstead depends on corral (PyPI name dbcorral). The first PyPI release under the new names is pending, so the beta installs from GitHub and names both packages; once published this is pip install netstead and corral is installed transitively. See Install and troubleshoot.

docs.title: API mapping
docs.text: GMNSpy v0.3 (removed) Netstead v1.0 (use this) Notes import gmnspy from netstead import Network Top-level helpers are gone — the entry point is the Network class. gmnspy.read_gmns_network(path) netstead.Network.from_source(path) Returns a Network (subclass of corral.Package) with lazy tables, not a dict[str, DataFrame]. gmnspy.read_gmns_csv(path, validate=True) corral.read(path) for any table; or Network.from_source(dir).<table> Format inference (csv / parquet / duckdb / zip-csv / URL) is automatic. gmnspy.validation.apply_schema_to_df(df, schema_file=...) net.validate() Schema, foreign-key, structural, and sync-state checks all run from one call. gmnspy.validation.validate_foreign_keys(...) net.validate() then keep the issues whose category is corral.validation.Category.FOREIGN_KEY (or use report.by_category()) Composite + self-referential FKs supported. gmnspy.validation._check_* helpers report = net.validate(); report.issues / report.by_severity() The Series-vs-bool truthiness bugs in constraint_checking.py are gone — predicates are ibis expressions now. gmnspy.schema.read_schema(path) corral.spec.load_package(path) / netstead.load_gmns_spec(version="0.97") Multi-version spec support; DEFAULT_SPEC = "0.97". gmnspy.schema.read_config(config_file, data_dir, schema_dir) Network.from_source(path) (auto-discovery) No more manual config wiring for the common case. gmnspy.schema.document_schemas_to_md(...) corral.docgen.schemas_to_md(package) / corral.docgen.package_to_md(package) Same idea, generalized; takes a corral.spec.DataPackage, so it honors version selection. gmnspy.utils.logger import logging; logging.getLogger("netstead") The utils grab-bag is gone. gmnspy.utils.list_to_md_table — Gone; see below. (no CLI) netstead validate <path> / netstead info <path> / netstead quality <path> / corral validate <path> Data commands accept --json; validate and convert also accept --yes to auto-approve gated ops. (no editing API) with corral.editing.Session(net) as s: netstead.clean.simplify_geometry(net, s) Atomic rollback + audit log. (no network-aware scope) netstead.scope.from_nodes(net, [...], path_between=True).apply() Network buffer, spatial buffer, connected component, zone filter — all chainable.

docs.title: What’s gone (no replacement)
docs.text:
These v0.3 surfaces were removed because they were either unsound or subsumed by the new engine:

  • gmnspy.validation.constraint_checking — the per-row validators there had latent Series-vs-bool truthiness bugs (if some_series:) that silently passed. Replaced by ibis-first predicates evaluated on pyarrow samples; the failure mode is structurally impossible.
  • gmnspy.utils — the grab-bag is gone. GMNS-specific name handling lives in netstead.semantics; logging is stdlib logging; the markdown table helper has no replacement (use corral.docgen for spec docs, or pandas.DataFrame.to_markdown).
  • Implicit pandas everywhere. Tables are lazy ibis expressions by default. If you mutated a returned DataFrame in v0.3 expecting the change to stick on the network, you must now go through an editing Session (see below).
  • read_gmns_network returning a bare dict. The Network object exposes the same tables as attributes (net.nodes, net.links, …) but those attributes return lazy Table wrappers, not DataFrames.

docs.title: What’s new
docs.text:
• Modern formats out of the box. Parquet (incl. partitioned), DuckDB, zip-CSV, and HTTP(S) URLs with a credentials cascade. Try corral.read("s3://bucket/network.parquet", credentials=...).
  • Multi-version GMNS spec. v0.95 / v0.96 / v0.97 ship side-by-side; default is 0.97. Per-call override: Network.from_source(path, spec_version="0.96").
  • Network-aware scoping. BFS, Dijkstra network buffer, spatial buffer from any link / point / node, connected-component, zone filter — chainable. See netstead.scope.
  • Data-quality framework. 7 GMNS rules out of the box; plugin pattern for custom rules. Surface: netstead quality <path>.
  • Editing with rollback. netstead.clean.simplify_geometry, merge_close_nodes, remove_orphans, recompute_lengths. All run inside an atomic corral.editing.Session with an audit log.
  • CLI + AI surface. netstead --help. Every data command takes --json for machine-readable output; netstead mcp serve runs the MCP server for Claude Desktop / Claude Code.
  • Reports. report.to_html(path) / report.to_json() / report.to_rich() render the same ValidationReport for humans, CI, or dashboards.

docs.title: Worked example: load + validate + filter a network
docs.text:
GMNSpy v0.3.5

import gmnspy
import pandas as pd

# Load — returns a dict[str, DataFrame], validates eagerly
network = gmnspy.read_gmns_network("path/to/gmns/dir")

nodes = network["node"]
links = network["link"]

# Re-validate one table by hand
gmnspy.validation.apply_schema_to_df(
    nodes,
    schema_file="gmnspy/spec/node.schema.json",
    originating_file="node.csv",
)

# Filter to a subnetwork — pandas only, no FK awareness
keep = nodes[nodes["zone_id"] == 42]["node_id"]
sub_links = links[links["from_node_id"].isin(keep) & links["to_node_id"].isin(keep)]

Netstead v1.0

from netstead import Network
from netstead import scope

# Load — lazy, format-agnostic, no eager validation
net = Network.from_source("path/to/gmns/dir")  # or .parquet / .duckdb / URL

# Validate everything (schema + FK + structural + sync-state) in one call
report = net.validate()
if not report.is_clean:
    report.to_rich()           # pretty-print to terminal
    report.to_html("report.html")
    raise SystemExit(1)

# Network-aware subnetwork: zone filter with FK pushdown to every related
# table (for a component, use scope.connected_component(net, seed_node_id))
sub = scope.from_zone(net, [42]).apply()

# Materialize only when you need to
nodes_df = sub.nodes.to_pandas()

Equivalent from the shell:

netstead validate path/to/gmns/dir --json > report.json
netstead info     path/to/gmns/dir
netstead quality  path/to/gmns/dir --json

docs.title: Breaking changes checklist
docs.text:
Before you upgrade, scan your codebase for each of these:

  • Requirement gmnspy replaced with netstead.
  • All from gmnspy import … and from gmnspy.* import … imports refactored to netstead — submodule paths changed too.
  • Calls to read_gmns_csv / read_gmns_network replaced with Network.from_source(...) (or corral.read(...) for a single table).
  • Code that mutated returned DataFrames in place now uses corral.editing.Session (or explicitly materializes with .to_pandas() and treats the result as a snapshot).
  • Validation call sites updated — they receive a ValidationReport, not bare lists or None. Check report.is_clean / iterate report.issues.
  • Tests that imported gmnspy.validation._check_* helpers switch to Network.validate() (or corral.Package.validate() for non-GMNS packages).
  • gmnspy.utils imports rerouted: logger → stdlib logging, markdown helpers → corral.docgen (spec docs) or removed.
  • Hard-coded references to gmnspy/spec/*.schema.json paths replaced with netstead.load_gmns_spec(version=...) or netstead.get_spec_path(version=...).

docs.title: Where to ask
docs.text:
• Issues: https://github.com/e-lo/netstead/issues
  • Discussions: https://github.com/e-lo/netstead/discussions
  • v1.0 tracking issue: https://github.com/e-lo/netstead/issues/97

If you hit a v0.3 pattern not covered above, please open an issue with the snippet — we want this guide to cover the long tail.

docs.title: netstead API reference
docs.text:
GMNS-specific surface. For the generic Frictionless data-package primitives (Package, Table, validation, editing framework, HTTP + MCP factories) see the corral API reference.

Auto-generated from package docstrings via mkdocstrings. Stable anchors match the codes in ai/api-index.json. This page covers the core surface — Network, spec, semantics, scope, quality, indexes, graph, clean — plus the builders, selection, map, settings and Workbench entry points; smaller helpers are documented in their modules’ docstrings.

docs.title: netstead.Network(spec_version=None) dataclass
docs.text:
Bases: Package

GMNS-aware :class:~corral.dataset.Package.

Subclass of :class:~corral.dataset.Package that defaults to the bundled GMNS spec (see :mod:netstead.spec) and exposes named accessors for the canonical GMNS resources (link, node, segment, lane, geometry, link_tod, signal_controller, …). Validation reports produced by :meth:validate carry the active :attr:spec_version so saved JSON / HTML reports are self-describing.

Attributes:

Name Type Description spec_version str | None

GMNS spec version this network was loaded against — one of :data:netstead.spec.SUPPORTED_SPECS. Populated by :meth:from_source; defaults to "" when the dataclass is constructed directly (the structural check still works, but :meth:validate’s stamp will be empty until the caller sets it).

Examples:

Load the bundled Leavenworth fixture, hit the named accessors, and run validation::

>>> from netstead import Network
>>> from netstead.fixtures import leavenworth
>>> from corral.engines.ibis_engine import IbisEngine
>>> net = Network.from_source(leavenworth.csv_dir(), engine=IbisEngine())
>>> net.links.name
'link'
>>> net.nodes.name
'node'
>>> net.segments is None  # Leavenworth has no segment table
True
>>> report = net.validate()
>>> report.spec_version == net.spec_version
True

docs.title: links property
docs.text:
The link table (required by GMNS).

Raises:

Type Description NetworkError

If the link resource is absent from the loaded package.

Examples:

>>> from netstead import Network
>>> from netstead.fixtures import leavenworth
>>> from corral.engines.ibis_engine import IbisEngine
>>> Network.from_source(leavenworth.csv_dir(), engine=IbisEngine()).links.name
'link'

docs.text:
The node table (required by GMNS).

Raises:

Type Description NetworkError

If the node resource is absent from the loaded package.

docs.title: geometry property
docs.text: The geometry table or None when absent.

docs.text: The lane table or None when absent.

docs.title: from_source(source, *, engine=None, spec_version=None, tables=None, credentials=None) classmethod
docs.text:
Load a GMNS network from source, defaulting the spec to gmns@spec_version.

Resolves spec_version (caller-provided or :data:netstead.spec.DEFAULT_SPEC), validates it against :data:netstead.spec.SUPPORTED_SPECS, loads the matching vendored spec via :func:netstead.spec.load_gmns_spec, then delegates to :meth:Package.from_source for the actual I/O. The returned :class:Network carries the resolved version on :attr:spec_version.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default source str | Path

Path / URL / directory pointing at the GMNS package — anything :meth:Package.from_source accepts.

required engine Engine | None

Engine to materialize through. Defaults to the corral default (typically :class:~corral.engines.ibis_engine.IbisEngine).

None spec_version str | None

GMNS spec version to validate against. Defaults to :data:netstead.spec.DEFAULT_SPEC. Must be a member of :data:netstead.spec.SUPPORTED_SPECS.

None tables Iterable[str] | None

Optional subset of resource names to load. Useful for memory-efficient partial loads (e.g. ["link", "node"]).

None credentials dict[str, str] | None

Optional explicit credentials for a URL source (fsspec storage options, e.g. {"key": ..., "secret": ...} for S3). Forwarded to :meth:Package.from_source; ignored for local paths.

None

Returns:

Type Description Network

A populated :class:Network with lazy

Network Network

Raises:

Type Description InvalidSpecVersionError

If spec_version is not in :data:netstead.spec.SUPPORTED_SPECS (subclass of :class:~corral.spec.errors.SpecLoadError).

Examples:

>>> from netstead import Network
>>> from netstead.fixtures import leavenworth
>>> from corral.engines.ibis_engine import IbisEngine
>>> net = Network.from_source(leavenworth.csv_dir(), engine=IbisEngine())
>>> "link" in net
True
>>> net.spec_version
'0.97'

docs.title: validate(**kwargs)
docs.text:
Run the inherited :meth:Package.validate and stamp :attr:spec_version on the report.

Pure composition — the orchestration (structural / schema / FK / sync-state passes) lives in :class:~corral.dataset.Package and is not duplicated here. The override exists solely so the returned :class:~corral.reports.ValidationReport advertises which GMNS spec version the data was checked against (renderers and saved JSON / HTML reports surface this in the header).

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default **kwargs Any

Forwarded verbatim to :meth:Package.validate.

{}

Returns:

Name Type Description A ValidationReport ValidationReport

Examples:

>>> from netstead import Network
>>> from netstead.fixtures import leavenworth
>>> from corral.engines.ibis_engine import IbisEngine
>>> net = Network.from_source(leavenworth.csv_dir(), engine=IbisEngine())
>>> report = net.validate(foreign_keys=False, sync_state=False)
>>> report.spec_version == net.spec_version
True

docs.title: netstead.NetworkError
docs.text:
Bases: PackageError

A GMNS-required resource is missing or violates GMNS semantics.

Specialises :class:~corral.dataset.PackageError so generic package-error handlers still catch it, while GMNS-aware callers can branch on the more specific type. Raised today by :attr:Network.links / :attr:Network.nodes when the underlying resource is absent from the loaded package; task 3.8 will reuse it for GMNS-semantics violations (broken connectivity, missing TOD references, …).

docs.title: netstead.semantics.is_connected(net)
docs.text:
Return True iff the network has exactly one weakly-connected component.

“Weakly connected” means we ignore link direction — a one-way pair of streets between two nodes counts as connected.

Examples:

>>> from netstead import Network
>>> from netstead.fixtures import leavenworth
>>> from corral.engines.ibis_engine import IbisEngine
>>> net = Network.from_source(leavenworth.csv_dir(), engine=IbisEngine())
>>> is_connected(net)
True

docs.title: netstead.semantics.connected_components(net)
docs.text:
Return the network’s weakly-connected components, largest first.

Each component is a set of node_ids. Sorted by len descending so connected_components(net)[0] is always the largest. Empty networks return [].

Examples:

>>> from netstead import Network
>>> from netstead.fixtures import leavenworth
>>> from corral.engines.ibis_engine import IbisEngine
>>> net = Network.from_source(leavenworth.csv_dir(), engine=IbisEngine())
>>> comps = connected_components(net)
>>> len(comps) >= 1
True
>>> all(len(comps[i]) >= len(comps[i + 1]) for i in range(len(comps) - 1))
True

docs.title: netstead.semantics.assemble_link_geometry(net)
docs.text:
Return (link_id, geometry, source) for every link in net.

geometry is WKB bytes (the canonical in-memory encoding; geometry ADR) or null. Resolution order per link row:

  1. Inline link.geometry (non-null) — source = "inline".
  2. link.geometry_id resolving in net.geometry — source = "geometry_table".
  3. Straight segment from from_node_id / to_node_id node coords, encoded as a WKB LINESTRING — source = "node_endpoints".
  4. None of the above (geometry column absent + geometry_id absent + endpoint nodes missing coords) — geometry = None, source = "missing".

Inline/table cells are pass-through when already WKB; a legacy WKT string is re-encoded, so the function is correct whether or not the network’s geometry was canonicalised on load.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default net Network

A loaded :class:netstead.Network.

required

Returns:

Name Type Description A Table Table

the link table’s id type), geometry (WKB bytes or null),

Table

and source (string from :class:GeometrySource).

Examples:

>>> from netstead import Network
>>> from netstead.fixtures import leavenworth
>>> from corral.engines.ibis_engine import IbisEngine
>>> from netstead.semantics import assemble_link_geometry
>>> net = Network.from_source(leavenworth.csv_dir(), engine=IbisEngine())
>>> tbl = assemble_link_geometry(net)
>>> set(tbl.column_names) == {"link_id", "geometry", "source"}
True
>>> # Leavenworth carries geometry via geometry_id, so all rows
>>> # should resolve through the geometry table.
>>> set(tbl.column("source").to_pylist()) <= {"inline", "geometry_table", "node_endpoints", "missing"}
True

docs.title: netstead.scope.NetworkScope(node_ids, link_ids, network, provenance='') dataclass
docs.text:
An immutable subset of a :class:Network’s links + nodes.

Built by the module-level constructors (:func:from_nodes, :func:from_node, :func:from_link, :func:from_point, :func:connected_component, :func:from_zone) and composed via :meth:union / :meth:intersect / :meth:subtract / :meth:buffer_network / :meth:buffer_spatial. :meth:apply materializes the scope as a fresh :class:Network with all FK-related tables pre-filtered.

Attributes:

Name Type Description node_ids frozenset[int]

frozenset of node ids in the scope.

link_ids frozenset[int]

frozenset of link ids in the scope.

network Network

the source :class:Network (used by composition ops to access the cached indexes; not re-validated on the return path of :meth:apply).

provenance str

short human-readable trail of how this scope was built (e.g. "from_nodes([1,2,3], path_between=True)"). Used in error messages and scope.repr.

Examples:

>>> import pytest
>>> _ = pytest.importorskip("scipy")
>>> from netstead import Network
>>> from netstead.fixtures import leavenworth
>>> from corral.engines.ibis_engine import IbisEngine
>>> from netstead.scope import from_nodes
>>> net = Network.from_source(leavenworth.csv_dir(), engine=IbisEngine())
>>> scope = from_nodes(net, [1, 2], path_between=True)
>>> isinstance(scope, NetworkScope)
True
>>> sub = scope.apply()
>>> sub.links.count() <= net.links.count()
True

docs.title: apply()
docs.text:
Return a new :class:Network whose tables are filtered to the scope.

Pushdown rules:

  • link -> rows where link_id is in :attr:link_ids.
  • node -> rows where node_id is in :attr:node_ids.
  • geometry -> rows whose geometry_id is referenced by any surviving link.
  • Other tables in :data:_FK_PUSHDOWN -> rows where any of their FK columns match the scope’s id sets.
  • Tables outside :data:_FK_PUSHDOWN (e.g. time_set_definitions, use_definition) pass through unfiltered — they are dimension tables, not network-keyed.

docs.text: Return the union of two scopes (same network).

docs.title: intersect(other)
docs.text: Return the intersection of two scopes (same network).

docs.title: subtract(other)
docs.text: Return the set-difference (self minus other) of two scopes (same network).

docs.title: buffer_network(distance)
docs.text:
Extend the scope by all nodes within distance network-distance of any current node.

Adds the induced links (any link whose endpoints are both in the expanded node set) so the result remains a proper subgraph.

docs.title: buffer_spatial(distance_m)
docs.text:
Extend the scope by all links within distance_m of any current link’s geometry.

Implementation note: builds a shapely union of the current scope’s link geometries, then queries the SpatialIndex with distance_m as a buffer. Endpoint nodes of any newly added links are folded in too.

docs.title: netstead.scope.from_nodes(net, node_ids, *, path_between=True)
docs.text:
Scope built from a set of seed nodes.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default net Network

The source :class:Network.

required node_ids Iterable[int]

Seed node ids. Unknown ids are silently dropped (the scope just gets smaller) so callers can pass loose lists without pre-validating.

required path_between bool

If True (default), expand the scope to include nodes + links on the shortest path between every pair of seeds (BFS-equivalent on uniformly weighted graphs; weighted by link.length on GMNS networks). If False, the scope is just the seed nodes plus the links directly incident on them.

docs.title: Quality (GMNS rule pack)
docs.text: The rule classes:

docs.title: netstead.quality.register_all()
docs.text:
Construct + register every rule in this module.

Wired as the corral.quality.rules entry point for the netstead distribution (see packages/netstead/pyproject.toml). Also callable directly from tests / ad-hoc scripts: register_all() returns the list of registered rule instances.

docs.title: netstead.quality.HighSpeedResidentialRule
docs.text:
Flag residential links with implausibly high free_speed.

Threshold keys:

  • speed_limit_mph (default 35) — anything above is flagged.

Looks at link.facility_type (matched against residential / local case-insensitively, ignoring surrounding whitespace) and link.free_speed. Skips links with null facility type or null free_speed (those belong to the MissingCriticalFieldsRule).

The free_speed unit is whatever the spec’s long_distance_units field declares — GMNS defaults to mph, so the threshold key is named speed_limit_mph for clarity. If your network uses km/h, set speed_limit_mph to your km/h threshold; the comparison is unit-agnostic from the rule’s point of view.

docs.title: applies_to(package)
docs.text: We need both the link table AND its facility_type + free_speed columns.

docs.title: run(package, report, rc=None)
docs.text: Filter the link table in the engine; emit one issue per offending row.

docs.title: netstead.quality.DisconnectedComponentsRule
docs.text:
Flag networks with more than one weakly-connected component.

Threshold keys: none (the presence of any extra component is the quality concern).

Emits a single Severity.INFO issue (not per-component) listing the component count + sizes. connected_components is delegated to :mod:netstead.semantics.connectivity so the same GMNSGraph (scipy) build is shared with any other connectivity caller in the session. No table is materialized here: the graph index reads only the columns it needs.

docs.title: applies_to(package)
docs.text:
We need link + node tables AND the columns GMNSGraph.build needs.

Skips silently on non-Network packages (no GMNS accessors) and on networks missing length on the link table — the upstream :class:~netstead.graph.GMNSGraph (built with cost="length") needs it and we’d rather no-op than blow up.

docs.title: run(package, report, rc=None)
docs.text: Build (or reuse) the GMNSGraph, count components.

docs.title: netstead.quality.LaneCountMismatchRule
docs.text:
Flag links where link.lanes disagrees with the lane table row count.

Threshold keys: none — any non-zero mismatch is flagged.

Skips links where either link.lanes is null OR the lane table has zero rows for that link (those cases are “underspecified”, not “wrong” — caught by :class:MissingCriticalFieldsRule). A fractional link.lanes is compared by its whole part.

docs.title: applies_to(package)
docs.text: Needs both the link table AND a lane table.

docs.title: run(package, report, rc=None)
docs.text: Count lane rows per link in the engine, join to link.lanes, emit the mismatches.

docs.title: netstead.quality.DuplicateNearNodesRule
docs.text:
Flag pairs of nodes within epsilon_units of each other.

Threshold keys:

  • epsilon_units (default 1e-5) — distance threshold in the node coordinate CRS units. The default is deliberately tiny so it means “effectively duplicate” in any CRS: ~1m for WGS84 at mid-latitudes; a hair’s breadth for projected coords. Tune it for your CRS. For projected networks (UTM, state plane) where coordinates are meters, 5.0 is a reasonable “near-duplicate” threshold. For WGS84 degrees, 0.0001 is roughly 10m. 0 flags only exact duplicates; a negative value raises :class:ValueError.

Implementation: a grid self-join in the engine. Each node is hashed to an epsilon-sized grid cell and joined against the nodes of the 3x3 block of cells around it, so the work grows with the number of nodes, not its square; only the pairs within epsilon reach Python.

docs.title: applies_to(package)
docs.text: Needs a node table with node_id + x_coord + y_coord columns.

docs.title: run(package, report, rc=None)
docs.text: Self-join node points on grid cells; flag every pair within epsilon.

docs.title: netstead.quality.SharpAngleBendsRule
docs.text:
Flag links whose geometry contains an interior turn angle below threshold.

Threshold keys:

  • min_angle_degrees (default 30.0) — any interior vertex with a turn angle below this is flagged.

Skips links without inline geometry (the geometry-table case is handled by :func:netstead.semantics.assemble_link_geometry callers who run this rule after assembly).

Requires shapely (clean extra). Angles need parsed geometries, which the engine can’t give us, so this rule materializes values: only the link_id and geometry of links with a non-null geometry. It finds candidates with vectorised shapely + numpy, then measures each candidate’s sharpest angle exactly as reported.

docs.title: applies_to(package)
docs.text: Needs a link table with an inline geometry column.

docs.title: run(package, report, rc=None)
docs.text: Parse link geometries (WKT or WKB), compute interior turn angles, flag sharp ones.

docs.title: netstead.quality.ImplausibleVcRule
docs.text:
Flag links with volume / capacity > threshold.

Threshold keys:

  • vc_max (default 1.5) — anything above is flagged.
  • volume_column (default "volume") — column name to read for volume. The base spec doesn’t define one; loaded networks often add it as an extension. The rule skips silently if the column is absent.

Skips rows where either capacity is null or zero (would be a divide-by-zero) — those should surface via the schema validator, not here.

docs.title: applies_to(package)
docs.text: Needs a link table with a capacity column (volume column is configurable).

docs.title: run(package, report, rc=None)
docs.text: Filter volume / capacity above vc_max in the engine; emit one issue per row.

docs.title: netstead.quality.MissingCriticalFieldsRule
docs.text:
Flag tables where a “should have” but spec-optional column is mostly null.

Threshold keys:

  • coverage_min (default 0.90) — minimum fraction of non-null rows required to NOT flag the column.

Emits one Severity.INFO issue per affected (table, column) pair, in column-name order. Targets the columns the GMNS community treats as effectively required even when the spec marks them optional — link.length, link.free_speed, link.capacity, link.lanes. The non-null counts are one aggregate query; NaN counts as null.

docs.title: applies_to(package)
docs.text: Needs a link table (we check the critical columns inside :meth:run).

docs.title: run(package, report, rc=None)
docs.text: For each critical column present, emit an Info issue if non-null coverage < threshold.

docs.title: netstead.quality.NonUniqueCombinationRule
docs.text:
Flag rows that repeat a combination of columns that should be unique.

GMNS 0.97 gives the time-of-day tables a surrogate primary key (link_tod_id, …), so two link_tod rows for the same link_id and time_day pass spec validation although they contradict each other. This rule groups each table by its natural key in the engine and reports every combination that occurs more than once.

Threshold keys:

  • combinations (default :data:DEFAULT_UNIQUE_COMBINATIONS) — a mapping of table name to a list of column combinations, each a list of column names. Setting it replaces the defaults, so include every combination you still want checked. A default combination whose table or columns are absent is skipped silently; a configured one is logged (a WARNING on the netstead.quality.rules logger), since it is probably a typo. It is not an issue, so severity_override never escalates it. A value that isn’t a mapping of table name to a list of column lists raises :class:ValueError (settings reject it when they load).

Rows with a null in any of the combination’s columns are skipped (a missing value is the schema validator’s concern, not a duplicate). Emits one issue per repeated combination: row is its first row, and extra carries columns, values (column → value), rows (the first 20 row positions) and count. Exact matches only: two time_day windows that overlap without being equal are not flagged.

(The code and threshold avoid the word “key”: the Workbench refuses setting names ending in key, which it reserves for credentials.)

docs.title: applies_to(package)
docs.text: Any package with tables: run resolves the configured combinations against what is present.

docs.title: run(package, report, rc=None)
docs.text: Group each configured table by each key combination; emit one issue per repeated combination.

docs.title: netstead.quality.OverlappingLinksRule
docs.text:
Flag pairs of links whose shapes run along each other for part of their length.

Threshold keys:

  • min_overlap_units (default 0.0) — a pair is flagged when the length they share is greater than this, in the geometry’s CRS units (degrees for WGS84; raise it to ignore digitising noise).

A shared stretch is a 1-D intersection: links that only touch at a node or cross each other are not flagged. Pairs with identical shapes are skipped too, since that is how GMNS encodes the two directions of a two-way street; a link lying along part of a longer one is flagged. Emits one issue per pair, on the first link’s row, with extra link_ids, rows and overlap_length.

Exact matching only. The test is GEOS’s exact DE-9IM relation with no snapping tolerance: only segments the two shapes share exactly are caught. Two digitisations of the same road a centimetre apart, or with vertices that don’t line up on a common segment, are not flagged. min_overlap_units filters short exact overlaps; it does not widen the match.

Shapes come from inline link.geometry when set, else from the geometry table through link.geometry_id (the first row of a repeated geometry_id); links with neither are skipped. Requires shapely (clean extra). The engine selects just the link ids and shapes; candidate pairs come from an STRtree bounding-box query, are cut down in numpy, and only the survivors get the exact DE-9IM test (about 0.2 s on a 100k-link grid). The cost grows with how many bounding boxes overlap with real area, so it can get slow on long or diagonal links whose boxes cover much of the network (long rural links in WGS84, say).

docs.title: applies_to(package)
docs.text: Needs shapely and a link shape source: inline geometry or geometry_id + a geometry table.

docs.title: run(package, report, rc=None)
docs.text: Index link shapes in an STRtree; emit one issue per pair sharing more than min_overlap_units.

docs.title: netstead.indexes.SpatialIndex(link_ids, geometries)

Wrap the assembled CSR + node/edge mappings.

docs.text:
